faqs.question: What is the first thing a Corniche household with two exam-year children should do?
faqs.answer: Collect both schools' calendars in September. For the Diploma student that means the internal assessment dates for all six subjects, the Extended Essay supervision schedule and the Theory of Knowledge deadlines. For the IGCSE candidate it means the awarding body, the syllabus codes, the entry tier, the paper numbers and the centre's administrative zone. Both schools will supply these if asked in writing, and together they are what makes a twelve-month plan possible instead of a sequence of reactions.

faqs.question: Where do the IB and IGCSE calendars actually collide?
faqs.answer: In three places. The autumn of the Diploma's final year, when coursework in six subjects falls due alongside university applications and a Year 11 sibling's mocks. Results, which arrive in August for the IGCSE summer series and in January for the autumn one, each demanding a decision within a fortnight. And the spring, when the Diploma exam window and IGCSE revision overlap so neither child can be the priority. All three are knowable a year ahead.

faqs.question: How should a two-child household handle Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Stack two late sessions after Iftar rather than suspending the month. School hours shorten and the useful study window moves late, which is actually easier online than at any other point in the year because nobody is driving to a tower at nine in the evening. Decide it before the month begins. The failure mode is a month quietly dropped and then resumed in a rush, with a coursework deadline four weeks closer than the plan assumed.

faqs.question: Does Ramadan fall in the same part of the school year each time?
faqs.answer: No, and this is why a plan cannot simply be reused. Ramadan shifts roughly eleven days earlier against the Gregorian calendar each year, so its position inside the academic year moves: in some years it lands in a relatively quiet term and in others it sits immediately before an exam window. A twelve-month plan written once and repeated unchanged will eventually place its heaviest weeks inside the month with the least available capacity.

faqs.question: Both children have a deadline in the same week. What do we do?
faqs.answer: Decide the priority before the week arrives rather than inside it. Counted coursework outranks a diagnostic mock, because one has permanent consequences and the other produces information. Then protect the lower-priority child's slot in reduced form, as a twenty-minute check-in rather than a cancellation, so they do not learn that their work is the thing that gets dropped. And settle the two quiet rooms in advance, because a Corniche flat cannot improvise them.

faqs.question: What is the summer actually for in a two-board household?
faqs.answer: It is the only block nobody has already claimed, and three jobs suit it. The transition from Extended or Higher tier into a Diploma Higher Level course, which is a predictable subject-specific gap. Settling an internal assessment topic and method so the autumn cluster starts with a viable question. And closing a content gap the mocks exposed, which is the only time of year a student can learn new material without revising old material at the same time.

faqs.question: How long should a summer block be?
faqs.answer: Three or four weeks with two sessions a week, aimed at one named target, with a written handover at the end. What does not work is running a full programme through July and August: a student who studies all summer arrives in September already tired, and that costs more than the original gap would have. The discipline is to define the target before the block starts and to stop when it is met rather than when term begins.

faqs.question: When are predicted grades decided, and can tuition change them?
faqs.answer: They are issued in the autumn of the Diploma's final year and they reflect work already done, which means tuition bought after they are issued cannot change them. The window in which predictions are actually earned is the first Diploma year and the spring following it. That is a year earlier than most families realise, and it is the strongest argument for light, early, well-targeted work rather than a heavy intervention in the term the applications are written.

faqs.question: Why does the university application season make coursework harder?
faqs.answer: Because it consumes the same resource. Applications are written in the autumn of the final year, in the same weeks as the coursework cluster, and both need sustained independent writing from the student plus administrative attention from a parent. Destinations have different rhythms too: a UK centralised autumn cycle, separate UAE admission timelines with their own tests, and North American rounds with standardised tests booked months ahead. A household applying in two directions is managing two of those at once.

faqs.question: Can two children on the Corniche have sessions at the same time?
faqs.answer: Technically yes, and physically it is the harder half of the question. Two simultaneous video lessons need two quiet spaces, which in a seafront flat usually means one child in a bedroom and one at the dining table with the rest of the household elsewhere for forty-five minutes. Many families find consecutive slots easier than simultaneous ones: 4:15pm and 5:30pm concentrates the disruption into one evening and needs only one quiet room at a time.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying for a tutor nearby if we can get one online?
faqs.answer: For the IGCSE side there is a genuine local pool around the Corniche and either route can work, so choose on tier and mark-scheme familiarity. For Diploma Higher Level sciences and Economics the local pool in Ajman is close to empty, and some of the best-placed local teachers are barred from tutoring students at their own school in any case. Planning on online delivery for the Diploma side and either for the IGCSE side saves a term of fruitless searching.

faqs.question: What should we ask a tutor who claims to cover both systems?
faqs.answer: Four questions per system, then a fifth for the Diploma. Which syllabus code did you last teach and when; which papers did your students sit; which topics did that cohort lose marks on; and do you hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit. Then: have you supervised an internal assessment through to submission, and what did you not do for the student. The last question is the most revealing one available, and a clear answer to it matters more than a confident answer to the others.

faqs.question: How does the permit work, and should we check it more than once?
faqs.answer: The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years, with MoHRE's own service page listing no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Because the validity is two years rather than indefinite, it is a reasonable thing to ask about again on a long engagement. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published.

faqs.question: Why are there no IB dates on this page when the IGCSE ones are specific?
faqs.answer: Because the sourcing is different. Cambridge and Pearson publish exam-administration pages that could be read and dated, so their positions appear here with the month they were read and with past dates keeping their year. The IB's own site returns an error to automated checking, so no IB exam or results date in this project has been verified from the board itself. Publishing an unverified date that a household plans a year around would be worse than publishing none at all.

faqs.question: Can tuition help with university applications as well as subjects?
faqs.answer: That is a different service and it should be described as one. Tutors here teach subjects: content, papers, criteria and feedback on the student's own work. Nothing on this page is a claim to manage admissions, write or edit a personal statement, or influence an outcome at any institution, and no provider can promise a place. Where a family needs application support, look for somebody who does that work explicitly rather than treating it as an extra from a subject tutor.

intro.heading: The search is about proximity; the problem is almost always about dates
paragraphs: A parent in Al Helio searching for a tutor nearby is rarely asking a geography question. They are asking a timing question in geographic words, because a mock result has landed, a coursework deadline has moved, or someone at the school gates mentioned that entries close soon. The useful reply is not a list of tutors within ten kilometres. It is a calendar, read backwards from the paper your child is actually sitting, with an honest line about what each remaining block of weeks can do.

So that is how this page is built. The anchor dates are the ones published by the boards. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in three windows through the year. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE sits in May/June and in November. Those two series, and the entry deadlines months ahead of them, are the fixed points. Everything a tutor does has to fit between them.

Two of those dates are worth writing down because they are already history and therefore checkable. Pearson's June 2026 International GCSE results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026. Its November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. That second one is the fact most families miss: a November entry does not produce a grade in time for a January application deadline. It produces a grade in January, which is a different thing entirely.

On the IB side the position is more cautious and this page will say so plainly rather than inventing certainty. The Diploma session UAE schools sit is the May session, with November available. We are not publishing a specific IB examination or results date here, because the IB's own site blocks automated checking and an unverified date on a page a parent plans around is worse than no date. Your child's IB coordinator holds the real internal calendar, which matters more anyway: the internal deadlines for the Internal Assessments, the Extended Essay drafts and the Theory of Knowledge essay are set by the school, not by the IB.

What follows, then, is a working calendar rather than a brochure. It covers the IGCSE year counted backwards, the Diploma year counted backwards, what eight weeks can and cannot fix, how a two-board household avoids a collision between an IGCSE mock week and an IA deadline, and when a November resit is the right call rather than a consolation. IB Gram teaches Al Helio students one-to-one online; we do not send a tutor to a UAE address, which is why a session can be in the diary for Tuesday rather than for whenever someone is free to drive out to Ajman.

ajman/ib-igcse-tutor-near-me-in-al-helio.programmesIntro: An Al Helio household can easily be running a Year 11 IGCSE candidate and a Diploma student at the same time, on two calendars that collide in predictable places. These are the four programmes that matter and the date pressure each one carries.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessed internally against criteria A to D in most subjects, with published descriptors rather than percentage marks. The date pressure here is continuous rather than terminal: unit assessments, the Personal Project in the final year, and interdisciplinary tasks spread across the year. Students who have only ever been assessed by criteria often struggle with their first timed external paper, which is why the MYP-to-DP and MYP-to-IGCSE transitions both need planning a term ahead.
programmes.countryNote: Ajman has fewer IB settings than Dubai, so some Al Helio families run MYP at one school and move a sibling to an IGCSE school, or commute into Sharjah for Diploma years. Where that happens, the two calendars are set by two schools with no coordination between them, and the clash usually lands in the spring term.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. The Extended Essay runs to a 4,000-word limit. Almost every component has an internal school deadline well before the external session, and the Internal Assessments are where a Diploma is quietly won or lost: they are marked against named criteria with published mark allocations, and they are completed under time pressure that nobody warns about in Year 12.
programmes.countryNote: UAE schools sit the May session, with November available. We publish no specific IB date here; the coordinator at your child's school holds the internal deadline sheet, and that sheet is the one a tutoring plan should be built around. Ask for it in September rather than in February.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Two or three written papers per subject in most cases, with June and November series for international centres. The entry decision, including Core or Extended tier, is made by the school months before the papers and is the single most consequential date in the two-year course. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative timetable zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone.
programmes.countryNote: Confirm your Al Helio school's timetable zone before planning revision from any downloaded timetable. Cambridge says it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after working from the wrong zone's version, and a tutor peaking a student a week late is a real and avoidable failure.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: May/June and November sittings, codes such as 4MA1, 4PH1, 4CH1 and 4BI1, with a modular pattern available on some courses so units can be banked across sittings. That modular option is a genuine planning tool: a student who is strong on one unit and weak on another can sequence them rather than meeting both in one week. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and then a final version.
programmes.countryNote: Work from the live official timetable on Pearson's site rather than a restated date, because provisional timetables are revised. The published history is the useful planning guide: the November 2026 final timetable ran to 19 November 2026, and the June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026.

ajman/ib-igcse-tutor-near-me-in-al-helio.subjectsIntro: Subject by subject, the calendar bites in different places. These are the courses Al Helio families most often ask about, each with the deadline or component that tends to catch a student out.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches (IB)
subjects.description: The Exploration is the dated component: a piece of the student's own mathematics with an internal school deadline usually in the second year. Students underestimate how long a viable topic takes to find, then write up in a fortnight. The written papers reward fluency rather than cleverness, so the revision block needs to start earlier than feels necessary.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation (IB)
subjects.description: Technology-heavy, statistics-heavy, and a better fit for many students than AA, but the route decision has to be made in Year 11 because some university courses specify AA. Ask the target universities before the option form goes in, not after. The Exploration carries the same internal deadline pressure as in AA.

subjects.name: Chemistry (IB)
subjects.description: The Internal Assessment takes longer than students plan for because the data collection has to work before the analysis can start. Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms are the recurring content weaknesses. An eight-week block before a session can rebuild calculation technique; it cannot rescue an IA that has not been started.

subjects.name: Physics (IB)
subjects.description: Fields, circular motion and the HL-only topics are where the grade separates, and the data-analysis skills in the IA transfer directly to the papers. Students who can describe an experiment but not quantify uncertainty lose marks in both places, which makes uncertainty work unusually good value in a short block.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.description: No coursework, so the whole grade sits on timed papers and the entry tier. That makes the mock result genuinely diagnostic: a Core-entered student scoring at the top of the range and an Extended-entered student scoring in the middle need completely different work in the remaining weeks.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Edexcel 4PH1)
subjects.description: Electricity and electromagnetism dominate the lost marks, and the alternative-to-practical paper is the most improvable component in the subject because it tests method writing rather than knowledge. Six focused sessions on method description and unit discipline move a grade more reliably than general revision.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Edexcel 4CH1)
subjects.description: Mole arithmetic and ionic equations are the separators; qualitative analysis is the cheapest set of marks on the paper and the first thing to secure when time is short. Organic chemistry is best left until the calculation work is reliable, because it rewards pattern recognition that builds on it.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Edexcel 4BI1)
subjects.description: A volume problem, not a difficulty problem, which makes it the subject most responsive to a structured eight-week schedule. Terminology precision is what the mark scheme pays for, so the productive drill is writing answers to the scheme's wording rather than rereading notes.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature (IB)
subjects.description: The Individual Oral has a school-set recording window, the HL Essay has an internal draft deadline, and both arrive while science IAs are being written. Of all the Diploma components this is the one most often left until the collision is unavoidable, so it belongs early in any calendar plan.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Studies (IB and IGCSE)
subjects.description: IB Economics carries internal commentary deadlines spread through the course; IGCSE Economics 0455 and Business Studies 0450 are terminal. Diagram accuracy decides the analysis marks in both, and an evaluation paragraph that actually weighs rather than restates is the most teachable single skill here.

ajman/ib-igcse-tutor-near-me-in-al-helio.regionsIntro: The neighbourhoods around Al Helio share an evening rhythm set by the Sharjah and Dubai commute, and that rhythm is what decides which session slots are realistic for a family keeping to a revision schedule.

regions.name: Al Nuaimiya
regions.note: Short hop to the Sharjah border, so parents are often home earlier and weekday sessions can start before 5pm. Useful during a mock fortnight, when an early start leaves the evening free for the actual past paper.

regions.name: Al Mowaihat
regions.note: Villa areas where students usually get home before 3pm. That makes a mid-afternoon slot workable, which matters in the final eight weeks when a 7pm session competes with fatigue rather than with traffic.

regions.name: Al Rawda
regions.note: Spread-out residential streets with several school options in reach. Families here often juggle two children on different school calendars, so the practical request is two short sessions on the same evening rather than one long one.

regions.name: Al Rashidiya, Ajman
regions.note: Closer to the older commercial centre and the Corniche, with slow through-traffic from mid-afternoon. A fixed weekly slot survives here only if it does not depend on anyone driving anywhere.

regions.name: Emirates City
regions.note: Towers on the Emirates Road side, heavily populated by Dubai commuters. The usable window is late, which during a revision block means protecting the 8pm session from becoming the 9.30pm session.

regions.note: One institutional and industrial, the other low-density and coastal, but with the same effect on scheduling: long approach drives and small school-age populations, so group revision classes rarely assemble at the right tier.

regions.name: Al Yasmeen
regions.note: Newer housing with young families and a growing Year 7 to Year 9 population. The calendar question here is mostly about the Checkpoint and tier-decision year rather than about an exam series.

schoolClusters.city: Ajman schools on the Al Helio run
schoolClusters.note: British, Indian and IB settings within reach of Al Helio, Al Nuaimiya and Al Mowaihat. Internal assessment calendars differ sharply between them, so the mock window one family is living through may be three weeks away for their neighbour.

schoolClusters.city: Sharjah and the Diploma commute
schoolClusters.note: Families needing a Diploma Programme place often look south, where the Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education and approves curricula, programmes and assessment methods. A cross-border school day compresses the evening study window considerably.

ajman/ib-igcse-tutor-near-me-in-al-helio.modesIntro: Pick the format by how many weeks are left, because that is the only variable that genuinely changes what is possible. The three below map onto a term, a run-in and a crisis.

modes.title: Full-term weekly, running slightly ahead of class
modes.description: One or two sessions a week from the start of a term, deliberately covering material shortly before the school teaches it. The student then meets each topic twice, which turns class time into consolidation. This is the only format that reliably moves more than one grade, and it needs a term or more to work.

modes.title: Eight-week run-in to a series
modes.description: Two or three sessions a week, built entirely from timed past-paper sections marked against the published scheme. No new content unless a gap blocks a paper. The output each week is a ranked list of what is costing the most marks and a plan for the next session. Suits a student whose knowledge is broadly there but whose marks are not.

modes.title: Deadline triage, two to four sessions
modes.description: For the week a coursework deadline or a mock result lands badly. The work is scoping and sequencing: what has to be done, in what order, and what can be dropped without consequence. For an IB student this means working on their own draft and their own data, never producing it for them.

sections.heading: What "near me" means once the exam date is fixed
paragraphs: Proximity buys one thing: the ability to start soon. That is not a trivial benefit when a deadline is six weeks out, and it explains why the search is phrased the way it is. But proximity in Ajman also narrows the pool sharply, and a tutor who can be at the door on Thursday is not necessarily a tutor who has taught the Higher Level paper your child is sitting.

Online delivery resolves the tension rather than splitting the difference. A live video session can be in the diary for tomorrow evening without anyone driving anywhere, which preserves the speed that made the search urgent, while the choice of tutor widens from whoever is in Ajman to whoever teaches that subject at that level. For Al Helio families this is the whole argument, and it is a scheduling argument rather than a technology one.

There is a second timing effect worth naming. In-home tutoring in Ajman is usually sold in two-hour blocks, because a two-hour visit justifies the drive. Two hours is a poor unit for exam preparation: the useful work is a 45-minute timed section followed by a marking discussion, which fits an hour. A plan built from weekly hours lands more sessions in the same month than a plan built from fortnightly double visits, and distribution matters more than total hours in the run-up to a paper.

So the honest answer to the search is this. IB Gram does not place a tutor at a UAE address and never has; this is online one-to-one teaching, on Gulf Standard Time. What you get instead of a car journey is a subject match and a start date, and in the weeks before a series those are the only two things that matter.

sections.heading: The IGCSE year counted backwards from the June papers
paragraphs: Read a school year forwards and the exams look far away. Read it backwards from the paper and the real deadlines appear, most of them months earlier than parents expect. The table below is the sequence in reverse order of urgency, built from what the boards publish and what UAE schools do internally. It is deliberately month-named rather than dated, because a timetable restated on a web page goes stale and the live official version does not.

The two dates worth holding onto are historical and therefore safe to quote. Pearson's June 2026 International GCSE results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026; its November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Those two numbers tell you everything about why a November entry is a resit route rather than a parallel option: the grade exists, but it exists in January.

The single most important line in the table is the entry deadline, because it is the last point at which tier can change. Once a Cambridge candidate is entered for Core in a tiered subject, the grade ceiling is fixed regardless of performance. Families who discover a child's potential in the spring term discover it too late to act in that series. A tutor cannot change this; a calendar read in the autumn can.

The mock window is the second anchor. A mock sat under real conditions and marked to the published scheme is the best diagnostic available, and it arrives with enough time to act on it. A mock treated as a formality produces a number and no information. If one thing on this page is worth acting on today, it is asking the school when the mocks fall and making sure the papers come home marked.

sections.heading: The Diploma year counted backwards, with the dates the school owns
paragraphs: A Diploma calendar has two layers and most of the pressure sits in the layer parents never see. The outer layer is the external session, which UAE schools sit in May with a November option. The inner layer is the school's own deadline sheet: first drafts and final versions of each Internal Assessment, the Extended Essay milestones, the Theory of Knowledge essay, the Individual Oral recording window, and the upload cut-offs that follow them. That inner layer is where a Diploma is actually lost.

This page publishes no specific IB examination or results date. The reason is simple and worth stating: the IB's own site cannot be checked automatically, and a precise date that turns out to be wrong is worse on a page a family plans around than no date at all. What we can say is structural, and the structure is what a plan needs. Ask the coordinator for the internal deadline sheet in the autumn term of the first Diploma year, and put it on a wall.

Counted backwards, the first Diploma year is where the leverage is. The Extended Essay topic and supervisor are settled there, the Internal Assessment subjects are chosen there, and a student who leaves that year with two IA data sets collected is in a completely different position from one who leaves it with none. The second year has no spare weeks: the IA write-ups, the Extended Essay final version, the TOK essay and the oral components all land in the same two terms as the final revision.

The tutoring implication is a sequencing one rather than a teaching one. Content support belongs in the first year and the first half of the second. Component support belongs to the point in the calendar where the component is live, and it must stay inside the academic-honesty boundary: a tutor asks questions about the student's plan, explains the criteria, and gives feedback on the student's own draft. Nobody at IB Gram writes, rewrites or completes an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay or a TOK essay, and any provider offering to is offering the student an expulsion risk.

sections.heading: Eight weeks out: what can be fixed and what cannot
paragraphs: Eight weeks is the most common starting point for a tutoring enquiry in Al Helio, and it is a genuinely useful amount of time if it is spent on the right things. It is enough to rebuild exam technique, to drill the three or four topics costing the most marks, to teach a student how to read a command term properly, and to convert a disorganised reviser into one with a schedule. It moves marks, sometimes substantially, because most lost marks in a mock are technique rather than ignorance.

It is not enough to learn a two-year syllabus. A student who has never met electromagnetic induction, moles or differentiation will not acquire all three in eight weeks alongside everything else. It is also not enough to rescue an unstarted Internal Assessment or Extended Essay, because those have their own non-negotiable deadlines and the data or reading cannot be compressed. Saying this clearly at the start of a plan is part of the job.

The productive eight-week shape is the same across boards. Week one is diagnosis from the student's own marked mock, producing a ranked list of lost marks by topic. Weeks two to six attack that list, one or two topics a week, each session ending with a timed section of a real paper. Week seven is full papers under conditions. Week eight tapers: no new material, light revision of the known weak spots, and sleep protected. The student should walk into the hall having already sat that paper several times.

What makes this work is marking to the published scheme rather than to a tutor's judgement. A student who learns that the scheme pays for a comparison, a unit, a labelled axis or a named process starts writing for the marker instead of writing what they know. That shift is the single largest gain available in a short block, and it is why the first thing we ask for is a marked paper rather than a list of topics.
bullets: Week 1: diagnose from marked work, rank lost marks by topic
Weeks 2-6: two topics a week, each closed with a timed section
Week 7: full papers under exam conditions, marked to the scheme
Week 8: taper, no new content, revisit the named weak spots only
Throughout: the student does the writing, the tutor does the feedback

sections.heading: Running two boards in one household without a collision
paragraphs: A fair number of Al Helio families have one child on an IB calendar and another on an IGCSE one, sometimes at two different schools in two different emirates. The two calendars are not coordinated and they collide in places that are entirely predictable once you look. Knowing where the collisions fall is most of the solution, because the fix is usually sequencing rather than more hours.

The first collision is the spring term. IGCSE mocks and Diploma Internal Assessment write-ups tend to occupy the same weeks, and both compete for the same parental attention and the same quiet room. The second is the run-in to the external sessions, when an IGCSE candidate needs timed papers in the evening and a Diploma student needs long uninterrupted blocks for revision. The third is the results gap: one child's grades arrive in August, the other's on a different schedule entirely, and the family plans twice.

The practical answers are unglamorous. Put both schools' deadline sheets on one wall calendar in September. Give the Diploma student the long weekend blocks and the IGCSE candidate the weekday evenings, because timed papers fit an evening and Extended Essay reading does not. Book tutoring for the IB components early in the first Diploma year, when there is slack, rather than in the second year when there is none. And resist the instinct to buy equal hours for both children; the one with a tiered entry decision pending has the more urgent deadline.

The table sets the two calendars side by side so the pressure points are visible. It uses months rather than dates, because the whole point of a planning table is that it stays true next year as well.

sections.heading: The mock result, and what to actually do with it
paragraphs: A mock is the most underused asset in the school year. Most families read the grade, feel something about it, and file the paper. The grade is the least informative part of the document. The information is in the distribution of lost marks: which topics, which question types, whether marks went missing at the start of long questions or at the end, whether the final pages were blank.

Three patterns show up again and again and each needs a different response. If marks are spread thinly across everything, the problem is usually fluency and the answer is volume of timed practice. If marks cluster in two or three topics, the answer is targeted teaching and the eight-week shape works well. If the last section is unfinished, the problem is pacing, and the fix is a stopwatch and a rule about when to abandon a question, not more content.

There is a fourth pattern that parents read as laziness and is usually something else: full marks on recall questions and nothing on the extended-response ones. That is a command-term problem. A student who treats describe, explain, compare and evaluate as synonyms will lose the same marks in every paper in every subject until someone shows them the difference, with the mark scheme open. It is a two-session fix and it is worth more than a term of content revision.

So the request we make of every Al Helio family at the start is the same: send the marked mock, not a description of it. Ten minutes with the actual paper produces a better plan than an hour of conversation about how the term has gone, and it costs nothing. Where no mock exists yet, a timed section of a past paper in the first session does the same job.

sections.heading: The November route, and when a resit is the right decision
paragraphs: Both boards offer a second window. Cambridge runs a November series alongside June for international centres; Pearson runs November alongside May/June. For a UAE candidate this is a real option rather than a technicality, and it is routinely misunderstood in both directions. Some families treat it as a free second attempt; others do not know it exists until after results.

The honest framing is that November is a resit route and a tier-correction route, not a parallel session. Its two constraints are timing and preparation. Pearson's November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, so a November grade is a January grade, which lands after many application deadlines. And the preparation window runs through the summer and the first autumn term, which is a thin stretch for a student who has just finished a difficult June.

Where November genuinely earns its place is in two cases. The first is a tier correction: a student capped by a Core entry who needs a higher grade for an AS Level course can sit Extended in November instead of carrying the ceiling forward. The second is a single-subject repair, where one grade out of nine has blocked a specific route and everything else is settled. In both, the work is narrow and the eight-week shape applies cleanly.

Where it does not earn its place is as a hedge. A student entered for June and planning on November tends to prepare for neither properly, and the summer disappears. Decide one way before the entry deadline, build the plan around that decision, and keep the November option as a response to a result rather than as part of the original strategy.

sections.heading: Term by term in an Ajman school year, Ramadan included
paragraphs: A revision plan that ignores the actual shape of the UAE school year fails in week three. Ajman's private schools sit under federal Ministry of Education oversight, and alongside the licensed international curriculum they teach the mandatory UAE subjects: Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies are the federal baseline that every private school works to. That means a Year 11 timetable already carries more subjects than the exam entries suggest, and the homework load is correspondingly higher than a British-school comparison implies.

Ramadan reshapes the day. School hours shorten, concentration moves either early or well into the evening, and a 5pm session that worked all year stops working. The practical answer is to move sessions after Iftar and to keep them shorter, because a 45-minute focused session after a meal beats a 90-minute one at the wrong time. Families who plan this in advance lose nothing; families who try to hold the old schedule lose three or four weeks.

The other recurring disruption is travel. Many Al Helio households travel during school breaks and sometimes during term, and an online plan survives that where an in-home one does not. A student on a live video schedule can keep a Tuesday session from anywhere with a connection, which matters most in the final term when continuity is worth more than intensity.

Put those three things together and the calendar for an Al Helio family looks like this: cover content in the autumn and winter terms when the timetable is stable, use the mock result to set a plan, shift to shorter post-Iftar sessions through Ramadan if it falls in the run-in, and protect the final fortnight as a taper rather than a sprint. None of that requires a tutor nearby. All of it requires a tutor who knows which paper your child is sitting.

process.title: Send the dates, not just the subject
process.description: The useful first message names the board, the subject code or level, and the date pressure: a mock result, an entry deadline, an IA deadline, a series. A tutoring plan is built backwards from a date, so the date is the most important thing in the enquiry.

process.title: Send the marked mock or one timed section
process.description: The paper tells us in minutes what a conversation takes an hour to approximate: whether the problem is content, technique, pacing or command terms. Where no mock exists, the first session includes a short timed section so the diagnosis comes from evidence rather than impression.

process.title: Free trial lesson, then a written plan
process.description: One 45 to 60-minute one-to-one lesson over live video, with no card details and no obligation. If it works, you get a written plan with a week-by-week shape and a finish line, built around your school's own deadline sheet rather than a generic term.

process.title: Hold the schedule through the disruptions
process.description: Ramadan, travel, assessment weeks and school events all land inside a revision block. We plan for them in advance: shorter post-Iftar sessions, a kept slot during a trip, and a deliberate taper rather than an accidental collapse in the final fortnight.

process.title: Review on marks, decide on the next window
process.description: Every few weeks, check whether past-paper scores in the named weak topics have moved. That review is also where the November question gets answered honestly, before the entry deadline rather than after results arrive in January.

whyPoints.title: Planning from published dates, not from guesses

Where a date is not verifiable, we say so rather than inventing it.

whyPoints.description: We publish no specific IB examination or results date, because the IB's own site cannot be checked automatically and a wrong date on a planning page is a real harm. We work from your school's internal deadline sheet, which is the document that actually governs an IB year.

whyPoints.title: A start date that does not depend on traffic
whyPoints.description: The reason the search says nearby is usually urgency. Online one-to-one gives you the urgency without the compromise: a session can be in the diary for tomorrow evening, and the tutor is chosen for the paper rather than for living in Ajman.

One site ranking on these searches sells finished Internal Assessments, which puts the student at risk rather than ahead.

whyPoints.title: Built for a two-board household
whyPoints.description: Al Helio families frequently run an IGCSE candidate and a Diploma student at once, on calendars set by two schools that do not talk to each other. We plan the pair together, which usually means unequal hours rather than equal ones.

IB Gram's own plan follows the free trial, not a rate card.

faqs.question: How late is too late to start tutoring before the June papers?
faqs.answer: Eight weeks is a strong starting point and four is still worth doing if the goal is narrowed properly. In eight weeks a student can rebuild exam technique, drill the three or four topics costing the most marks and learn to read command terms, which together move more marks than most parents expect. In four weeks the realistic target is pacing, mark-scheme wording and the two highest-value topics. What no short block can do is teach a two-year syllabus from scratch or rescue an unstarted Internal Assessment.

faqs.question: When do IGCSE entry deadlines actually fall for a school in Ajman?
faqs.answer: Months before the papers, and your school sets an internal cut-off earlier still. The date matters more than it sounds because it is the last point at which tier can change: once a Cambridge candidate is entered for Core in a tiered subject, the grade ceiling is fixed whatever happens in the exam room. Ask the examinations officer for the internal deadline in the autumn term rather than the spring. Families who discover a child's Extended-tier potential after that date cannot act on it in that series.

faqs.question: Why do November results arrive so much later than June ones?
faqs.answer: Because the marking cycle sits after the papers, and the November papers are late in the calendar year. Pearson's June 2026 International GCSE results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026. Its November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. That gap is the whole reason November is a resit and tier-correction route rather than a parallel session: the grade exists, but it exists in January, after many application deadlines have closed.

faqs.question: Does my child in Al Helio sit the same exam series as students in India?
faqs.answer: No, and this trips up revision plans found online. Cambridge's February/March series is offered to India only. UAE candidates sit the June series, with November as the resit route, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. Any schedule built around a February exam window belongs to a different country. Check one more thing while you are asking: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative timetable zones, and says it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone.

faqs.question: Who sets the deadlines for the IB Internal Assessment and Extended Essay?
faqs.answer: Your child's school, not the IB, and that is the document a plan should be built from. The school issues a deadline sheet covering draft and final dates for each subject's Internal Assessment, staged Extended Essay milestones, the Theory of Knowledge essay and the recording window for oral components. Ask the coordinator for it in the autumn term of the first Diploma year and put it somewhere visible. The external session is fixed and distant; the internal sheet is what causes the actual crises.

faqs.question: What should we do with a disappointing mock paper?
faqs.answer: Read the distribution of lost marks rather than the grade. Marks spread thinly across everything points to fluency, and the answer is volume of timed practice. Marks clustered in two or three topics points to targeted teaching. An unfinished final section is a pacing problem that a stopwatch fixes faster than content revision. Full marks on recall questions and nothing on extended responses is a command-term problem, usually a two-session fix once a student sees what describe, explain, compare and evaluate each pay for.

faqs.question: Can we get both an IB student and an IGCSE student tutored on the same evening?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in Al Helio households that is a common request. Two consecutive one-hour online sessions work better than one long shared slot, because the two curricula need different work: timed past-paper sections for the IGCSE candidate, longer component or content blocks for the Diploma student. Our usual advice is to resist splitting hours evenly between children. The one with an entry or tier deadline pending has the more urgent calendar, and the other can be front-loaded earlier in the year when there is slack.

faqs.question: Will sessions keep running through Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the timing moved. School hours shorten, concentration shifts, and an afternoon slot that worked all year stops working. The practical pattern is shorter sessions after Iftar, often 45 minutes rather than an hour, planned before the month starts rather than rescheduled week by week. Families who plan around it lose nothing from a revision block; families who try to hold the old schedule typically lose three or four weeks at exactly the point in the calendar where those weeks are most expensive.

faqs.question: Is a November entry a sensible backup if June goes badly?
faqs.answer: As a response to a result, yes. As a hedge planned in advance, usually not. A student preparing for June while assuming November will catch them tends to prepare properly for neither, and the summer vanishes. November earns its place in two specific cases: correcting a tier, where a Core-capped candidate sits Extended for a grade an AS Level course requires, and repairing one subject that has blocked a route while everything else is settled. In both the work is narrow and an eight-week plan fits well.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help my child finish an IA that is behind schedule?
faqs.answer: A tutor can help the student finish it; a tutor cannot finish it. That distinction is the whole rule. Legitimate help is scoping what remains, sequencing it against the deadline, explaining the assessment criteria, asking questions about the student's method and responding to the student's own draft. Writing a section, rewriting prose or editing to completion is malpractice, and the consequence lands on the student rather than the provider. Any service offering completed Internal Assessments is selling a risk, not a shortcut.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week makes sense in the run-in to a series?
faqs.answer: Two or three, kept to an hour each, distributed across the week rather than stacked. Distribution matters more than total hours this close to a paper, because the gains come from repeated retrieval and from acting on feedback between sessions. Two separate hours with marked work in between beats one two-hour block almost every time, which is also why in-home double visits are a poor unit for exam preparation even when the tutor is good. The final ten days should taper rather than intensify.

faqs.question: Which parts of the Diploma are hardest to rescue late?
faqs.answer: Anything requiring data or reading that cannot be compressed. An Internal Assessment where the experiment has not been run, an Extended Essay with no sources read, a Theory of Knowledge essay chosen in the final weeks. These have school deadlines that do not move and workloads that cannot be parallelised. By contrast, timed-paper technique, mark-scheme discipline and content gaps in specific topics all respond well to a short focused block. The lesson is to put component work early in year one, where there is slack.

faqs.question: How quickly can a session actually start for a family in Al Helio?
faqs.answer: Usually within a few days, because nothing depends on anyone driving to Ajman. That speed is most of the reason the search is phrased as a hunt for someone nearby, and online one-to-one preserves it while widening the choice of tutor from whoever is local to whoever teaches that paper. Where the exact subject, level and board combination has thin availability close to a series, we say so rather than substituting a generalist and letting you discover the mismatch in week three.

faqs.question: What does the Ajman school day do to the usable study window?
faqs.answer: It compresses it from both ends. Private schools here teach the mandatory UAE subjects alongside the licensed international curriculum, since Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies are the federal baseline, so the homework load is heavier than the exam entries suggest. Many Al Helio parents also commute to Sharjah or Dubai, pushing supervised study later into the evening. The workable pattern is a mid-afternoon session for a student who gets home early, or an 8pm slot where a parent wants to be in the room.

intro.heading: Two calendars, one evening, one set of parents
paragraphs: Al Jurf households are often busy in a specific way. The district sits beside the university and hospital area, with the courts nearby and an industrial zone beyond, and a high proportion of families here work academic or clinical hours. When two children in such a household are sitting examinations in the same year, the binding constraint is rarely money. It is attention: whose deadline gets the Tuesday evening, who gets the parent at the kitchen table on Saturday morning, and which crisis gets absorbed when both arrive in the same fortnight.

The two calendars genuinely do not align. An IGCSE candidate's year is built around a June series with November available behind it, an entry that closed months earlier, and a tier decision taken in Year 10. A Diploma candidate's year is built around a May session, four internal deadlines converging in the autumn of DP2, a winter mock window, and no mid-year repair route at all. Those are different shapes with different pressure points, and a household plan that treats them as one revision problem will serve neither child.

What makes it manageable is knowing which pressure points overlap. The autumn is the Diploma's worst term and the IGCSE child's quietest. The winter mock window hits both at once, which is the hardest fortnight of the year in a dual-curriculum house. The spring belongs to the Diploma. The summer after results belongs to whichever child has a decision to make. Mapped out, the year has two or three genuinely contested periods rather than nine months of competition.

On delivery, the answer to the search term is direct. IB Gram does not provide in-home visits anywhere in the UAE; home tutoring is a service we offer only in India. Lessons for Al Jurf families are live, one-to-one, over video on Gulf Standard Time. In a two-child household that format has a practical advantage beyond the obvious: two consecutive slots on the same evening with two different specialists costs one disrupted evening rather than two visits, and neither child waits for a tutor stuck on the Ajman ring road.

The rest of this page is the map. The two calendars side by side, month by month. What the transition year looks like when one child finishes IGCSE in June and starts the Diploma in September. What happens on results days and the decisions they force. Why the November series gives one child a second chance that the other does not have. How Ramadan and the holiday structure land on both calendars. How to allocate scarce hours when two children need help in the same term. And where the coursework honesty line sits in both qualifications, since it is the same line.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme

The Personal Project in the final year is the first extended independent piece a student attempts, and it competes with subject criterion deadlines throughout. Process criteria, not content, are where most marks are lost.

The practical fix for Al Jurf families is a fixed weekly slot that cannot be reallocated to whichever sibling is in crisis, since a term of reallocated slots is a term of nothing.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two years with terminal examinations in a June series, November available as a resit route, and syllabus codes that fix the papers and often the tier. programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Internal assessments carry roughly a fifth to a quarter of each subject grade and their deadlines converge in the autumn of DP2 alongside the first mocks. There is no equivalent of a November resit within the same academic year.

subjects.name: Physics (IB HL and SL; Cambridge 0625; Pearson 4PH1)

subjects.description: Mole calculations at IGCSE are the foundation of Diploma stoichiometry, so a gap carried across the transition compounds immediately. Organic chemistry is taught late at IGCSE and early at Diploma level, which produces a predictable September problem.

subjects.description: Case-study response under time pressure at both levels, with evaluation marks lost in the same way: the theory described, the judgement never made. The Higher Level pre-released case study creates a defined preparation window that has no IGCSE counterpart.

subjects.description: Deadlines with no examination behind them, which is why they are deferred and why they then collide with everything else. In a household with a second child's mocks in the same window, these are the components that quietly slip and cost the most.

subjects.name: Computer Science (IB HL and SL; Cambridge 0478)
subjects.description: Algorithm tracing and pseudocode conventions at IGCSE; a documented solution assessed on planning and evaluation at Diploma level. Students arrive able to code and unable to document at both levels, and the documentation is where the marks sit.

sections.heading: One household, two examination calendars
paragraphs: The first thing to do in a dual-curriculum household is put both calendars on a single page. Not two plans next to each other, but one grid showing what each child faces in each month. Almost no family does this, and the families who do usually discover that the year contains two or three genuinely contested periods rather than the continuous competition it feels like from inside.

The grid needs four inputs. For the IGCSE child: the board, the syllabus codes, the tier, the mock window and the series. For the Diploma child: the subject internal assessment deadlines, the Extended Essay checkpoints, the Theory of Knowledge dates and the mock window. Schools issue all of this, though rarely in one document and often at different points in the term. Asking both schools in September costs two emails.

What the grid reveals is usually counterintuitive. The autumn term, which feels like the start of the year and therefore low pressure, is the Diploma child's worst term by a distance, because four internal deadlines converge there. The IGCSE child's autumn is comparatively light. By the spring the position reverses. The one period where both are at full stretch is the winter mock window, and knowing that in September is the difference between planning for it and surviving it.

The allocation rule that follows is unglamorous and works: hours follow the calendar, with a floor under each child. A floor matters because the younger child's continuous assessment has no dramatic deadline to defend it, and a term in which their slot is given away three times is a term in which nothing was taught. One fixed weekly session that cannot be reallocated, plus a flexible pool that follows whichever deadline is nearest, serves both children better than an attempt at fairness measured in equal hours.

sections.heading: The same month, seen from both sides
paragraphs: The table below sets the two years against each other by term rather than by date, because dates differ between schools and between Ajman and Sharjah cohorts. It is the document a dual-curriculum household should build for itself with real dates filled in, and it answers the only question that matters in a crowded week: whose deadline is closest and least recoverable.

Read the last column, which is the allocation advice. It is not an attempt to be even-handed. It follows a simple principle: the hours go where the loss would be permanent. A Diploma internal assessment deadline that passes badly is closed; the component is submitted and moderated and cannot be revisited. An IGCSE mock that goes badly is a diagnostic with a June series still ahead of it and a November series behind that. Those two are not equivalent losses, and treating them as equivalent is the usual mistake.

The exception is the final term, where the June series and the May session sit close together and both children have fixed, unrecoverable papers ahead. That is the one period where there is no clever allocation, only honest triage and, if the budget allows, more hours. Families who have planned the previous nine months well arrive at that term needing fewer of them, which is the main argument for building the grid in September rather than February.

One practical note on building your own version. Fill in real dates rather than terms, and include the school's own assessment weeks as well as the board deadlines, because an internal school test that carries a report grade will consume an evening whether or not it matters externally. Families who include those discover that the contested fortnights are not always the ones the board calendar predicts.

sections.heading: The transition year: IGCSE in June, Diploma in September
paragraphs: The hardest version of the dual-calendar problem is when it is the same child twice: finishing IGCSE in June and starting the Diploma or AS Level in September. The summer in between is treated as a holiday, which is understandable and expensive, because the new course assumes knowledge the old one did not always deliver.

The gaps are specific rather than general, and they are predictable by subject. A student entering Standard Level Diploma mathematics from Core IGCSE rather than Extended is missing algebraic fluency the course assumes from the first week. A student entering Diploma chemistry from Coordinated Science has not met the organic depth or the mole work that stoichiometry builds on. A Diploma biology student arriving from IGCSE has almost never handled statistics, which is where the internal assessment will be weakest a year later.

What makes the summer the right moment is that these gaps are cheap to close before the new course starts and expensive afterwards. Closing an algebra gap in August takes a handful of sessions with no competing deadlines. Closing the same gap in November of DP1 means doing it alongside new content, and the new content keeps arriving. The table below sets out the common transitions and the gap each leaves.

The other summer task is the first internal assessment. Diploma students who use August to settle a research question, rather than waiting to be chased in DP2, remove a large part of the autumn convergence described earlier on this page before it arrives. It is the single cheapest intervention in the two-year programme and it happens in a month when nobody wants to think about school.

sections.heading: Results days and the decisions they force
paragraphs: Two results events can land on a dual-curriculum household in the same year, and they force different decisions. The IGCSE results day in August is a decision point: whether a grade one below a subject requirement blocks an A Level or Diploma subject choice, whether to query a result, and whether to enter the November series. The Diploma results day is a different kind of event, mostly confirming a university place rather than opening a new choice.

The dates that can be stated here are the board ones. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE results from the June 2026 series reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 series results reached students on 22 January 2026. Those are the published figures and they define the decision windows. No International Baccalaureate date is published on this page, because the organisation's own site blocks automated retrieval and nothing could be verified; the school's coordinator holds that information.

The practical advice for the August window is to decide in advance what would change your plan, before the result arrives. If a grade of 6 in a science blocks the intended A Level, what is the alternative, and is a November resit compatible with starting Year 12? If a grade is one mark from a boundary, does the school intend to request a review, and by when must that be done? Families who ask these questions in July make decisions in August; families who do not spend August gathering information under time pressure.

The November resit question deserves its own answer because the timing is awkward. A November result reaching students in January may arrive after a sixth-form or university deadline, and re-entry means sitting the full paper set for the subject rather than the single weak paper. For some students it is clearly right. For others, protecting the start of Year 12 matters more than repairing a grade that nobody will ask about again.

sections.heading: Why one child has a second chance and the other does not
paragraphs: This asymmetry drives most of the allocation decisions on this page, so it is worth stating plainly. The IGCSE year has a structural repair route: Cambridge runs June and November series for UAE candidates, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May and June and again in November. A disappointing summer grade can be re-sat within the same academic year, with results in January.

The Diploma has no equivalent. Candidates at UAE schools sit the May session, and while retake sessions exist in principle, a Diploma result arriving after a university cycle has closed is a different proposition from an IGCSE grade repaired in January. More importantly, the Diploma's internal assessments are closed components: once submitted and moderated they cannot be revisited, which means a significant fraction of each subject grade is fixed before the written papers are sat at all.

That is why, in a contested autumn, the hours should generally go to the Diploma child. The loss there is permanent and the loss for the IGCSE child, at that point in the year, is not. It is also why the IGCSE child needs a protected floor rather than nothing: continuous erosion of their slot through the autumn produces a Year 11 student who arrives at the spring with a term's worth of unaddressed gaps and no diagnostic.

There is one honest caveat. If the IGCSE child's position is genuinely precarious, with a tier decision in play or several subjects at risk of falling below a sixth-form requirement, that changes the arithmetic. The rule is not age-based, it is loss-based, and a family should reassess it at the mock window rather than deciding once in September and defending the decision all year.

sections.heading: Ramadan, holidays and both calendars at once
paragraphs: Ramadan affects both children and affects them differently. School days shorten, fasting afternoons are low-energy, and productive hours move to after Iftar. For the Diploma child in the final term this collides with paper practice; for the IGCSE child it collides with the same. In a two-child house the post-Iftar window becomes the most contested hour of the day, and it is a narrow window.

Two household patterns work. The first runs both children in the same evening after Iftar, in consecutive slots from around 9pm, which is tiring and effective for timed paper work and poor for new teaching. The second splits the children across alternate days, giving each three sessions a fortnight rather than one a week, which preserves focus at the cost of frequency. Either beats leaving the ordinary timetable in place and watching both children work badly for a month.

Holidays are the recovery mechanism and the most underused asset in both calendars. A holiday week is the only realistic window for sitting full papers under proper timed conditions, and in a dual-curriculum household it is the only week where both children can have two or three intensive sessions without competing for the same evening. Families who schedule into breaks rather than treating them as entirely free reliably arrive at the next term in better shape.

The summer is where the two calendars finally cooperate. The IGCSE child's results-driven decisions and the Diploma child's internal assessment groundwork both belong in July and August, and neither competes with a school timetable. It is also the only point in the year when a family can afford to do the cheap, calm, preventative work that the rest of this page describes as the alternative to crisis spending.

sections.heading: Allocating hours when both children need help
paragraphs: Budget and attention are separate constraints and they bind at different times. A household can usually fund two weekly hours; it cannot always supervise them, particularly where parents work clinical or academic shifts, as many do in this part of Ajman. The table below is a working allocation model rather than a rule, and it assumes a fixed total number of hours rather than an expanding budget.

The model has three components. Each child has a protected floor that is never reallocated, because a slot given away three times in a term teaches nothing. A flexible pool follows whichever deadline is nearest and least recoverable. And a reserve, usually two or three hours, is held for the fortnight when something goes wrong, which it will. Families without a reserve end up buying emergency hours at short notice, which is both expensive and dependent on a specialist being free.

What this model does not do is divide hours equally. Equal division feels fair and serves the calendar badly, because the two qualifications place their pressure in different terms. A family that gives both children the same hours every month will over-serve one and under-serve the other in every term of the year, which is the outcome the grid at the top of this page exists to avoid.

One further refinement is worth the trouble. Review the allocation at the start of each half-term rather than each week, because weekly reviews drift towards whichever child has had the worse seven days, and that is exactly the signal the model is designed to ignore. A half-term horizon is long enough to follow the calendar and short enough to respond when a tier decision or a mock result genuinely changes the picture.

sections.heading: The honesty line is the same in both qualifications
paragraphs: Both children are subject to the same rule, and it is worth saying once for the household rather than twice for each child. Assessed work must be the student's own. That covers Diploma internal assessments, the Extended Essay and the Theory of Knowledge essay, and it covers any IGCSE coursework or controlled assessment component. A tutor teaches, questions and gives feedback. A tutor does not write, complete or supply text for submission.

The pressure to cross that line peaks exactly where this page says the calendars converge. A market exists in these search results that sells completed Internal Assessments at a published price, and the same offer exists in less visible forms for coursework at every level. What is being sold is a risk transferred onto the student: submitting work that is not their own is an academic-honesty breach, and for a Diploma candidate the consequence can extend to the Diploma itself.

Legitimate help under pressure is narrower and better. The tutor reads the draft and asks where the evidence supports the claim. They explain what a criterion descriptor actually requires, because terms such as evaluation and personal engagement have specific evidence requirements rather than general ones. They cut a research question to something answerable in the word count. They teach the student to read their own paragraph the way a moderator will. Those are the interventions that move marks, and they are available at the price of an ordinary hour.

For a household running two calendars, the practical value of a stated boundary is that it removes an argument at the worst moment. When a deadline is two days away and somebody suggests a shortcut, the answer has already been given in writing. A tutor who declines clearly is protecting the certificate that two years of effort was for, in both qualifications at once.
bullets: Diploma internal assessments carry roughly a fifth to a quarter of each subject grade
