sections.heading: Where the marks sit: the weightings families misread
paragraphs: A surprising amount of wasted revision in Al Ain comes from not knowing what each component is worth. Parents hear that a paper is hard and buy tuition for it, when the component actually losing the grade is a coursework piece marked months earlier, or a paper that carries nearly half the subject and gets a third of the practice. The weightings are published by the IB for every subject; they are not a secret, they are simply never put in front of parents.

In the current Diploma sciences, both Standard and Higher Level sit at Paper 1 for 36 per cent, Paper 2 for 44 per cent and the scientific investigation for 20 per cent. Read that again: the investigation is worth more than double a strong performance on any single long-answer question, and it is the one component the student controls completely, in their own time, with feedback allowed. A family deciding between coursework support and exam cramming should usually take the coursework first.

Mathematics splits differently by level. At Standard Level, Papers 1 and 2 take 40 per cent each with the exploration at 20 per cent. At Higher Level, Papers 1 and 2 drop to 30 per cent each and Paper 3 takes 20 per cent, which means the HL paper students practise least carries as much as the exploration they agonise over. Economics shifts even harder: Higher Level moves Paper 1 down to 20 per cent and brings in the quantitative Paper 3 at 30 per cent.
The table lists the splits we work from. Weightings are revised between syllabus cycles, so check the current subject guide or ask the school's coordinator before building a plan around them.

sections.heading: The Internal Assessment, criterion by criterion, with the marks attached
paragraphs: No competitor page in this market names a single assessment criterion, which is remarkable given that the Internal Assessment is where a fifth of most Diploma subject grades is decided. The criteria are published by letter with marks attached, and a student who has not read them is marking blind. The first thing we do in IA coaching is put the criteria next to the draft and have the student mark their own work. It is usually an uncomfortable twenty minutes and it saves weeks.

In the current science guides the scientific investigation is marked out of 24 across four criteria of six marks each: research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation. The pattern of loss is predictable. Research design loses marks for a vague methodology and an unjustified range of values. Data analysis loses them on uncertainty handling and unlabelled graphs. Conclusion loses them when the student restates results instead of comparing them with accepted values and published literature. Evaluation loses them on generic limitations: writing that there was human error is worth nothing.

The Mathematics exploration is out of 20, split across presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics, with that last criterion worth 6 marks and depending on the mathematics being commensurate with the level studied. An exploration that uses nothing beyond the first year of the course caps itself regardless of how neat it looks. The Economics portfolio is three commentaries of 800 words each, marked out of 14, with explicit marks for diagrams, terminology, application, a named key concept and evaluation. The Extended Essay is 4,000 words out of 34, and critical thinking alone carries 12 of those marks.
Read those numbers once and the priorities invert. The student who spends a weekend formatting an essay is protecting 4 presentation marks while leaving 12 critical-thinking marks untouched.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with an IA, EE or TOK essay
paragraphs: This has to be said plainly, because at least one provider selling to UAE families offers completed Internal Assessments at a fixed price. That is not tutoring. Submitting work that is not your own is malpractice under the IB's academic integrity rules, the school is required to act on it, and the consequence falls on the student, not on the person who sold the document. A family paying for that is buying a risk to the whole Diploma.

The honest boundary is easy to describe. A tutor may teach the subject content the coursework rests on, explain what each criterion rewards, discuss the suitability of a research question, show the student how to mark a draft against the descriptors, point out where a paragraph describes instead of argues, and check that referencing meets the school's required style. All of that is ordinary teaching and all of it is allowed.

A tutor may not write, rewrite or redraft any part of the submitted text, supply paragraphs for the student to insert, produce or alter data, choose the research question for the student, write reflection or process-journal entries, or edit a draft line by line until the voice is no longer the student's. The last one is where well-meaning help usually crosses over, and it is also the easiest for a supervisor to spot, because the writing stops matching everything else the student has produced that year.
We tell students this in the first coursework session and we tell parents the same thing. If a provider cannot say where its own line is, that is the answer to the question.

sections.heading: MoE equivalency, UAEU and what an Al Ain leaver needs on file
paragraphs: Al Ain is a university city. The United Arab Emirates University sits in the Asharej area, and a meaningful share of local Diploma and IGCSE students apply to it or to another UAE institution rather than going abroad. That makes one piece of paperwork more important here than in most Gulf cities, and it is one that no competitor page in this market mentions: the Ministry of Education certificate of equivalency.

The principle is straightforward. A UAE university needs to know that a foreign school-leaving qualification is equivalent to the national secondary certificate, and the Ministry issues an equivalency decision on that basis. For an IB student the question is usually whether the full Diploma was awarded rather than a certificate of individual subjects, and whether the subject spread and points total meet the published threshold. For a British-curriculum student it is a count: a required number of IGCSE or GCSE passes alongside a required number of AS or A-level subjects, in a recognised combination. For students required to study Arabic and Islamic Education, those subjects form part of the file.

Where this goes wrong is almost never academic. It is a certificate issued under a previous passport name, a transcript that was never attested, a student who sat a resit at a centre the school did not record, or a family that only discovers at application time that the subject combination does not satisfy the rule. Start the MoE equivalency certificate file in DP1 or Year 11, not in July. Keep the originals, keep every statement of entry, and check the current requirements on the Ministry's own equivalency portal, because the rules are revised and this page is not the authority on them.

UAE University admissions, like other national institutions, also publish their own entry tests and English-language thresholds alongside the equivalency requirement, and those are a separate matter from the Diploma score. Deal with them as a separate deadline, because a student can hold the points and still miss the intake on a language score nobody flagged.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and UAE Social Studies alongside the Diploma
paragraphs: Something that is almost completely absent from tutoring pages aimed at UAE families: an IB or IGCSE student in Al Ain is not only studying IB or IGCSE. ADEK requires private schools in the emirate to teach Arabic, Islamic Education for Muslim students, and UAE Social Studies or moral education, in specified amounts and for specified year groups. These sit on top of a six-subject Diploma, and the hours are real.

For Emirati families, particularly in districts such as Falaj Hazzaa and Al Muwaiji where Arabic as a first language is standard, this means the week already contains a demanding literacy load before any Diploma subject is counted. For expatriate families it often means a child studying Arabic as an additional language to a standard the school sets, with marks that appear on the school report but not on the Diploma. Parents are regularly surprised by how much of a term's grade pressure comes from this side of the timetable.

Practically, this changes how we schedule rather than what we teach. Arabic and Islamic Education support sessions a school runs are usually fixed, so tuition goes around them. We ask for the full school timetable, not just the subject in question, before fixing a slot, and we do not book a DP Chemistry session into the one evening a student already has school Arabic support. A tutor who ignores this side of the week ends up competing with it, and the student loses either way.

We also keep the honest limit visible. Where the requirement is a school-set Arabic course rather than an examined IB or IGCSE syllabus, the school's own department sets the standard and the materials, and our role is scheduling around it and supporting study skills, not second-guessing what the school assesses.

process.title: Send the report and the inspection page
process.description: Share the most recent school report, any marked assessment, and if you have it the section of the ADEK report covering teaching and achievement in your child's phase. Twenty minutes of reading replaces an hour of guessing, and it frequently changes which subject we recommend starting with.

process.title: Confirm board, level and entry
process.description: We check the statement of entry or the school's confirmation: Diploma level, or Cambridge and Edexcel codes and tiers for IGCSE, plus the practical arrangement for sciences. This is the step that prevents a term of revision from the wrong board's past papers, which is commoner in Al Ain than anyone admits.

process.title: One diagnostic session on a real paper
process.description: The first session is a marked past paper or a marked piece of coursework, not an introduction. The tutor identifies whether the gap is content, technique, coursework or timing, and tells you which. If the answer is that your child does not need weekly tuition, you will hear that too.

process.title: Fix a slot in Gulf Standard Time
process.description: We set a weekly slot around the school run, the school's own Arabic or Islamic Education support, and sibling timetables. Zakher, Hili and Al Foah families usually land on a later start. Ramadan moves sessions to post-Iftar automatically rather than cancelling them.

process.title: Written feedback the parent can read
process.description: After every second session you receive a short note: what was covered, what the student got wrong, and what changes next. Marked work is annotated on screen and saved where you can open it. No scores are promised, and a session that went badly is reported as a session that went badly.

process.title: Reset before each exam block
process.description: Ahead of mocks and of the May or November session we rebuild the plan backwards from the first paper: the date new content stops, which papers are sat timed, and which error types are being drilled. Blocks end when the exam ends rather than rolling on by default.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the syllabus, not to the district
whyPoints.description: The question is not who can reach Al Towayya by five. It is who has taught the paper your child is sitting, in the current guide, with the markscheme in front of them. Online delivery means the answer to that question is not limited to the people living within driving distance of your street.

whyPoints.title: We read the ADEK report with you
whyPoints.description: Al Ain schools are inspected by ADEK, and the report says more than the headline band. We read the achievement and teaching judgements for your child's phase with you and say which gaps tuition can realistically close and which belong to the school. That conversation is free and sometimes ends in us recommending nothing.

whyPoints.title: A stated line on coursework
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach content, explain criteria and mark drafts. They do not write, redraft or supply any part of an Internal Assessment, Extended Essay or TOK essay, and they do not produce data. The student hears that boundary in the first coursework session, in the same words a supervisor would use.

whyPoints.title: Market pricing shown, not hidden
whyPoints.description: The AED bands on this page are figures other providers publish, attributed to them, so you can see where any quote you receive sits. We do not pretend a monthly bundle and an hourly rate are the same product, and we would rather you compared cost per contact hour than per month.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that respects the Al Ain week
whyPoints.description: Sessions are booked in Gulf Standard Time, planned around the school's own Arabic and Islamic Education commitments, moved to post-Iftar slots in Ramadan, and arranged back to back for siblings sharing one quiet room. Scheduling is where most tuition quietly fails, so we treat it as part of the teaching.

whyPoints.title: Told plainly when nobody is free
whyPoints.description: Specialist availability is finite, particularly for minority languages and some Higher Level options. If no tutor who teaches your child's syllabus has a slot that works, we say so and give you an honest timeframe rather than offering a near-match and hoping. A wrong tutor costs more than a wait.

faqs.question: What does an ADEK inspection rating tell me about the tutoring my child needs?
faqs.answer: It tells you where the school's own capacity sits, which narrows what you should buy. The overall band is a weighted summary of a whole school, so read one level down: the judgements on students' achievement and on teaching and assessment for your child's phase and subject group. If feedback quality is criticised, an outside tutor marking your child's work to the published markscheme fills a real gap. If subject availability is the problem, no rating fixes that and an online specialist is the practical answer. Check the current report on ADEK's own site rather than an old summary.

faqs.question: Why is Al Ain inspected by ADEK rather than KHDA?
faqs.answer: Because Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, not Dubai. Private schools in Abu Dhabi, Al Ain and Al Dhafra are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge. KHDA covers Dubai only, and Sharjah's private schools answer to SPEA, while the northern emirates sit with the federal Ministry of Education. This matters when you read advice online: guidance written for Dubai families about KHDA fee rules, inspection cycles or school ratings does not transfer directly to your child's school in Al Ain.

faqs.question: How much should I expect to pay per hour for a tutor in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Market rates published by other UAE providers give the range. Budget online tuition runs from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, a qualified subject teacher online between about AED 150 and AED 300, and visiting in-home tuition from around AED 180 to AED 500 because travel is priced inside the hour. Named IB and IGCSE specialists are quoted from AED 200 to AED 450 and above. Those are other companies' figures, not ours. Compare any quote per contact hour, since monthly bundles package very different amounts of teaching.

faqs.question: Is a visiting home tutor in Al Ain worth the extra cost over online lessons?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it depends on the age. For primary-age children and some students with additional needs, having an adult in the room genuinely helps with focus in a way a screen does not. For Diploma and IGCSE students the calculation usually flips, because what decides the grade is whether the tutor has taught that exact paper. In a city with a smaller specialist pool, insisting on someone who can drive to your district on a Tuesday evening shrinks the list sharply. IB Gram delivers UAE tuition as live one-to-one online lessons; home visits are part of our India service only.

faqs.question: Al Ain has fewer IB schools than Abu Dhabi island. Can my child still get a Higher Level specialist?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the clearest reason local families use online tuition. A smaller private-school set means some Higher Level sciences and the less common languages are taught to a single small group, or are not offered at all. Online lessons remove geography from the match, so a Chemistry HL tutor who has taught the current guide can work with a student in Zakher as easily as one in Abu Dhabi. If no specialist in your child's exact syllabus has a workable slot, we will tell you that and give a realistic timeframe rather than substituting a near-match.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in the UAE need a permit, and should I ask to see one?
faqs.answer: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated, and a permit for individual private tutors is issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. Every regulatory source we checked states that the permit itself carries no fee. Employed residents generally need their employer's agreement before tutoring privately. It is reasonable to ask any individual tutor working in the UAE about their permit position and their qualifications. Rules and processes change, so check the current requirements on the ministry's own channels rather than relying on a tutoring company's summary, including this one.

faqs.question: Which exam board does my child's school in Al Ain actually use?
faqs.answer: Check the statement of entry rather than assuming, because mixed entries are common here. Cambridge subjects carry four-digit codes such as 0580 for Mathematics, 0625 for Physics and 0620 for Chemistry. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE codes look like 4MA1, 4PH1 and 4CH1. Cambridge IGCSE 0580 also tiers into Core and Extended, and the tier caps the grade available, so it matters as much as the board. One family can easily have two children on different boards, and one student can carry both across subjects. Send us the entry document and we check it before the first session.

faqs.question: How are the marks split between the papers and the Internal Assessment in Diploma sciences?
faqs.answer: Under the current guides both Standard and Higher Level sit at 36 per cent for Paper 1, 44 per cent for Paper 2 and 20 per cent for the scientific investigation. The investigation is the component a student controls completely, in their own time, with feedback permitted, and it is worth a fifth of the grade. Families frequently buy exam cramming while that 20 per cent goes unsupervised. Weightings are revised between syllabus cycles, so confirm the current split with your school's coordinator or the published subject guide before planning around it.

faqs.question: When should a Diploma student in Al Ain start the Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: Roughly nine months before the first paper, which for a May session means the spring and summer of DP1. The work that matters at that stage is not writing; it is narrowing the research question until the criteria are actually reachable. A question that is too broad, or that depends on data the student cannot collect, costs weeks that cannot be recovered later. Once a workable question exists, the drafting is manageable. Students who start in the autumn of DP2 collide with the Extended Essay, the TOK essay and four other investigations in the same twelve weeks.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Internal Assessment without breaking the rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear line. A tutor may teach the underlying content, explain what each criterion rewards, discuss whether a research question is feasible, show the student how to mark their own draft against the descriptors, point out where a paragraph describes rather than argues, and check referencing against the school's required style. A tutor may not write or redraft any passage, supply text to insert, produce or alter data, choose the question, or write reflection entries. Any provider offering to supply a finished Internal Assessment is offering malpractice, and the consequence lands on the student.

faqs.question: Does my child still have to study Arabic and Islamic Education alongside the Diploma?
faqs.answer: In the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, ADEK requires private schools to teach Arabic, Islamic Education for Muslim students, and UAE Social Studies or moral education, for specified year groups and in specified amounts. Those hours sit on top of a six-subject Diploma or a full IGCSE set, and they carry real grade pressure on the school report even when they do not appear on the Diploma. We ask for the complete school timetable before fixing a slot, so a tuition session never collides with the school's own Arabic support. Your school's registrar can confirm exactly what applies to your child's year.

faqs.question: What is the Ministry of Education equivalency certificate, and when should we start it?
faqs.answer: It is the decision that a foreign school-leaving qualification is equivalent to the UAE national secondary certificate, which a UAE university will expect from an IB or British-curriculum applicant. For a Diploma student the usual question is whether the full Diploma was awarded and whether the subject spread meets the published threshold; for an IGCSE and A-level student it is a count of passes in a recognised combination. Start the file in DP1 or Year 11. Most problems are administrative: unattested transcripts, a name change, or a resit the school never recorded. Confirm current rules on the ministry's own portal.

faqs.question: Should my child take Maths AA or AI for UAE University admissions?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a degree decision rather than a difficulty decision, because Applications and Interpretation is not the easy option; it is the modelling and statistics route with heavy technology use and a great deal of written interpretation. Engineering, physics and some computing programmes commonly expect Analysis and Approaches, while economics, business and many life-science routes accept either. Published entry requirements change between intakes, so read the current page for the specific degree at the specific university rather than relying on what an older sibling was told. We check the route against the degree plan before a student commits.

faqs.question: Do Al Ain students do better with sessions moved to after Iftar during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for most Al Ain students that is the better slot anyway. School days shorten during Ramadan and the productive hours for a teenager shift later, so we schedule lighter content work in the afternoons and move the demanding sessions to after Iftar. Because lessons are delivered online there is no travel to fit around the timing change, which is one practical advantage of the format during the month. We agree the revised timetable before Ramadan begins rather than rescheduling week by week, and go back to term timings afterwards.

faqs.question: We live in Zakher and the school run finishes late. When can sessions realistically start?
faqs.answer: Plan for a 6pm start on weekdays rather than 4.30pm. Zakher sits on the southern edge of the city towards Jebel Hafeet, and families whose children attend central or northern campuses have the longest run in Al Ain. Many Zakher families also shift the heavier subject to Friday or Saturday morning, when there is no commute at either end and a student can work for ninety minutes properly. We set the first few sessions deliberately late, see what arrival time actually looks like, then move it earlier if the family wants.

faqs.question: How does online tutoring handle practical work and the alternative-to-practical paper?
faqs.answer: The practical examination itself is run by the school or the examination centre, and no tutor replaces laboratory time. What tuition does cover is the written assessment of practical skills, which is where most of those marks actually sit: describing apparatus and method, identifying variables and controls, spotting anomalous results, handling uncertainty, and following table and graph conventions. We work through past practical and alternative-to-practical papers on screen, annotating the student's answers against the published markscheme. For the Diploma investigation, the design and analysis work is exactly what online sessions suit.

faqs.question: What happens if the first Al Ain tutor we try is not the right match for my child?
faqs.answer: Tell us after the first or second session and we change the tutor, not the plan. A mismatch is usually about pace or explanation style rather than competence, and it shows up quickly: a student who answers in single words, or who leaves a session without a clear next task. We would rather re-match in week two than discover in week ten that nothing moved. The diagnostic session exists partly for this reason, because it gives both the tutor and the parent something concrete to judge the fit against.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start if the first paper is six weeks away?
faqs.answer: It is late for content and useful for technique. Six weeks before a paper, teaching new topics rarely pays; marking timed papers does. A short block in that window works when it is built around whole past papers, marked to the published markscheme, with errors logged by type rather than by topic, so the student keeps meeting the same mistake until it stops. What a six-week block cannot do is close a year-wide content gap, and we will say so plainly rather than selling a package that cannot deliver. No tutor can promise a particular score.

al-ain.closingHeading: Start with the report, then choose the subject specialist
al-ain.closingBody: Send us the last school report, the ADEK inspection page for your child's phase if you have it, and the statement of entry. We will read them, tell you whether the gap is content, technique, coursework or scheduling, and match an online IB tutor in Al Ain who teaches that exact syllabus. The first session is a marked paper, not a sales call, and if the honest answer is that your child does not need weekly tuition, that is what you will hear. Lessons are live one-to-one video, booked in Gulf Standard Time, with written feedback you can read.

Families searching for IB and IGCSE tutors in Al Jimi are frequently solving an availability problem: a Higher Level subject not offered, an option block that collides, a cohort of five. This page covers what a small school can timetable, Higher against Standard Level dimension by dimension, and the private candidate route. Lessons are one-to-one over live video.

al-ain/al-jimi.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are matched to subjects rather than to a city, which is the point of the format. A Higher Level Chemistry specialist does not have to live in Al Ain to teach a student in Al Jimi, and in practice there are considerably more of them elsewhere.

intro.heading: In a small school, the gap is often a whole subject
paragraphs: Al Jimi sits in the central-western part of Al Ain, around the mall and the oasis, with Al Qattara, Al Mutawaa and Al Muwaiji adjoining it. Al Ain itself is part of the Abu Dhabi emirate and therefore regulated by the Department of Education and Knowledge, 130 kilometres inland from the capital, and its private-school set is substantially smaller than the island's. That single structural fact changes what tutoring is for here.

In a large city school the gap a tutor fills is usually narrow: a topic that did not land, a technique that was never corrected, a coursework draft nobody read twice. In a smaller school the gap is often categorical. The Higher Level subject your child wants may not run, because a viable set needs a minimum number of students and the cohort is thin. An option block may place two subjects your child needs in the same column. A subject may run with five students and a teacher covering it alongside two others. None of those is a failing on the school's part; they are arithmetic.

What that produces is a different set of parental questions from the ones competitor pages answer. Not how do I find a maths tutor, but can my child take Higher Level Physics at all, and if not, what are the options. Not how much does tuition cost, but what does it mean to study a subject the school does not teach. Not is online as good as in person, but is there anybody in Al Ain who teaches this subject, and if not, does that matter.

The honest answer to the last of those is that it does not matter much, because the format removes the geography. A Higher Level Economics specialist teaching from anywhere in the time zone is available to a student in Al Jimi in exactly the way a locally resident generalist is, and there are considerably more of the former. The 130 kilometres is a constraint on who can arrive at a door and no constraint at all on who can teach on a screen.

There is a timing point that runs through all of it and deserves saying on its own. Every response to an availability problem requires notice. Moving a subject between option blocks, finding a centre that will enter an external candidate, teaching a two-year course from outside the school, changing school: each of those is possible in November of Year 11 and impossible in June of Year 12. The families who come out of this well are not the ones with the most money. They are the ones who asked for the timetable a year early.

So this page sets out what Al Ain schools typically can and cannot timetable, compares Higher and Standard Level properly across seven dimensions rather than in a sentence, explains the private candidate route for a subject the school cannot offer, and says plainly what self-teaching a subject actually requires. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, and that is also the practical reason any of this is possible from here rather than a matter of preference.

al-ain/al-jimi.programmesIntro: The notes below are written around availability, because in a smaller school set the question of whether a course runs at all comes before any question about how it is taught.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. The structure is the constraint in a small school: a student must find three Higher Level courses that actually run and that do not collide in the option blocks, which narrows real choice considerably.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain Diploma cohorts are small, which has genuine advantages, more teacher attention and a closer group, and one serious disadvantage. If the Higher Level subject your child needs for a university course does not run, the decision has to be made in Year 11 rather than discovered in Year 12. Ask the school for its option blocks a full year ahead.

programmes.name: IGCSE
programmes.description: Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel both operate here, with Cambridge tiering several subjects into Core and Extended and capping Core at grade C. IGCSE option lists are usually wider than Diploma ones because the cohort is larger and the teaching load per subject is lower.
programmes.countryNote: The practical Al Ain issue at IGCSE is the less common subjects: a second science, a specific language, computer science or a creative subject may not run at all. The subject your child drops at fourteen can close a Higher Level door at sixteen, which is why the Year 9 options conversation matters more here than in a larger city.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups marked against four lettered criteria, each out of eight, with process assessed alongside content. In a small school the same teacher often carries a subject across several year groups, which means consistency is good and specialist depth at the top end can be thinner.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Ain family the MYP matters mainly as preparation for a narrow Diploma choice. A student who keeps a second science and a language going through MYP preserves options that a thin Diploma option block will otherwise close for them two years later.

programmes.name: A Level
programmes.description: Linear qualifications with all assessment at the end and little coursework in most subjects. Three or four subjects studied deeply, which in a small school can be easier to timetable than a full Diploma because there are fewer courses to staff.
programmes.countryNote: Where a Diploma option block cannot accommodate a student's needs, A Level is sometimes the better route in Al Ain simply because it requires fewer simultaneous courses. It also satisfies the Ministry of Education's British track, which asks for one accredited A Level at grade E or better, or two AS Levels at the same grade, alongside five IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3.

al-ain/al-jimi.subjectsIntro: The notes below say something about availability as well as content, because in Al Ain the first question about a subject is often whether anybody nearby teaches it at all.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Papers 1 and 2 carry 36% and 44% in the Diploma with the investigation at 20%. Higher Level organic mechanisms and energetics are the most frequently requested gap from Al Ain, partly because Higher Level sets here are small and partly because the material needs hand-drawn repetition.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Higher Level Physics is one of the courses most likely not to run in a small school, because the cohort rarely reaches a viable size. Where it does run, fields and the Higher Level extension topics are the standard loss points.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Usually available because demand is higher. Built on unifying themes at Diploma level with heavy unseen-context questioning, where students lose marks describing a trend when the command term asked them to explain a cause.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Standard Level sits two papers at 40% each with a 20% exploration; Higher Level adds Paper 3 at 20%. Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is frequently the single hardest course to staff in a small school and the one most often requested from outside.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics with the graphic display calculator throughout. More commonly offered in smaller schools than Analysis and Approaches because it suits a broader cohort, which makes the route choice partly an availability question rather than purely a preference.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Standard Level is Paper 1 at 30%, Paper 2 at 40% and the portfolio at 30%, with a quantitative Paper 3 added at Higher Level. Higher Level Economics is a common gap in smaller schools and a subject several UAE university routes expect.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Higher Level sits Paper 1 at 35% and Paper 2 at 40% with the project at 25%. The project needs real organisational access, and in a small cohort students often choose the same two or three local businesses, which produces generic analysis.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen analysis, comparative essay, and the Individual Oral at 30% of Standard Level, with the HL essay at 20% added at Higher Level. Reliably available, and the loss point is summarising a text rather than analysing the writer's choices.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: One of the least likely subjects to run at Higher Level in a smaller school, and increasingly requested. It is also one of the thinner subjects in the regional tutor pool, so it is worth asking about a long way in advance.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first and additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the international programme under the federal rules, with separate provision and different expectations for Arab and non-Arab students. Arabic A at Diploma level is better served in Al Ain than many other subjects.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: A frequent Diploma choice that smaller schools often cannot staff, and one where students underestimate the research-methods component. The internal assessment is an experimental replication with strict ethical constraints that trip up the unprepared.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A 1,600-word essay on a prescribed title plus the exhibition with its 950-word commentary. In a small school it is often taught by a teacher carrying it alongside a full subject load, so it is the component most likely to be under-supported.

al-ain/al-jimi.regionsIntro: Al Ain is a compact, low-rise city, so these districts are all within a short drive of Al Jimi and the school choice is made across them.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji
regions.note: Immediately west of Al Jimi, residential and largely Emirati, with the historic fort at its centre. Short school runs in both directions, and households here face the same thin Diploma option lists.

regions.name: Al Towayya
regions.note: North-east towards Tawam, with the hospital and medical community nearby. A significant number of families here work shifts, which shapes when tutoring can happen in a way it does not elsewhere in the city.

regions.name: Al Khabisi
regions.note: East of Al Jimi, with established school provision including some of the city's longest-standing private schools. One of the main school destinations for Al Jimi families.

regions.name: Hili
regions.note: North of the city centre, residential with the archaeological park nearby. Reachable within a few minutes, and part of the same small set of school options.

regions.name: Al Maqam
regions.note: South-east, where the UAE University campus sits. Relevant academically because it shapes what local families aim at and which subject prerequisites matter for their applications.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: South of the city on the way towards the Omani border, residential and spread out. Longer runs into the central school cluster, which pushes tutoring towards weekends for these households.

regions.name: Falaj Hazza
regions.note: West towards the Jebel Hafeet side, residential with local provision. Another district drawing on the same central school cluster, with the same Higher Level availability constraints.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: Central and close to Al Jimi, with easy access to the main school sites. One of the better districts for keeping a weekday afternoon session, because almost nothing in the city is far away.

schoolClusters.city: Central Al Ain: Al Jimi, Al Khabisi and Al Mutawaa
schoolClusters.note: The city's main private-school concentration, spanning British, SABIS and national-curriculum routes. Strong, long-established schools working with year groups far smaller than the capital's, which is the source of both the attention and the option-block constraint.

sections.heading: What a smaller private-school set actually means for a Diploma student
paragraphs: Start with the arithmetic, because it explains everything else. A Diploma Higher Level course needs a teacher with subject depth, a timetable column and enough students to justify both. In a school with a year group of sixty, a Higher Level subject chosen by four students is difficult to run and a subject chosen by two is usually impossible. The school is not refusing; it is solving a staffing problem with the resources it has.

The consequences arrive in a sequence that parents rarely anticipate. First, the option blocks are tighter: subjects are grouped into columns and a student can take one from each, so two subjects your child needs may be in the same column with no way around it. Second, the available Higher Level set is narrower than the brochure suggests, because a brochure lists what the school can offer and a timetable shows what actually runs this year. Third, the subjects that do run may be taught by someone carrying three courses, which affects depth at the top end rather than competence.

Against that, small schools give something larger ones cannot. A teacher who knows every student in the cohort. Coursework drafts read more than once. A pastoral attention that is genuinely different in kind. Families who move from a large city school to an Al Ain one often find the teaching relationship better and the subject menu worse, which is a real trade rather than a complaint.

The practical move is to get the option blocks in writing a full year before they bind. A Year 11 family who sees next year's Diploma columns in November has time to change course, consider a different school, plan a private candidate entry or adjust their university thinking. The same family in July has none of those options, and that timing difference is the single most valuable thing on this page.

sections.heading: Subjects Al Ain schools can and usually cannot timetable
paragraphs: The table below describes the pattern across a smaller school set rather than any single school, and it should be checked against your own school's current timetable rather than assumed. It exists because families arrive at the options conversation with no sense of what is normal, and therefore cannot tell a reasonable constraint from one worth pushing back on.

The broad shape is consistent. Core subjects run everywhere and at both levels: Mathematics, English, Biology, Business and a local-language option. The mid-tier subjects run at Standard Level reliably and at Higher Level only when the cohort allows, which in practice means Chemistry and Physics are the ones most often capped. The specialist subjects, Computer Science, Psychology, the less common second languages, Design Technology and some creative courses, are the ones that most often do not appear at all.

That matters because of the prerequisite chain. A UAE or international university engineering route that expects Higher Level Mathematics and Physics is closed to a student whose school caps Physics at Standard Level, unless something is done about it. Medicine routes expecting Higher Level Chemistry and Biology face the same issue. These are not small inconveniences; they are route-level decisions, and they are made by a timetable rather than by the student.

The right-hand column is the useful one. Every constraint in the table has at least one response available, and all of them require time. The response that requires the most time, a private candidate entry for a subject taught entirely outside school, is covered in its own section below.

sections.heading: Higher Level against Standard Level, dimension by dimension
paragraphs: Most pages in this market reduce the Higher and Standard Level distinction to a sentence about difficulty. It is more useful than that, and in a school where the Higher Level menu is restricted a family needs the full comparison in order to make a reasoned substitution rather than a resentful one.

The differences are not uniform across the dimensions. Teaching hours and content depth differ substantially. The number of papers differs, with Higher Level sciences and Mathematics adding a third paper. Internal assessment weighting is frequently the same at both levels, which surprises people: a science investigation carries 20% whether the course is Higher or Standard, which means the coursework work a tutor can protect is identical in value at either level.

The dimension that decides most decisions is the university prerequisite. A course that asks for Higher Level Chemistry will not accept Standard Level, and no amount of achievement at the lower level substitutes. A course that asks for a science at either level opens up a much wider set of options. So the first step in any Higher Level conversation is to read the actual entry requirements for two or three target courses, not to reason in the abstract about ambition.

The last dimension in the table is the honest one: the signal from prior attainment that a student is ready for Higher Level. A student finishing IGCSE at a comfortable grade 6 or B in a subject will find the Higher Level course demanding but viable with support. A student who scraped a pass is being set up to fail, and in a small school where the Higher Level set is tiny there is nowhere for them to hide while it happens.

sections.heading: When the school cannot offer the subject: the private candidate route
paragraphs: If a subject your child needs does not run, one option is to study it outside school and sit the examination as a private candidate through a centre that accepts external entries. It is a real route, it is used every year, and it is also the route most often attempted carelessly. The two things that go wrong are the practical requirements and the deadlines.

Practical requirements come first because they are the hard constraint. Science subjects carry assessed practical or internal assessment components that generally require laboratory access and a supervising teacher, and a private candidate cannot simply skip them. Some boards offer alternative-to-practical papers; the Diploma's internal assessment requirements are different again and are administered through a school. Before any teaching starts, establish in writing what components the subject requires and whether a centre will administer them for an external candidate. If the answer is no, the route is closed whatever the teaching arrangements.

Deadlines come second and bite harder. Entries close months before examinations. Cambridge examines IGCSE, O Level and International A Level in a June series and a November series, and an Al Jimi family effectively chooses between them rather than between dates in the same term. June is the main series almost every school enters; November is the resit and second-attempt route, far enough after August results to act on them but close enough that the entry decision has to be made within weeks of opening the June grades. Pearson Edexcel runs May and June plus November and publishes provisional timetables ahead of each, with its November 2026 window finishing on 19 November 2026. Entries for either board close well ahead of the papers, so a family that waits until the term of the exam to decide has usually already lost the choice, and nobody is going to warn them.

The sequence that works is therefore backwards. Find a centre that will accept an external candidate and administer the required components. Confirm the entry deadline for the series you want. Then count back the teaching time needed, which for a two-year Diploma course is two years and for a one-year IGCSE is not realistically less than a year done properly. Only then decide whether the route is viable. Doing it in the other order produces a well-taught student with no entry.

sections.heading: The option block collision, and what to do in Year 11
paragraphs: Option blocks are the mechanism by which a small school fits a wide curriculum into a narrow timetable. Subjects are grouped into columns and a student takes one subject from each column. It is an entirely reasonable system and it produces an entirely predictable problem: the two subjects a particular student needs sometimes sit in the same column.

When that happens, the responses available are limited and all of them require time. The school may be able to move a subject between columns if enough students are affected, which is why raising it early and finding out who else has the same clash is worth doing. The student may substitute a subject, which requires knowing whether their target university courses accept the substitution. The family may consider a different school, which is a large decision and a real one. Or the student may take one subject outside school as a private candidate, with all the constraints the previous section describes.

What does not work is waiting. Timetables are built over months, and a request in November when next year's blocks are being drafted is a different conversation from the same request in June when they are set. Parents often hesitate because they do not want to seem demanding; the result is that a decision about their child's university options gets made by a scheduling spreadsheet.

There is one further point worth making to Year 11 families specifically. The subject your child drops at the end of Year 9 or Year 11 closes doors quietly, and in a school with a thin Higher Level menu it closes them earlier. Keeping a second science or a language going for one more year, even without enthusiasm, is cheap insurance against an option block nobody can see yet.

sections.heading: Self-teaching a subject, honestly assessed
paragraphs: Families sometimes propose that a motivated student simply teaches themselves a subject the school does not offer. It can be done and it is done, and the honest version of the advice is that it works for a specific kind of student in a specific kind of subject and fails badly outside those conditions.

It works best in subjects that are content-led, well documented and examined on written papers with no practical component: Business, Economics at Standard Level, some humanities, and mathematics for an unusually self-directed student. It works worst in the sciences, where practical and internal assessment requirements need laboratory access and supervision, and in languages, where the speaking components need a trained interlocutor and regular interaction.

The student it works for is not simply the clever one. It is the student who can hold a schedule for eighteen months without external deadlines, who will mark their own work honestly against a scheme, and who will ask for help before a problem compounds. Most sixteen-year-olds cannot do all three, and saying so is not a judgement about ability. It is a judgement about what unsupervised long-horizon work asks of anybody.

If a family goes ahead, the structure that makes it survivable is a weekly external deadline, which is what a weekly tutored hour actually provides. Not the teaching so much as the obligation: someone will look at this week's work on Tuesday. Students who had that obligation finish the course. Students who relied on their own motivation generally arrive at February having covered a third of the syllabus, and by then the entry has usually been made and the money spent.
bullets: Works in content-led subjects examined on written papers only
Fails in sciences with practical requirements and in languages with speaking
Needs a student who can hold eighteen months without external deadlines
A weekly external obligation is what makes it survivable

sections.heading: What tuition costs in Al Ain, and why the local pool is smaller
paragraphs: This market publishes very little about price, which is unhelpful everywhere and especially in a city with fewer providers. Three of the six competitor pages examined for this project quote no figure at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars. The bands below are market rates as of October 2026 with the source attached, and none of them is an IB Gram price list.

Budget online tutoring runs AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52 at entry tiers. A qualified subject tutor working online is AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one visits are AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the figure, on Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table and comparable listings. Genuine IB, IGCSE or A Level specialists are AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and premium named tutors at AED 650.

The Al Ain difference is on the supply side rather than the price side. The city is 130 kilometres from the capital and its resident teaching population is smaller in absolute terms, so the pool of people who could arrive at a door in Al Jimi to teach Higher Level Chemistry is genuinely small, and in some subjects it is empty. Scarcity in a local market usually raises the price of the few available providers while reducing the quality floor, which is a poor combination for a parent.

That is the clearest practical argument for the online format in this particular city, and it is an argument about availability rather than about convenience. The relevant pool is not the people who live within driving distance of Al Jimi; it is the people who teach that syllabus in this time zone. For a Higher Level subject not taught locally, that difference is the whole of whether the subject is possible at all.
bullets: Qualified subject tutor, online, market rate: AED 150 to 300 an hour
In-home visits run AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the rate
Al Ain's resident specialist pool is small and in some subjects empty
The relevant pool online is everyone who teaches the syllabus, not the locals

sections.heading: A home tutor in Al Jimi against a specialist on screen
paragraphs: Families here do search for a home tutor and the reasoning is perfectly sound in a city of villas and short drives. So the question deserves a proper answer rather than a deflection. A visiting tutor in Al Jimi is cheaper to reach than one in a remote district, because Al Ain is compact and nothing is far. The constraint is not travel time; it is who exists to travel.

For a core IGCSE subject the local pool is adequate and a visiting tutor is a reasonable option, with market in-home rates of roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour against AED 150 to AED 300 online. For a Higher Level Diploma science, Higher Level Mathematics, Higher Level Economics or Computer Science, the honest position is that the number of people in Al Ain who teach that syllabus to that level is very small, and choosing from them is not really choosing.

IB Gram does not make home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Lessons for Al Ain families run one-to-one over live video. In this city that is less a compromise than the mechanism by which a Higher Level specialist becomes available at all, which is a different argument from the one usually made for online tuition.

The honest limitation is the same as everywhere. A younger child who needs an adult physically present to stay on task is harder to hold on video, and for that age we recommend shorter sessions more often with a parent within earshot. For a sixteen-year-old working on Paper 3 technique with a specialist, the screen is simply the better arrangement.
bullets: Al Ain is compact, so travel is not the limiting factor; supply is
Core IGCSE subjects have an adequate local pool; Higher Level subjects do not
No home visits in the UAE; lessons run one-to-one over live video
Younger children need shorter sessions with a parent nearby

sections.heading: Coursework in a cohort where everyone picks the same topic
paragraphs: Small cohorts produce a specific coursework problem that larger ones do not. When six students in a Diploma class choose an internal assessment topic, and the obvious local options are limited, several of them converge on the same idea. That is not malpractice and it is not a crisis, but it does produce a set of near-identical investigations, and it caps the personal engagement and originality marks for all of them.

The fix is to have the topic conversation earlier and wider. A good internal assessment question comes from something the student actually has access to and some curiosity about, and in Al Ain that can be genuinely distinctive: local water and soil conditions, the agricultural economy, heat effects on materials and systems, the city's own tourism and transport data. Those are better starting points than a textbook investigation that forty thousand students worldwide also chose.

The boundary on what a tutor may do is the same everywhere and worth restating. A tutor interrogates the research question until it can be answered inside the word limit, says when a method will not generate data capable of supporting a conclusion before any data exists, reads a draft against the published criteria and names the criterion that is unevidenced, teaches the missing skill and returns the work, and asks the student to justify a paragraph aloud.

A tutor does not supply text, rewrite a section into something the student could not have produced, edit a draft to completion, or hand over a topic, structure or data set ready-made. Nothing is bought in. One operation in this market sells completed Diploma internal assessments; the malpractice finding falls on the student and can cost the diploma. We also do not reproduce or supply subject guides, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables, which belong to the boards and which your child's school holds legitimately.
bullets: Small cohorts converge on the same topics, which caps originality marks
Local conditions make genuinely distinctive investigation questions available
Questions, methods and criteria coaching, placed early in the process
No supplied text, no rewriting to completion, no ready-made topics or data

sections.heading: Starting from Al Jimi
paragraphs: The first request is unusual compared with most tutoring enquiries, and it is the right one for this city: ask the school for next year's option blocks and the list of subjects actually running at each level this year. Not the prospectus. The timetable. That document tells a family what their real choices are, and in a smaller school it is also the document that quietly determines which university routes remain open.

Second, the most recent marked work in the subject that worries you, because the question of whether a student is ready for Higher Level is answered by evidence rather than by ambition. A comfortable grade in the subject at IGCSE means Higher Level is demanding and viable. A scraped pass means more hours than the gain justifies, and in a tiny Higher Level set there is nowhere to hide while that plays out.

Then a diagnostic session rather than an introduction. The tutor works through the marked work with your child, assesses readiness for the level being considered, and writes down what a term or a course of work would consist of. If the honest conclusion is that a subject should be taken at Standard Level, or substituted, we say that. It is less profitable advice and it is better advice.

Two limits stated plainly. Coverage for the rarer Diploma subjects and languages is thin in this time zone, Higher Level Computer Science among them, and if there is no honest match we say so rather than putting a generalist in front of a Higher Level paper. And in this market generally, ask any tutor whether they hold the private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, with eligibility covering registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published.
bullets: Ask for the option blocks and the subjects actually running, not the prospectus
Readiness for Higher Level is settled by marked evidence, not by ambition
The diagnostic may conclude that Standard Level is the correct choice
Ask any tutor whether they hold the MoHRE private tuition permit

process.title: Get the option blocks in writing
process.description: Next year's Diploma or sixth-form columns, plus the list of subjects actually running at each level this year. In a smaller school this document determines which university routes stay open, and a family who reads it in November has choices that the same family in July does not.

process.title: Check the prerequisites for two target courses
process.description: Read the actual entry requirements for two or three courses your child might apply to, including at UAE universities. A course asking for Higher Level Chemistry by name will not accept Standard Level. That single check converts an abstract argument about ambition into a concrete decision.

process.title: Send the marked evidence
process.description: The most recent marked work in the subject under discussion. Readiness for Higher Level is answered by a grade that was comfortable rather than scraped, and in a Higher Level set of four students there is nowhere to hide while an unwise choice plays out over two years.

process.title: Confirm whether the route is even possible
process.description: If a subject is to be taken outside school, establish first what practical or internal assessment components it requires, whether a centre will administer them for an external candidate, and when entries close. A well-taught student with no valid entry is the worst outcome available.

process.title: Fix a weekly obligation, not just a lesson
process.description: For any subject studied outside the school timetable, the weekly session is as much a deadline as a lesson: someone will look at this week's work on a known day. Students with that obligation finish the course. Students relying on motivation alone usually do not.

whyPoints.title: We answer the availability question first
whyPoints.description: In Al Ain the first real question is often whether a subject can be taken at all, not how it should be taught. This page publishes what a smaller school set typically offers, what it usually cannot, and what a family can actually do about each constraint, with the timing for each decision named.

whyPoints.title: The subject pool is not local
whyPoints.description: A Higher Level Chemistry specialist does not need to live in Al Ain to teach a student in Al Jimi. The relevant pool is everyone who teaches that syllabus in this time zone rather than the small number who could drive to your door, and in several subjects that is the difference between possible and not.

whyPoints.title: Higher and Standard Level compared properly
whyPoints.description: Seven dimensions rather than a sentence about difficulty: taught hours, papers, content depth, internal assessment weighting, grade ceiling, university prerequisites and the honest readiness signal from prior attainment. Internal assessment weighting is the same at both levels, which surprises most families.

whyPoints.title: The private candidate route, with its failure points
whyPoints.description: Components first, centre second, entry deadline third, teaching time last. A Cambridge June entry has to be lodged in the spring, and the November resit entry has to be lodged within weeks of August results, so both deadlines land in a holiday. Families who plan in the other order end up well taught with no valid entry, which is the one outcome nobody recovers from.

whyPoints.title: Advice that sometimes recommends less
whyPoints.description: If marked evidence says Higher Level is the wrong choice, we say so. If self-teaching a science is not viable because of the practical requirements, we say that too. Both are less profitable conclusions than the alternative, and both are the correct ones.

whyPoints.title: No borrowed authority
whyPoints.description: We explain what the Department of Education and Knowledge does and point to the Ministry for equivalency. IB Gram holds no accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, operates no UAE office, and claims none of it.

faqs.question: Why does my child's Al Ain school not offer Higher Level Physics?
faqs.answer: Almost always because the cohort is too thin to justify it. A Higher Level course needs a teacher with subject depth, a timetable column and enough students to make both viable. In a year group of sixty, a subject chosen by three students is very difficult to run. That is arithmetic rather than a judgement about your child, and the response is to ask early: request next year's option blocks in November when they are being drafted, and find out how many other students have the same problem.

faqs.question: What are option blocks and why do they limit my child's choices?
faqs.answer: They are the mechanism by which a school fits a wide curriculum into a narrow timetable. Subjects are grouped into columns and a student takes one from each column, so two subjects your child needs can sit in the same column with no way around it. In a smaller school the columns are tighter and the collisions more frequent. Schools can sometimes move a subject between columns if enough students are affected, which is why raising it with numbers behind you is more effective than raising it alone.

faqs.question: Is the internal assessment worth less at Standard Level than at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: No, and this surprises most families. In the current science guides the investigation carries 20% of the final grade at both Standard and Higher Level, and the Mathematics exploration carries 20% at both levels too. What differs between the levels is the taught content, the number of papers and the depth of the extension material. The practical consequence is that coursework supervision is equally valuable whichever level your child is taking, which is useful to know when a budget is limited.

faqs.question: Can my child sit a subject the school does not teach?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, as a private candidate through a centre that accepts external entries, and the order of the checks matters more than anything else. First establish what practical or internal assessment components the subject requires and whether a centre will administer them for an external candidate, because that can close the route outright in the sciences. Then confirm the entry deadline, which sits months before the papers. Only then count back the teaching time needed. Doing it in the other order produces a well-taught student with no valid entry.

faqs.question: How early do examination entries close for an external candidate?
faqs.answer: Months before the papers, and the two live sessions in the UAE are June and November. For the Cambridge June series, entries close in the spring, several months ahead of the first paper; the exact deadline belongs to your centre and is confirmed on the statement of entry the school issues, so ask the exams officer for it in writing rather than working from a date found online. Pearson Edexcel runs May and June plus November, with provisional timetables published in advance and its November 2026 window finishing on 19 November 2026. Pearson results give a sense of the lag at the other end: June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. A family that starts the conversation in the term the exam falls in has usually left it too late to enter at all.

faqs.question: Can a motivated student teach themselves an IB subject?
faqs.answer: In some subjects and for some students, yes. It works best in content-led courses examined on written papers alone, such as Business or Standard Level Economics. It works badly in the sciences, where practical and internal assessment requirements need laboratory access and supervision, and in languages, where speaking components need a trained interlocutor. The student it suits is not simply the able one but the one who can hold a schedule for eighteen months without external deadlines, which most sixteen-year-olds cannot.

faqs.question: Should my child take a subject at Standard Level instead of switching schools?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and the way to decide is to read the real entry requirements for two or three target university courses rather than to reason about ambition. A course that asks for Higher Level Chemistry by name will not accept Standard Level, and no achievement at the lower level substitutes for it. A course asking for a science at either level opens up much wider options. That check turns a difficult conversation into a factual one, and it takes about twenty minutes.

faqs.question: Does a small Diploma cohort help or hurt my child?
faqs.answer: Both, in different places. A small cohort means a teacher who knows every student, coursework drafts read more than once, and pastoral attention that is genuinely different in kind from a large school. It also means a narrower Higher Level menu, tighter option blocks, and teachers carrying several courses at once, which affects depth at the top end rather than competence. Families moving from a large city school often find the relationship better and the subject menu worse, which is a real trade.

faqs.question: Why do several students in my child's class have the same internal assessment topic?
faqs.answer: Because small cohorts converge. When six students choose a topic and the obvious local options are limited, several arrive at the same idea independently. It is not malpractice, but it does cap the personal engagement and originality marks across the group. The fix is an earlier and wider topic conversation, and Al Ain offers genuinely distinctive starting points: local water and soil conditions, the agricultural economy, heat effects on materials, the city's own transport and tourism data.

faqs.question: Are there enough Higher Level tutors living in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: For the core IGCSE subjects, yes. For Higher Level Diploma sciences, Higher Level Mathematics, Higher Level Economics or Computer Science, the honest answer is that the number of people resident in the city who teach that syllabus to that level is very small, and in a few subjects it is zero. That is the clearest argument for online delivery in this particular city, and it is an argument about availability rather than convenience: the relevant pool is everyone who teaches the syllabus, not everyone who can drive to your door.

faqs.question: Do tutors visit homes in Al Jimi?
faqs.answer: Not through us. IB Gram does not make home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India, and Al Ain lessons run one-to-one over live video. Independent in-home tutors do work in the city, and for core IGCSE subjects they are a reasonable option at market rates of roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour against AED 150 to AED 300 online. For a thinly covered Higher Level subject, choosing from the handful of local people who teach it is not really choosing.

faqs.question: What should we keep going in Year 9 to protect Diploma options?
faqs.answer: A second science and a language, even without much enthusiasm for either. In a school with a thin Higher Level menu, the subject dropped at fourteen closes a door at sixteen, and the family usually cannot see which door at the time. Keeping both running for one extra year costs some effort and buys real insurance against an option block that has not been drafted yet. It is the cheapest protective decision available at that stage.

faqs.question: Which authority regulates private schools in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: The Department of Education and Knowledge, because Al Ain is part of the Abu Dhabi emirate. It supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection ratings. Dubai schools fall under a different authority, Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah have their own, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Equivalency of certificates goes to the Ministry of Education wherever the school sits.

faqs.question: Can a tutor teach a whole subject rather than top up what the school does?
faqs.answer: Yes, where a subject does not run at all and the student intends to sit it. That is a different commitment from supplementary support: the syllabus is mapped and sequenced against the official specification, work is set and recorded weekly, and the course should begin when the cohort's does rather than part-way through. Before any teaching starts we confirm the practical and internal assessment requirements and the entry arrangements, because a course with no viable entry is not worth teaching.

faqs.question: What if there is no tutor available for the subject we need?
faqs.answer: We say so, rather than offering a near-equivalent. Coverage for the rarer Diploma subjects and languages is genuinely thin in this time zone, Higher Level Computer Science among them, and some combinations may have no match at all. The alternatives we can offer are a different hour, a tutor working from another time zone, or a component-focused block rather than a full course. Putting a generalist in front of a Higher Level paper is the one thing we will not do.

al-ain/al-jimi.closingHeading: Ask for the timetable, not the prospectus
al-ain/al-jimi.closingBody: The most useful document available to an Al Jimi family costs one email: next year's option blocks, plus the list of subjects actually running at each level this year. A prospectus says what a school can offer; a timetable says what runs, and in a smaller school the timetable quietly decides which university routes stay open to your child. Read it in November rather than July, check the real entry requirements for two target courses, and send us the most recent marked work. From there we can say honestly whether Higher Level is the right choice, whether a subject can be taken outside school, and who actually teaches it, delivered one-to-one over live video.

al-ain/al-khabisi.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the requests that arrive from central Al Ain: Year 10 and 11 mathematics and science for students who have just changed board, Diploma mathematics and sciences, and English writing for students strong in content and weak on extended answers.

intro.heading: Four kinds of household, four different first questions
paragraphs: Al Khabisi sits in the middle of Al Ain, within walking distance of the city's main retail cluster and a short drive from the oldest group of private schools in the emirate's inland city. It is one of the more mixed districts in Al Ain: walled family villas on the quieter streets, apartment blocks on the main roads, and a population that includes long-settled Emirati households, Indian and Pakistani families working in the city's hospitals, schools and businesses, Arab expatriate families, and a rotating group of new arrivals who were in another country last August.

That mix matters because it means there is no single Al Khabisi question. A page that answers one of these households answers none of the others. The family whose child has just moved from a CBSE school into Year 10 IGCSE has a content-sequencing problem. The Emirati family choosing between an Arabic first-language stream and an additional-language stream has a placement problem that will decide which Diploma courses are open in three years. The Diploma parent has a coursework-deadline problem. The new arrival has a map problem.

What they share is a city with a small private-school set. Al Ain has far fewer campuses than the capital, which has two consequences for every household on that list. Subject choice at sixteen is narrower than it would be in Abu Dhabi or Dubai, so a wanted combination sometimes does not exist locally. And when a child arrives mid-course from another system, there is often no parallel class to move them into, so the gap has to be closed around the timetable rather than inside it.

The most expensive mistakes in this district are made at transitions rather than inside a course. A student who was comfortable in a system that rewarded recall meets a system that rewards command terms and loses a grade before anyone diagnoses why. A student who has never written four hundred words of continuous argument meets an IGCSE English paper that requires it. Neither problem is about intelligence and both are fixable in a term, which is why identifying them early is the highest-value thing a parent can do.

This page is organised around that. It begins with who lives here and what each household asks, moves to a subject-by-subject transition map, covers what the Ministry of Education will actually require from a school leaver, puts the real cost of tutoring next to the fees already being paid, and ends with the limits on what a tutor may do with assessed work. All of it is written for a family who wants to make one decision well rather than read a brochure.

Delivery is one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE and nobody will be sent to an Al Khabisi address; that service exists only in India. The honest case for the online format in a city this size is set out in a comparison table rather than asserted, because the argument is about which specialist your child gets, not about which format sounds more attentive.
bullets: Four distinct household profiles generate four different first questions
Transitions, not courses, are where most lost grades in this district begin
