al-ain/al-khabisi.programmesIntro: Central Al Ain households are spread across the British route, the Indian boards, the IB continuum and the American diploma. These are the four programmes that generate enquiries from Al Khabisi, described by what each one demands of a student who has just arrived in it.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson International GCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined by terminal papers, with several subjects tiered into Core and Extended or Foundation and Higher. Marks are allocated against command terms: describe, explain, compare and evaluate each want a different shape of answer, and a student who writes everything as a description caps out well below their understanding.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain this is the programme most often joined mid-stream, because families arriving in the city rarely arrive in September. A student entering Year 10 from a different system needs the first term spent on answer structure and on the two or three topics their previous syllabus never covered, rather than on general revision.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at two levels, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internal assessment is marked by the teacher against published criteria and moderated externally. The programme rewards students who can sustain independent work over months, which is a different skill from performing well in a weekly test cycle.
programmes.countryNote: The number of Diploma campuses in Al Ain is small, so a student wanting a particular Higher Level combination may find it offered in a single set at a single school. That is worth checking in Year 10 rather than discovering during option choices, because the alternative is a campus change or a different programme entirely.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, scored out of eight and converted to a 1-7 grade. Criteria are skills rather than topics, so a report describing criterion D as a three is telling you about reflection or evaluation, not about a missed chapter. The Personal Project closes the programme.
programmes.countryNote: Students moving from an Indian or national-curriculum middle school into MYP in Al Ain usually find the content familiar and the assessment language foreign. Translating a criterion-based report into something a parent can act on is a short piece of work and is where the first useful tutoring hour often goes.

programmes.name: American diploma with Advanced Placement
programmes.description: A credit-based high-school diploma with grade point average carrying weight across four years, and optional Advanced Placement examinations for subject depth. Continuous assessment means a weak quarter is permanently on the transcript, which changes the tutoring calculus: the work is to protect the average month by month rather than to peak in May.
programmes.countryNote: Families on this route in Al Ain are usually planning towards universities that read a transcript rather than a single examination result, and the Ministry's own equivalency route for American curricula has specific test requirements. Those are set out in the equivalency table further down this page.

al-ain/al-khabisi.subjectsIntro: Requests from Al Khabisi concentrate on the subjects where a change of system shows up fastest: quantitative subjects where the method differs, and written subjects where the expected length and register differ. Each entry below names the assessment and the usual point of loss.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580)
subjects.description: Extended entry assumes fluent algebraic manipulation and a willingness to show structured working. Students arriving from systems that rewarded a correct final answer lose method marks steadily. The first repair is always written layout, before any new topic is introduced.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Same subject, different paper architecture and a different formula sheet. Higher tier questions escalate within a single question rather than across the paper, so students who stop at the first unfamiliar part leave accessible marks behind in every section.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: Taken alongside the main mathematics course by students heading for a quantitative Diploma or A Level route. Calculus and trigonometric identities arrive early and without ceremony, and it is the clearest signal of readiness for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: Electricity and the practical component take most of the lost marks. The alternative-to-practical paper is coachable without a laboratory, because what it tests is reading apparatus diagrams, spotting a controlled variable and handling a real result table.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 and Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and qualitative analysis carry the paper. Students who can define a term but cannot lay out a calculation lose marks in both papers, and structured working closes that gap faster than additional content revision does.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 and Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: The volume subject. Reading notes repeatedly feels productive and changes nothing; answering past questions and comparing against the mark scheme line by line changes a grade. Diagram labelling and experimental design are the two reliably underpractised areas.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 and 0511)
subjects.description: The paper many transferring students are placed into and then outgrow, or are not placed into and should be. Reading comprehension technique and the structured writing task are both trainable, and placement is worth questioning in the first term rather than the last.

subjects.name: English First Language (Cambridge 0500)
subjects.description: Directed writing and composition at a register most transferring students have not been asked for before. The gap is rarely vocabulary; it is paragraph architecture and the ability to hold an argument for four hundred words without restating the question.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The Diploma route for students who will study a quantitative subject at university. Proof and calculus dominate, and the exploration needs a topic the student can genuinely model rather than one that sounds impressive in a title.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and heavy calculator use. The failure pattern is a correct hypothesis test followed by an interpretation that does not answer the question asked, which costs marks in every paper and is fixable in a few sessions.

subjects.name: Chemistry and Physics at Diploma level
subjects.description: Where a small Al Ain cohort depends on one teacher carrying both levels. The Higher Level extension material and the internal assessment are the two places a second explanation is most often needed, and neither is available twice at most campuses.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first and as an additional language
subjects.description: Two distinct courses under one name. Placement is made by the school and is worth questioning: a child who speaks dialect at home but has never studied formal Standard Arabic can be misplaced in either direction, and the consequence appears three years later at option choices.

al-ain/al-khabisi.regionsIntro: Al Khabisi families consider campuses across the whole city, and enquiries from here regularly mention the districts below. What each one means in practice is a different journey, a different school cluster and a different set of local requests.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: The adjacent district and the densest school concentration in Al Ain. Most Al Khabisi children attend a campus here or pass through it, and it is the cluster families compare against when deciding whether a move is worth it.

regions.name: Al Towayya
regions.note: North of here, beside the city's major hospital campus. Households there frequently include a parent on a clinical rota, which is why the scheduling conversation with those families looks different from this one.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: West towards the oasis, older and quieter, with large plots and a long-settled population. Requests from there lean towards Diploma work rather than mid-course transitions, because families have usually been in the same school for years.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji
regions.note: West of the centre, with a mix of established campuses and a high share of bilingual households. Arabic stream placement questions arrive from there more often than from anywhere else in the city.

regions.name: Hili

sections.heading: Who lives in Al Khabisi, and what each household asks first
paragraphs: Enquiries from this part of Al Ain sort themselves into four recognisable groups, and the useful first move is working out which one you are in, because the right answer differs completely between them. The groups are not about income or nationality so much as about where the child was educated eighteen months ago and what the family is planning towards. A tutoring plan that ignores that distinction will be generic, and a generic plan on a narrow timetable wastes the one hour a week a family has.

The first group arrived recently from an Indian board, usually CBSE or ICSE, and has a child in Year 9 or 10. Their child is often ahead on mathematical content and behind on how marks are awarded. The second group is long-settled, frequently Emirati or Arab expatriate, and is deciding between Arabic streams or weighing a bilingual load against an international timetable. The third has a Diploma student and a coursework calendar that nobody at home has seen before. The fourth moved to the city this year and is still learning which campus offers what.

Each group also has a characteristic mistake. The transferring family buys general mathematics tutoring when the problem is answer structure. The long-settled family accepts a stream placement made in Year 7 and discovers in Year 11 that it closed a Diploma option. The Diploma family starts coursework support in the month the draft is due. The new arrival chooses a campus on reputation and finds out in Year 10 that the subject combination they wanted is not timetabled there.

The table below sets out the four profiles with the question each one actually asks and the first thing that helps. It is deliberately blunt, because the purpose is to let a parent recognise themselves in a row and skip the three sections that do not apply to them. Al Ain is a small enough city that most families in this district will recognise at least one neighbour in each of the four rows.

sections.heading: The transition map, subject by subject
paragraphs: Changing education system is not a single event with a single gap; it is a different gap in every subject. A student moving from CBSE into Cambridge IGCSE may be two terms ahead in algebra and two terms behind in extended writing. A student moving from an American middle school into MYP may find the content lighter and the independent-work expectation much heavier. Treating all of it as one problem called settling in is how a term gets lost.

The table that follows breaks the common moves into subject-level work with an honest estimate of how long each takes. Those estimates assume one focused hour a week and a student who does the practice between sessions. They are not promises, and no tutor can commit to a timescale for another person's learning, but they are the ranges that actually recur. A family that knows the realistic figure makes better decisions than one told everything takes six weeks.

Two patterns are worth naming because they come up in almost every transition from this district. First, the recall-to-command-term shift: systems that reward reproducing a method well do not prepare a student for a paper that asks them to evaluate, compare or justify, and that shift accounts for a large part of the first term's lost marks. Second, extended writing stamina: a student who has never been asked for four hundred continuous words of argument cannot produce them because they have not practised, not because they cannot think.

The practical approach is to run a transition as a defined block rather than as an open-ended arrangement. Identify the gaps, work through them, hand over a written summary and stop. If a standing weekly arrangement is still useful afterwards, that is a separate decision made with evidence. Blocks that never end are how families in a small city find themselves paying for a second school.

sections.heading: Arriving from an Indian board into Year 10
paragraphs: This is the most common transition in central Al Ain and the most commonly misdiagnosed. A student arrives from a CBSE or ICSE school with genuinely strong mathematical content, sits their first IGCSE assessment and comes back with a grade that does not match what the family knows their child can do. The conclusion drawn at home is usually that the new school is harder or the teaching is worse. Neither is typically true. The marks are being awarded for something the student has not been trained to do.

Indian boards reward accurate reproduction of a method and a correct final answer. Cambridge and Pearson papers award marks against command terms and against visible method. A question that says explain is asking for a causal chain and will not accept a description. A question worth four marks expects roughly four distinct creditable points, and a student writing a dense paragraph that contains two of them earns two. None of this is hidden; it is in the mark scheme, and almost no transferring student has read one.

The second half of the problem is written English, and it is not a vocabulary issue. Students arriving from Indian-board schools in Al Ain are frequently fluent and accurate, and then struggle with a composition that needs a sustained argument across several paragraphs with a deliberate structure. That is a practised skill. Six to eight weeks of weekly writing with marked feedback usually moves it a grade, and it also improves the extended-response marks in science, which nobody expects.

The third element is specific uncovered content. Every pair of syllabuses has two or three topics the previous one treated lightly or not at all, and they are predictable once the two specifications are compared. Finding them takes a tutor twenty minutes with both documents. Discovering them in a mock examination takes a term and costs a grade, which is the entire argument for doing the comparison in the first fortnight.

sections.heading: The bilingual household and the stream decision nobody revisits
paragraphs: Private schools in the UAE are not required to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. For a bilingual household in Al Khabisi that means a child carries subjects belonging to no international syllabus alongside the international course, and that the school places them into a stream for those subjects, usually in primary or early secondary.

The decision that matters is which Arabic stream. Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language are different courses with different expectations and different end points. A child who speaks dialect confidently at home but has never studied formal Standard Arabic can be placed in the first-language stream and spend five years struggling with literary register. A child placed in the additional-language stream because the family moved mid-primary can coast and then find that Arabic A at Diploma level is not realistically available to them.

The reason this persists is that nobody revisits it. The placement was made by a teacher who no longer teaches the child, in a year the family barely remembers, and no event in the school calendar triggers a review. The useful intervention is one consultation in Year 8 or 9 that looks at what the child can actually produce in writing, compares it against both streams' expectations and produces something a parent can take to the school. That is an hour, not a course.

The constraint on tutoring in these subjects should also be stated. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is not permitted. So support in Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies works on the school's own material: vocabulary, written structure, reading technique and assessment format. A tutor offering an alternative syllabus for these subjects is offering something a parent should turn down.

sections.heading: What the Ministry will require from an Al Ain school leaver
paragraphs: Equivalency is the step families in this district discover last and should plan for first. It is the Ministry of Education process that recognises a foreign school certificate for use in the UAE, and it has specific, published subject and grade requirements that depend on which curriculum your child followed. It is not something a tutoring platform performs, guarantees or accelerates, and no provider should imply otherwise. What a family can do is make sure the subjects taken satisfy it.

For the British track the requirement is concrete. A student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and must show either one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects, which regularly surprises families who assumed they counted.

For the American track the requirement is test-based. English proficiency is satisfied by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL internet-based test, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT. Mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Mathematics test before applying. Those are the published figures, and a family on this route should be planning the test calendar in Grade 11 rather than after graduation.

For the Diploma there is no figure on this page, deliberately. No IB points threshold for equivalency has been read on the Ministry's own site, and one competitor already publishes an incorrect subject count for the British track. Rather than inherit somebody else's error, this page says what is sourced and sends you to the authority for the rest. Verify your own child's position with the Ministry or the emirate's attestation channel before relying on anything written by a tutoring company, including this.

sections.heading: Tutoring cost in context, next to the fees you already pay
paragraphs: Most pages in this market either publish no price or publish one in US dollars. The figures below are in AED and attributed to whoever put them in public. They are market rates rather than an IB Gram price list, and your own quote should come from a consultation. Published online bands run from AED 45 to 65 at EdFlik and AED 33 to 52 at Tutopiya, AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB at Unitors, AED 270 at TutorChase, AED 200 to 450 and above in the Bestimate survey, and AED 650 at BartyED.

Those numbers mean little on their own, which is why the table below sets them against the other education costs an Al Khabisi household already carries. Read that way, the question stops being whether tutoring is affordable and becomes which single hour is worth buying. One Higher Level subject taught by a specialist for a year costs a fraction of a term's fees, and sampling four subjects lightly for the same money reliably achieves less.

Two cautions on quotes. First, ask whether a rate is per hour or per session, because a sixty-minute hour and a forty-five minute session at the same price are different products, and this market contains both. Second, ask whether the figure includes value added tax, because that is a question for the provider rather than for a web page; the tax treatment of tuition is a matter for the Federal Tax Authority and should not be asserted by a tutoring company.

The monthly package patterns seen in this market are worth knowing because they reveal how providers think about volume. Around AED 799 a month buys eight online sessions at some providers, and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month buys four two-hour home visits. The per-hour arithmetic on those is not always better than the hourly rate, and a package that locks a family into a frequency they cannot sustain is a worse deal than a slightly higher hourly figure.

sections.heading: Online lessons from central Al Ain, and the in-home alternative
paragraphs: A family in Al Khabisi searching for a home tutor is asking a reasonable question. In-home tutoring in Al Ain is advertised, and market rates sit between roughly AED 180 and AED 500 an hour with travel built into the figure. What it delivers is an adult in the room, which some younger children genuinely need. What it cannot deliver in a city this size is choice, because the list of people who can reach a central Al Ain street at four in the afternoon and still get home is short.

That is the honest argument for the online format here, and it is a supply argument rather than a technology one. Al Ain has a much smaller private-school set than the capital, so there are fewer resident teachers of any given subject, and the rarer the subject the shorter the list becomes. For Core IGCSE Mathematics the local pool is adequate. For Higher Level Chemistry or a less common Diploma language it may be one person, or nobody, and no amount of searching changes that.

IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE and will not send anyone to an Al Khabisi address; home visiting exists only as an India service. UAE lessons are one-to-one over live video, with the student sharing their own exercise book or screen and writing while the tutor watches. The annotated work stays available afterwards, which gives a parent something to look at rather than a verbal report at the door.

Neither format is universally right. A Year 2 child who will not engage with a screen needs a person in the room. A Year 11 student working through a past paper, or a Diploma student whose data file and write-up need to be visible at the same time, is better served online. The table compares them on the dimensions that genuinely differ in this city rather than on the ones a brochure prefers.

sections.heading: What a tutor may do, and what this platform does not claim
paragraphs: A tutor may teach the skills a piece of assessed work needs, explain what each criterion is asking for, question a draft the student has written and point at a section that does not yet answer its own research question. A tutor may not write, draft, complete or edit to completion an internal assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or a Personal Project. The practical test is whether comments arrive in conversation or inside the document, and only the first of those is acceptable.

This is worth stating in blunt terms because one page competing for these searches sells completed internal assessments. The student is the person who carries a malpractice finding, and a finding at Diploma level can cost the whole diploma. No saving in time is worth that exposure, and any provider willing to cross the line on coursework should be assumed to be relaxed about other things too.

Materials follow the same rule. Official syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables and subject guides belong to the awarding bodies, and a tutor cites and links the official source rather than redistributing it. Working from whatever your child's school has legitimately issued is both legal and more useful, because it is the version the school's own assessments are built from.

On status, the position is simple and worth putting in writing. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the labour ministry, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. It runs no office, centre or branch anywhere in the UAE. It publishes no self-assessed rating, no success percentage and no student headcount, because a statistic without a sample, a date and a method is not information. Where this page states a figure, it names who published it.

process.title: Say which of the four household profiles fits you
process.description: A recent arrival from an Indian board, a bilingual household weighing stream placement, a Diploma family facing coursework deadlines, or a family new to the city choosing a campus. Naming the profile skips three conversations and gets to the one that matters, because the right first action differs completely between them.

process.title: Bring the last two school assessments and the specification
process.description: The most recent marked work shows where marks are being lost, and the specification or syllabus code shows what the paper will actually ask. With both, a transition gap can be identified in one session. With neither, the first month is spent guessing, which is the most expensive way to begin.

process.title: Define the work as a block or as a standing arrangement
process.description: A transition is a block with an end point and a written handover. A thinly staffed Higher Level subject is a standing weekly arrangement. Deciding which one you are buying prevents the common outcome in a small city, where a six-week fix quietly becomes a second school fee.

process.title: Check the options and streams before the choices close
process.description: Year 10 option forms decide which Diploma and A Level combinations are reachable, and in Al Ain some combinations are not offered locally at all. An Arabic or English stream placement made years earlier may also need revisiting. Both reviews are an hour of work and both have a three-year shadow.

process.title: Review against the school's own marks, not a feeling
process.description: Progress is measured against your child's next school assessment and, in an examination year, against timed papers marked to the published scheme. If the review shows the school is already covering the gap, the arrangement should end. That is a better outcome than an arrangement nobody can evaluate.

whyPoints.title: The first question is which household you are
whyPoints.description: Four profiles live within a few streets in Al Khabisi and each needs a different first action. Sorting that before anything is booked is why a transition family gets structure work rather than general revision, and why a Diploma family gets a deadline map rather than weekly content coverage they do not need.

whyPoints.title: Transitions are scoped as blocks with an end
whyPoints.description: A change of education system produces a different gap in every subject, and each of those gaps has a realistic timescale. Work is scoped against those timescales with a written handover at the finish, because an open-ended arrangement in a small city is how families end up paying twice for the same year.

whyPoints.title: Equivalency rules are quoted, not paraphrased
whyPoints.description: The five-subject British-track requirement, the grade floor and the exclusion of Arabic and Islamic education are published requirements and are stated here as such. The IB points figure is absent because no sourced version exists, and one ranking competitor already publishes a wrong subject count. Inheriting that error is not an option.

whyPoints.title: Costs shown next to the costs you already carry
whyPoints.description: An hourly rate in isolation tells a parent nothing. Setting the published market bands against school fees and against the alternative uses of the same money turns the question into which single hour is worth buying, which is the question that actually improves a grade.

whyPoints.title: Stream and option placements get reviewed
whyPoints.description: A decision made in Year 7 by a teacher who no longer teaches your child still governs which Diploma courses are available in Year 12, and nothing in the school calendar triggers a review. One consultation that compares what the child can produce against both streams' expectations is among the cheapest useful hours available.

whyPoints.title: No claimed approvals and no invented numbers
whyPoints.description: IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform with no regulator or awarding-body approval, no UAE premises, and no self-published rating or success statistic. Every figure on this page carries the name of whoever published it, and where nothing is sourced the page says so instead of estimating.

faqs.question: My child moved from CBSE to IGCSE and the grades dropped. What is going on?
faqs.answer: Almost always mark allocation rather than ability or teaching. Indian boards reward accurate reproduction of a method and a correct final answer; Cambridge and Pearson award marks against command terms and visible method. A question that says explain wants a causal chain and will not accept a description, and a four-mark question expects roughly four creditable points. Your child is probably producing two of them inside a dense paragraph. Read one mark scheme together in the first month, and compare the two specifications to find the two or three topics the previous syllabus skipped.

faqs.question: How long does it take to close the gap after changing education system?
faqs.answer: It differs by subject, which is why treating it as one problem wastes a term. With one focused hour a week and practice in between, extended writing after an Indian-board move usually takes eight to twelve weeks, mathematics and science answer structure four to six, and a move from MYP into the Diploma six to ten with the work front-loaded into the first term of Year 12. Those are recurring ranges, not promises, and no tutor can commit to a timescale for somebody else's learning. Knowing the realistic figure stops a family expecting six weeks to fix everything.

faqs.question: Which Arabic stream should my child be in, and who decides?
faqs.answer: The school decides, usually in primary or early secondary, and almost nothing in the calendar triggers a review afterwards. Arabic as a first language assesses literary analysis in formal Standard Arabic; Arabic as an additional language assesses prescribed themes, productive writing and a conversation. A child who speaks dialect at home but never studied formal Arabic can be misplaced into the first-language stream and struggle for years. A child misplaced the other way can lose the option of Arabic A at Diploma level. One consultation in Year 8 or 9 that looks at written output is the fix.

faqs.question: Why are the mandatory UAE subjects taught separately from my child's main curriculum?
faqs.answer: Because private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That federal baseline sits underneath every emirate's requirement, which is why a Diploma or IGCSE student in Al Ain also carries subjects belonging to no international syllabus. Tutoring in those subjects is limited to the school's own material, because the use of different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is not allowed, so a tutor offering an alternative syllabus should be declined.

faqs.question: What exactly does the Ministry require from a British-curriculum leaver?
faqs.answer: The published requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. One ranking competitor states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the published rule. Verify your own child's position with the Ministry rather than relying on any tutoring company, including this page.

faqs.question: What does the Ministry ask of a student on the American diploma route?
faqs.answer: Test scores rather than subject counts. English proficiency is satisfied by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL internet-based test, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT. Mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Mathematics test before applying. That means the test calendar belongs in Grade 11, not after graduation, because a retake needs a sitting date and sittings are not weekly. Equivalency is a Ministry process that no tutoring platform performs, accelerates or guarantees.

faqs.question: Why does this page not give an IB points figure for equivalency?
faqs.answer: Because no sourced figure exists for it here. The British-track numbers were read from a published report of the Ministry's clarification, but no IB points threshold has been read on the Ministry's own site, so publishing one would mean passing on somebody else's unverified number across hundreds of pages. A competitor in this market already publishes an incorrect subject count for the British track, which is what inheriting unverified figures looks like. Ask the Ministry or the emirate's attestation channel directly, and treat any tutoring page that quotes an IB threshold with caution.

faqs.question: Can one tutor teach two children on different boards in the same evening?
faqs.answer: Possible, rarely advisable. A tutor who genuinely knows Cambridge 0580 Extended and Pearson 4MA1 Higher well enough to teach both is unusual, and a tutor who claims six subjects across four year groups is usually a generalist. Separate specialists with staggered slots costs the same per hour and produces better results, and it avoids the sibling dynamic where one child performs for the other. What can be shared is the review: a single written progress summary covering both children, read against each school's own assessments.

faqs.question: Should we book several subjects at once or start with one?
faqs.answer: Start with one, in nearly every case. Families who book three subjects at once spread the hours thin, the child attends six appointments a fortnight and nothing improves enough to be visible. One subject taught properly by a specialist moves a grade, and the study habits it builds often lift the others at no extra cost. The exception is the final two terms before a series, when a second subject can be added as timed-paper practice rather than as teaching. Choose the subject where the gap is widest and the consequences are largest.

faqs.question: Is the quoted rate per hour or per session, and does it include tax?
faqs.answer: Ask both questions explicitly, because this market contains providers doing it both ways. A sixty-minute hour and a forty-five-minute session at the same price are different products, and the difference across a year is substantial. On tax, the treatment of tuition fees is a matter for the Federal Tax Authority and not something a tutoring page should assert. What you can reasonably ask any provider is whether their own quoted figure is inclusive, and to have the answer in writing before the first payment.

faqs.question: Should an Al Ain family take a monthly bundle or pay per session?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the arithmetic is worth doing rather than assuming. Patterns advertised in this market include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions, and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour home visits. Divide by the hours and compare against the published hourly bands of AED 150 to 300 for a qualified online tutor. A package is only good value if the frequency it assumes is one your household can actually sustain through an examination term, including the weeks when school assessments take over.

faqs.question: How does a small city limit my child's subject choices at sixteen?
faqs.answer: Al Ain has far fewer private campuses than the capital, so a particular Higher Level or A Level combination may be timetabled in a single set at a single school, or not offered locally at all. That is worth checking in Year 10 while option forms are still open, rather than discovering it during subject selection. The realistic responses are choosing a different combination, changing campus, or in some cases entering a subject as a private candidate through an approved centre. All three are manageable; none is manageable in June.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send tutors to houses in Al Khabisi?
faqs.answer: No. No home visits are sold anywhere in the UAE, and nobody will be sent to an address in this district; that service exists only in India. Every UAE lesson runs one-to-one over live video, with the student sharing their own exercise book or screen and the annotated work remaining available afterwards. In a city the size of Al Ain the trade is usually favourable: instead of choosing from whoever can reach a central street at four in the afternoon, you choose a tutor by subject, level and board, which for a rare Higher Level subject may be the difference between someone and nobody.

faqs.question: What should a first session with a transferring student actually cover?
faqs.answer: Three things, in order. A look at the last two pieces of marked school work to see where marks are being deducted and for what. A comparison of the old and new specifications to identify the two or three genuinely uncovered topics. And one short piece of work under examination conditions, marked against the published scheme, so the student sees the difference between what they wrote and what earned credit. The output is three written priorities and a realistic timescale, not a verdict on the child.

faqs.question: Can a tutor write part of my child's internal assessment if we are short of time?
faqs.answer: No, and a provider willing to do it is selling your child a problem. A tutor may teach the skills the task needs, explain what each criterion asks for, question a draft the student has written and identify a section that does not answer its own research question. Writing, drafting, completing or editing to completion is malpractice, and the student is the person who carries the finding. The practical test is where comments live: spoken and questioned is acceptable, typed into the document is not, however it is described on the invoice.

faqs.question: What approvals does IB Gram actually hold?
faqs.answer: None, and that is stated deliberately rather than buried. IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform with no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the labour ministry, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. It operates no office, centre or branch in the UAE. It publishes no self-assessed rating, no success percentage and no student headcount, because a figure without a sample, a date and a method is not information. Any provider claiming regulator approval for tutoring should be asked to produce the permit number.

al-ain/al-khabisi.closingHeading: Start by naming the move, not the subject
al-ain/al-khabisi.closingBody: The quickest way to a useful answer from Al Khabisi is to tell us what changed: a new board, a new country, a new programme, or a coursework calendar nobody at home has seen before. Add the last two pieces of marked school work and the syllabus code, and we can usually identify the actual gap in one session rather than three. If the honest conclusion is that your child's school is already covering it, we will tell you that and stop. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, no home visits are sold in the UAE, and IB Gram holds no regulator approval of any kind. The first conversation is free and ends with a written next step.

al-ain/al-maqam.tutorsIntro: The tutors here work on assessed components rather than on general content coverage: internal assessment design in the sciences and mathematics, Extended Essay process coaching, Theory of Knowledge argument structure, and the written and practical components at IGCSE.

intro.heading: The parts of the course with no lesson attached
paragraphs: Al Maqam lies on the southern side of Al Ain, past the oasis belt, on the road out towards the mountain and with the main university campus close at hand. It is a district of larger plots and newer housing where families have often chosen space and a quieter street over being five minutes from a school gate. Children travel into the city's central school cluster, and older siblings frequently study at the university nearby, which makes this one of the few districts where a Diploma student has an undergraduate in the house.

The request that arrives from here more than any other concerns the assessed work that sits outside the taught timetable. Every programme has it. The Diploma has internal assessments in every subject, the Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay and exhibition, the Group 4 project and CAS. The Middle Years Programme ends with the Personal Project. IGCSE has coursework or practical components in several subjects. All of it is marked, none of it has a weekly lesson, and most of it is supervised by a teacher carrying twenty other supervisees.

That structure produces a very particular failure. A student who is organised, well taught and perfectly capable arrives at the week a draft is due with nothing written, because nothing in their week ever said write it. The school set a deadline in October, the student noted it, and then eight weeks of lessons, tests and homework happened in between with no scheduled hour for the one thing that had no lesson. This is not a motivation problem. It is a calendar problem with a predictable shape.

The second failure is about criteria. Internal assessments are marked against published criteria, labelled by letter, each carrying a defined number of marks. Students routinely produce work that is strong on the criterion they find interesting and silent on two others, then cannot understand why the mark is mid-range. Reading the criteria with the marks attached, before starting, changes the piece that gets written. It is the cheapest single intervention available on the Diploma and almost nobody does it early.

The third is limits. Every written component has a word or page limit, and exceeding it has consequences that vary by component and by subject. Students write long because they are anxious, and then cut badly under time pressure, losing the structural clarity the criteria reward. Knowing the limit at the planning stage produces a different plan, and a different plan produces a better piece of work than any amount of editing at the end.

Everything described here is delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE and nobody will be sent to an Al Maqam address; that service exists only in India. On coursework the format is an advantage rather than a compromise, because a draft, a data file and a criteria sheet can all be on screen at once, which is awkward at a dining table and impossible across a desk.

al-ain/al-maqam.programmesIntro: Al Maqam households sit mainly on the IB continuum and the British route. Each programme is described below by its assessed components rather than by its philosophy, because the components are what this page is about.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level, each with an internal assessment marked by the teacher against published criteria and externally moderated. Alongside them sit three core components: the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge, and CAS. Internal assessment generally carries twenty to thirty per cent of a subject grade, which makes it the largest single piece of work most students have ever been marked on.
programmes.countryNote: A Diploma student travelling into central Al Ain from Al Maqam has a long day, and the core components compete with that journey for the same evenings. Schools here set internal deadlines that tend to cluster, so two internal assessments and an Extended Essay draft can land in the same fortnight unless the year has been mapped backwards from those dates.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, converted to a 1-7 grade. The programme closes with the Personal Project, an extended independent piece with its own criteria and its own supervisor. It is the first time most students manage a long deadline themselves, and it is excellent preparation for the Extended Essay if it is taken seriously.
programmes.countryNote: The Personal Project is the component Al Ain families most often underestimate, partly because it carries no examination and partly because it falls in a year already crowded with other things. Students who treat it as a rehearsal for Diploma coursework arrive in Year 12 with a genuine advantage over those who did it in a fortnight.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson International GCSE
programmes.description: Mostly terminal papers, with practical or coursework components in several subjects and an alternative-to-practical route in the sciences where laboratory assessment is not taken. Each component has its own mark allocation and its own conventions, and the practical papers reward specific trained habits rather than general scientific ability.
programmes.countryNote: Which science route a school enters a student for matters a great deal and is often not explained to families. The alternative-to-practical paper tests reading apparatus, identifying variables and handling real result tables, all of which are coachable without laboratory access, and students in Al Ain frequently sit it without ever having practised one.

programmes.name: International AS and A Level
programmes.description: Papers carry nearly all the weight, with practical assessment in the sciences and coursework in a minority of subjects. The step from IGCSE is mainly in how much of an answer has to be constructed from scratch, and in how much independent reading is assumed rather than set.
programmes.countryNote: Some Al Ain campuses continue to A Level rather than the Diploma, which means fewer assessed components outside the timetable but a heavier reliance on the student's own question practice. Families switching between the two routes at sixteen should understand that the coursework load is genuinely different, not merely differently named.

al-ain/al-maqam.subjectsIntro: Requests from Al Maqam cluster around subjects whose internal assessment or practical component is doing the damage. Each entry below names the component and the recurring mistake rather than restating the syllabus.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The exploration is where this subject is won or lost outside the papers. Students choose a topic that sounds impressive and cannot be modelled with the mathematics they have, then produce a description of someone else's work. Topic selection is the session that matters most, and it belongs early.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Explorations here fail on data rather than on mathematics: a dataset too small for the test applied, or a statistical procedure used without its assumptions checked. Reflection and personal engagement are the criteria most often left thin, and both are easy to plan for in advance.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Internal assessments founder on investigations with no genuine independent variable, or on a research question too broad to answer in the available pages. Uncertainty handling and evaluation are the criteria that separate a mid mark from a high one, and both are coachable without a laboratory.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The common failure is an investigation that produces a straight line and no analysis worth writing about. Error propagation, graph choice and a genuine evaluation of method are where the marks are, and students who plan for those criteria design a better experiment in the first place.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Statistical treatment is the recurring weakness, together with research questions that cannot be answered with the equipment available. The Group 4 project also lands in this subject most often, and students rarely understand that it is assessed on collaboration and reflection.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Commentaries need articles chosen for the theory they permit, not for how interesting they are. Each commentary has a tight word limit, and students who choose a broad article write an overview that touches three concepts shallowly rather than one properly.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The research project requires a real organisation, genuine data and a defensible research question. Students pick an organisation they cannot get information from, discover it late, and then write around the gap. The feasibility check is a twenty-minute conversation that saves a term.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The individual oral is assessed on a global issue and two extracts, and it fails on structure rather than on insight. A student who arrives with observations and no argument will not reach the higher bands however well they read the texts.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: An essay on a prescribed title and an exhibition of three objects. The essay fails when it becomes an opinion piece, and the exhibition fails when the objects are chosen before the prompt is understood. Both are argument-structure problems rather than knowledge problems.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Four thousand words on a self-chosen research question in a chosen subject, with a supervisor and a reflection process. Most failures trace back to a question that is either unanswerable or answerable in four hundred words, and that is decided in the first fortnight.

subjects.name: Sciences at IGCSE (0620, 0625, 0610 and Pearson equivalents)
subjects.description: The practical or alternative-to-practical component carries real marks and is rarely practised. Reading apparatus diagrams, identifying variables and processing an untidy result table are trainable skills, and they are the difference between a predicted and an actual grade.

subjects.name: MYP Personal Project
subjects.description: Assessed on planning, applying skills and reflecting rather than on the product itself, which is the opposite of what most students assume. A beautiful outcome with no process evidence scores poorly, and a modest outcome with rigorous documentation scores well.

modes.title: A design session before anything is written
modes.description: The highest-value hour available on any assessed component, and the one families book last. The research question, the method, the feasibility and the criteria are examined before a word exists. A question that cannot be answered in the available pages is identified here rather than in March, when the only options left are bad ones.

Nothing is typed into the document and no replacement text is supplied. The student leaves knowing what to change and does the changing themselves, which is the only version of this that is permissible.

sections.heading: The components nobody timetables, and who is actually responsible
paragraphs: Start by writing down every piece of assessed work your child owes this year that does not have a weekly lesson attached to it. For a Diploma student in Year 12 that list usually runs to six internal assessments at various stages, an Extended Essay with a supervisor, a Theory of Knowledge essay and exhibition, a Group 4 project and a CAS record. For a Year 11 student in the Middle Years Programme it is the Personal Project plus subject criteria work. For an IGCSE student it is practical or coursework components in several subjects.

Then write down who is responsible for each one. The answer, in almost every case, is the student, with a supervisor who checks in. That is by design: these components exist to assess independent work, and a supervisor who did more would be compromising the assessment. The problem is that nobody states the arrangement plainly to the family, so parents assume the school is managing the schedule and the school assumes the student is.

The consequence is the single most common Diploma crisis in this city. A capable, organised student reaches the week a draft is due with nothing written, because at no point did their week contain an hour whose purpose was writing it. Lessons, homework, tests and a long bus journey filled every hour that was scheduled, and the only unscheduled work was the work that mattered most. Blaming the student for this is both unkind and inaccurate.

The table sets out the components with their supervision arrangements and the characteristic point of failure for each. It is worth going through it with your child and marking which rows are genuinely in hand. In practice the rows that are not in hand are usually the ones with the most distant deadline, which is exactly the wrong way round and entirely human.

sections.heading: Internal assessment criteria, by letter, with the marks attached
paragraphs: Internal assessments are not marked holistically. They are marked against criteria, each labelled by a letter, each carrying a defined number of marks, and each assessed independently of the others. A student can write something genuinely interesting and score in the middle because two criteria were barely addressed. This is the most consequential thing a Diploma student can understand about coursework, and almost none of them understands it before the first draft is returned.

The practical implication is that criteria should be read at the planning stage, with the mark allocations visible, and the plan should allocate space in proportion. If a criterion carrying a quarter of the marks concerns evaluation of method, then evaluation of method needs planned space rather than whatever is left at the end when the word count is nearly gone. Students do the opposite: they write the parts they enjoy at length and compress the criteria they find difficult.

The second implication concerns the criteria students consistently neglect. Across subjects, the ones that go thin are reflection, evaluation and personal engagement, because they feel like padding to a student who thinks the mathematics or the data is the real work. They are not padding; they carry marks, and they are the easiest marks on the component to secure because they require honesty rather than brilliance.

The table below is written generically on purpose, because the exact criterion letters, counts and mark allocations differ by subject and are set by the current subject guide. Confirm the figures against the guide your child's school holds before planning against them. What does not change is the principle: find the letters, find the marks, allocate space accordingly, and do it before writing rather than after.

sections.heading: Word and page limits, and what exceeding them costs
paragraphs: Every written component has a limit, and most students treat it as a target to approach from above. The anxious instinct is to write long and cut later, which produces a piece whose structure was designed for a different length and whose cuts fall wherever cutting is easiest rather than where it is least damaging. Planning to the limit from the start produces a better piece of work, and it is a free decision made in the first session.

The published upper limit for the Extended Essay is four thousand words, and for the Theory of Knowledge essay sixteen hundred. Subject internal assessments are usually governed by page counts rather than word counts, with ranges set in the subject guide; mathematics explorations and science investigations both sit in the low-to-mid teens of pages in most current guides. Economics commentaries and the Business Management research project each carry their own tight limits.

The figures above are the widely published ones, and they should still be confirmed against the current subject guide your child's school holds, because limits are revised between syllabus cycles and the school's copy is the authoritative one. This project does not reproduce awarding-body documents, and it does not publish IB dates at all, because the IB's own site could not be checked programmatically. Treat any tutoring page that states a limit without that caveat with mild suspicion.

What a limit should change is the plan. A four-thousand-word essay has room for roughly five substantial sections and no room for a literature review that was interesting to write. A sixteen-hundred-word essay has room for two knowledge arguments properly developed, which is why students who attempt four end up with four assertions. Deciding the section structure and its word allocation before drafting is the whole technique, and it takes twenty minutes.

sections.heading: The internal deadline calendar, counted backwards
paragraphs: Schools set internal deadlines for coursework, and those deadlines are the ones that actually govern a student's year. They exist because teachers need time to mark, moderate and upload, and they therefore sit well before any external date. A family planning against an external examination window rather than against the school's internal calendar is planning against the wrong document, and will be surprised twice.

The clustering is the part worth anticipating. Because every subject's internal assessment has to be marked in the same term, schools tend to place drafts and finals in the same few weeks, and the Extended Essay reflection sessions land in among them. The result is a fortnight in which a student owes three substantial pieces of work and has the same number of evenings as any other fortnight. That fortnight is visible in September and invisible in January.

Counting backwards is the fix, and it is arithmetic rather than inspiration. Take each internal deadline, subtract the time the work genuinely needs, and put the start date in the calendar as an event rather than an intention. A science investigation needs its design approved, its data collected, a false start absorbed and a write-up drafted: that is weeks, not a weekend, and the weeks have to be real ones with hours in them.

This is also where an honest conversation about external dates belongs. Cambridge and Pearson publish their timetables and key dates, and those can be worked from. In the UAE that means two Cambridge series, June and November, and a Pearson International GCSE calendar of May/June and November: Pearson's November 2026 timetable, for example, runs from late October to 19 November 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. One caution on the Cambridge side is that every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones with its own version of the timetable, so the dates that matter to an Al Maqam student are the ones on their centre's zone timetable and statement of entry, not a generic published window. The three Checkpoint windows in March, May and October are Primary and Lower Secondary tests, not IGCSE sittings, and are easy to mistake for an exam series. IB session dates are deliberately absent from this page, because none has been verified from the IB itself, and a wrong examination date would be a genuinely harmful thing to publish.

sections.heading: Practical work and the Group 4 project when lessons are online
paragraphs: A fair question arrives from every science family: if the tutoring happens over video, how does practical work get supported? The honest answer is that practical work happens at school, in the school laboratory, under the school's supervision, and that is where it should happen. What a tutor can do is everything around it, and that turns out to be most of the marks.

Design is the first part. An investigation that produces no analysable variation cannot be rescued by good writing, and the commonest internal assessment failure in Al Ain is a method approved late and never interrogated. Working through the design before the laboratory session means the student arrives knowing which variable they are controlling, what range of values will produce a usable graph, and how many repeats the analysis will need.

Analysis is the second and larger part. Uncertainty propagation, graph selection, curve fitting, statistical testing and the honest evaluation of limitations are all screen work, and they are where the higher criteria marks live. A student can share a spreadsheet of their own results and work through the processing with a specialist watching, which is considerably more useful than doing it alone at eleven at night.

The alternative-to-practical paper at IGCSE deserves separate mention because it is routinely neglected. It is a written paper about practical work, testing whether a student can read an apparatus diagram, identify variables, spot a flaw in a method and process an untidy result table. All of that is trainable on paper with marked feedback, and students in this city regularly sit it without having practised a single one. The Group 4 project, similarly, is assessed on collaboration and reflection rather than on the science, and the reflection is the part nobody documents until it is too late.

sections.heading: Theory of Knowledge: an essay and an exhibition, both unlike anything else
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge is the component students find hardest to get help with, because it looks like a subject without content and therefore like a subject that cannot be taught. It has content: it has a structure, a vocabulary, and a set of moves that an argument has to make. What it does not have is material to memorise, which is why students who are strong at memorising find it uncomfortable.

The essay fails in a predictable way. A student takes a prescribed title, forms an opinion, and writes an opinion piece with examples attached. What the assessment wants is a knowledge argument: a claim about how knowledge is produced or justified in a particular area, supported, then tested against a counterclaim, with the implications drawn out. The difference between those two pieces of writing is structural, and it can be taught in a few sessions with a plan and a counterargument.

The exhibition fails differently. Students choose three objects they like and then try to attach a prompt to them, which produces three paragraphs explaining why an object is interesting. The assessment wants the prompt understood first and objects selected because they illuminate it, with each object's link to the prompt made explicit. Choosing in the right order is most of the work, and it takes one conversation.

On both components the tutoring boundary is the same as everywhere else and worth repeating here because this is the component where the temptation is strongest. A tutor may teach the structure of a knowledge argument, question the student's claim, point out that the counterclaim is a restatement rather than an opposition, and explain what each assessment band asks for. A tutor may not write the essay, supply paragraphs, or compose the argument for the student to reproduce.

sections.heading: What coursework support costs, and what it must never include
paragraphs: Published market figures first, in AED and attributed. EdFlik advertises online tutoring from AED 45 to 65 an hour, Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52, Unitors lists IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, TutorChase shows AED 270, the Bestimate rate survey puts specialist IB and IGCSE work at AED 200 to 450 and above, and BartyED publishes AED 650. Those are the market's own numbers, not an IB Gram price list.

Coursework support prices differently from weekly subject tutoring because it is not weekly. The pattern that works is a small number of sessions placed where they change the outcome: one design session before anything is written, one or two draft reviews, and a final conversation about the criteria the student has still not addressed. Four sessions placed well beat twelve placed badly, and they cost a third as much.

There is a tier in this market that should be avoided entirely, and it is not defined by price. One page ranking for these searches sells completed internal assessments at a published figure. That is not an expensive tutoring service; it is a different product, and the product is a malpractice finding waiting to be issued. The student is the person who carries it, and at Diploma level the consequence can extend to the whole diploma.

The useful question to ask any provider is therefore not what it costs but what happens to the document. If the answer involves anyone other than the student typing in it, the service is one to decline regardless of the price. If the answer is that feedback is spoken, questioned and acted on by the student, the price is worth comparing against the published bands above.

sections.heading: A school supervisor and a tutor on screen: who does what
paragraphs: Families worry, reasonably, about whether bringing in a tutor undermines or duplicates the supervisor's role. It does neither when the division of labour is clear, and understanding that division is also how a family avoids the awkward situation of a student receiving contradictory advice from two adults a fortnight before a deadline.

The supervisor owns the formal process. They approve the research question, hold the required reflection sessions, confirm the work is the student's own, and submit it. They are the only person who can authorise a change of topic or sign off a declaration. Nothing a tutor says overrides them, and where their advice conflicts with a tutor's, the supervisor's view is the one that governs because they are accountable for the submission.

A tutor owns neither process nor product. What a tutor can do is spend time the supervisor does not have: interrogating a research question for scope, reading criteria with the student and asking which sentence serves which criterion, working through data processing, and questioning a draft paragraph by paragraph. A supervisor with twenty supervisees cannot do that, and is not expected to.

The table sets the two roles out explicitly, which is worth having if only so a student can answer the question honestly when a supervisor asks what help they have had. That question should be easy to answer, and if it is not, the help was the wrong kind. IB Gram holds no approval or accreditation from any awarding body or regulator, operates no UAE premises, and makes no claim to any relationship with your child's school.
