sections.heading: The private candidate route from Al Ain
paragraphs: Sometimes a subject a student needs is not entered by their school, or a student is studying outside a school altogether, or a resit is wanted in a series the school is not entering. In those cases the route is to sit as a private candidate at a registered Cambridge examination centre, which is a different arrangement from being entered by one's own school and comes with its own conditions.

Three things determine whether it is feasible. First, a centre must be willing to accept private candidates, which not all do, and the acceptance usually has to be arranged well before the entry deadline. Second, not every syllabus is available to private candidates, because some have components that require a centre to assess coursework or speaking. Third, the fees are the candidate's own and are set by the centre rather than by the board, so they vary and must be asked for directly.

For an Al Ain family this is a logistical question before it is an academic one, since the nearest centre accepting private candidates may be in Abu Dhabi rather than in the city. That turns each paper into a journey on a date fixed by the zone timetable. Planning that around a multi-paper series is the part families underestimate, and it is worth mapping before committing to the route rather than after.

Where tuition fits is straightforward: a private candidate has no class, no school mock and no teacher submitting forecast grades, so the structure that a cohort provides has to be built deliberately. That means a schedule with fixed checkpoints, full papers sat to time at the right intervals, and an honest external view of where the student actually stands. It is demanding, and it works for the right student with the right subject.
bullets: Not every centre accepts private candidates; arrange it early
Some syllabuses are unavailable privately because of their components
Entry fees are set by the centre, not the board, so ask directly

sections.heading: What Cambridge tuition costs in this market, and the limits on this page
paragraphs: Published UAE tutoring rates range widely and most pages competing for this search print no AED figure. The bands below are market rates taken from providers' own published pricing and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table. They describe the market rather than IB Gram's price list, and they are here so that an Al Ain quote can be measured against something checkable. Budget online tutoring from university students is advertised from roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from roughly AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor working online sits at AED 150 to 300, where Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one with travel runs roughly AED 180 to 500, with Bestimate at 180 to 350 and independent home tutors at 200 to 500. IGCSE and A Level specialists run AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270, and premium named tutoring reaches AED 650, as BartyED publishes.

Bestimate's monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions are AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist examination-year support. Monthly packages seen in the market include AED 799 for eight online sessions. For a Cambridge candidate the sensible shape is usually a steady weekly hour through Year 10 and the first part of Year 11, then a heavier pre-series block. Paying specialist examination-year rates from the first week of Year 10 is a common overspend, and the exception worth making is the tier-decision diagnostic, where a small number of hours early can change the grade ceiling for two years.

The limits on this page are worth stating plainly. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from Cambridge International, Pearson, ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education or the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, and there is no IB Gram office, centre or branch anywhere in the UAE. No grade is promised by anyone here and no statistic appears without a named source. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service available only in India. Where no UAE-based specialist is free for a syllabus, the match comes from the wider tutor pool at Gulf Standard Time and that is disclosed before any lesson is booked.

One further point applies to any tutor an Al Ain family hires, from us or anywhere. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. The Ministry's service is Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, listing no fees and a two-working-day completion time, applied for through its smart app, website and e-services system. Anyone tutoring without a permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount is quoted here.

process.title: Send the specification sheet or statement of entry
process.description: Not the subject list from the school website. The specification sheet or statement of entry carries the four-digit codes, the tiers and the components actually entered, and it is the only document that reliably describes what your child is sitting. Everything else in the process follows from it.

process.title: Get the zone timetable from the examinations officer
process.description: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and warns that the correct zone timetable must be used. Ask which zone the centre sits in and work from the issued timetable for the whole series, then check it against the statement of entry paper by paper.

process.title: Settle the tier question with evidence
process.description: If Core or Extended is in doubt, a short diagnostic produces a written view of what the student can currently do at Extended standard. The tier is the centre's decision, but a case made with evidence in the first term of Year 10 lands very differently from a preference raised in January.

process.title: Meet the matched tutor for a trial lesson at no charge
process.description: One introductory session once a tutor is matched to the exact syllabus code, with nothing charged and no card required to book. Watch whether the tutor asks for the code and the practical component before teaching, which is the clearest signal that the match is real rather than nominal.

process.title: Review after each school assessment
process.description: Mock results and marked school papers are the review points, because they show component marks rather than impressions. Diagnose by component and by question type, and change the plan when the evidence says so rather than persisting with a diagnosis that the last paper contradicted.

whyPoints.title: The code comes before the teaching
whyPoints.description: Matching a tutor to 0580 Extended or 0607 or 0606 is not pedantry. The papers, tiering, calculator expectations and mark schemes differ, and a tutor working from the wrong one teaches confidently in the wrong direction.

whyPoints.title: Administration treated as part of the grade
whyPoints.description: Zone timetables, entry deadlines and tier decisions decide outcomes before any teaching happens. Most pages competing for this search mention none of them, and most of the avoidable grade losses in Al Ain each year sit here.

whyPoints.title: Dates taken from the board, not aggregated
whyPoints.description: The Cambridge and Pearson dates on this page come from each board's own published key dates and timetable pages, with the series named. No IB session date appears anywhere here, because the IB's own site is the only reliable source for those.

whyPoints.title: Al Ain's regulator, correctly identified
whyPoints.description: Al Ain private schools are inspected by ADEK, not KHDA. Almost all online tutoring content is written about Dubai, which points a local parent at the wrong authority and the wrong inspection framework.

whyPoints.title: Rates with sources attached
whyPoints.description: Every AED band here is attributed to the provider or rate table that published it and kept separate from anything IB Gram charges. Three of the six pages competing in this market publish no price at all.

whyPoints.title: Official materials referenced, not distributed
whyPoints.description: Past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and boundary tables stay on Cambridge's own site. Sessions work from them by link and by reference, which is both the lawful position and the only version guaranteed current.

faqs.question: What do Cambridge syllabus codes like 0580 and 0620 tell me?
faqs.answer: They identify the exact syllabus, which the subject name does not. The code fixes how many papers are sat, whether the subject is tiered into Core and Extended, how practical work is assessed and which grading scale the result is reported on. Cambridge publishes paired syllabuses for several subjects, one reported A* to G and one 9 to 1, each with its own code. Take the code from your child's specification sheet or statement of entry, and verify it on Cambridge International's own subject pages, because syllabuses are revised and codes retire.

faqs.question: Which Cambridge administrative zone is Al Ain in, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: The zone belongs to the centre rather than to the city, so ask your school's examinations officer which zone it sits in. It matters because Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, states that using the correct zone timetable is essential, and says it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. Examination windows across zones differ by days, which is subtle enough that a parent planning travel from a timetable found online may not notice until it is too late.

faqs.question: Which Cambridge series does a student in Al Ain actually sit?
faqs.answer: June or November. Cambridge runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in those two series in the UAE, and the winter sitting that appears in some search results is offered to candidates in India rather than here. The Checkpoint tests that sit in March, May and October are Primary and Lower Secondary assessments, not IGCSE, which is where most of the confusion comes from. The practical difference between the two real series is resit timing: November means a student who misses a target in the summer can retake within months rather than waiting a year. Which series your school enters is a centre decision, so ask rather than assume, and work only from the official timetable issued for that series and that zone.

faqs.question: How long before the first paper do Cambridge final entries close?
faqs.answer: Months, not weeks. For a June series the final entry closes in the spring, roughly four months ahead of the first paper, and for a November series it closes over the summer; the exact day for your centre is on the statement of entry, which is the document to ask the examinations officer for rather than a date lifted from a website. Pearson's published timetables show the same gap in hard numbers, with the November 2026 International GCSE series examined from late October to 19 November 2026. The gap is the point: subject and tier decisions are effectively locked long before the papers. If you want a tier changed, the conversation belongs in the first term of Year 10, not in the term the entries are already submitted.

faqs.question: What is a forecast grade and who submits it to Cambridge?
faqs.answer: A forecast grade is the centre's professional judgement of the grade a candidate is expected to achieve, submitted by the school to Cambridge as part of administering a series. The deadline sits some weeks before the first paper of whichever series the candidate is entered for, and the examinations officer holds the current date for your centre. It is part of the results process rather than the university admissions process, which is where predicted grades belong, and the two are often confused. No tutor can influence a forecast grade directly, and any offer to do so misunderstands how the mechanism works.

faqs.question: Is my child's Cambridge IGCSE graded 9 to 1 or A* to G?
faqs.answer: It depends on which syllabus code the centre entered, because Cambridge attaches the scale to the syllabus rather than deciding it at results time. The numeric scale subdivides the top of the older scale more finely, which is why it exists, so a 7 is not simply an A. Keep a single sheet listing each subject's code and scale, because school and university entry requirements may be written in either form. The Ministry of Education's British-track equivalency rule names grade E or grade 3 precisely to cover both.

faqs.question: How are Cambridge IGCSE science practicals assessed?
faqs.answer: Either through a laboratory test or through a written alternative, with the centre choosing which and choosing separately per subject. In both cases what is examined is practical reasoning rather than manual dexterity: identifying controlled variables, spotting what makes a result unreliable, reading scales, choosing apparatus and justifying repeats. That reasoning is teachable on a shared screen using methods, results tables and graphs. The hands-on work stays in the school laboratory under the school's own supervision and safety arrangements.

faqs.question: Can my child sit Cambridge IGCSE as a private candidate in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, with three conditions. A registered Cambridge centre must be willing to accept private candidates, and not all do, so the arrangement has to be made well before the entry deadline. Not every syllabus is available privately, because some components require centre assessment. And entry fees are set by the centre rather than the board, so ask the centre directly. For Al Ain families the nearest accepting centre may be in Abu Dhabi, which turns each paper into a journey on a date fixed by the zone timetable.

faqs.question: Is Cambridge IGCSE or Pearson Edexcel International GCSE better for a UAE student?
faqs.answer: Universities treat them as equivalent, so the better board is whichever your child's centre has entered. What differs is the experience: series timing, question styles, tiering arrangements and how practical science is assessed. Pearson runs May or June and November series and publishes provisional then final timetables; Cambridge runs June and November for UAE candidates and allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones. A student changing school mid-course between boards is making a real transition and usually benefits from a short block of support.

faqs.question: Which Cambridge IGCSE subjects do Al Ain students most often resit?
faqs.answer: Mathematics first, then the individual sciences, with English First Language appearing more often than families expect. Mathematics resits are frequently a tier issue rather than a teaching issue: a student capped by Core entry who needed Extended for a sixth-form or Diploma route. The November series makes a resit possible within months rather than a year, which is worth knowing before results day so the decision can be made quickly. Ask the school which subjects it will enter in November before assuming the option exists.

faqs.question: How many Cambridge IGCSE subjects does the Ministry of Education count?
faqs.answer: Five. As reported when the UAE clarified its equivalency requirements, a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. The British track also requires proof of one accredited Advanced Level subject at no less than E, or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. One ranking competitor tells UAE families six subjects are required; the sourced figure is five. Confirm the current rules on the Ministry's own site.

faqs.question: What is Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint and does it matter?
faqs.answer: Checkpoint is a set of diagnostic tests taken in the years before IGCSE, available in March, May and October sittings. It is not a qualification and no university sees it. Its value is that it produces subject-level evidence of where a student stands against the Cambridge framework before the Core or Extended decision has to be made, which is the single most consequential decision of the IGCSE years. Where an Al Ain school does not run it, families often ask for a diagnostic session instead before Year 10 starts.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover Cambridge IGCSE Maths 0580 and Additional Maths 0606?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and it is one of the more sensible pairings to keep with a single tutor, because 0606 builds directly on Extended 0580 and introduces calculus and trigonometric identities that 0580 does not contain. Ask when the tutor last taught 0606 specifically, since the calculus content and question style differ enough that general mathematics teaching does not automatically cover it. For a student heading towards A Level Mathematics or Higher Level Analysis and Approaches, 0606 is the most useful bridge available in Al Ain.

faqs.question: How long before a Cambridge paper should tutoring start?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most families start, and for a different reason than they expect. The highest-value early work is not content but the tier decision, because Core entry caps the achievable grade and the entry is effectively locked months before the paper. After that, a steady weekly hour through Year 10 and the first part of Year 11 costs less and achieves more than a heavy final block alone. A pre-series intensive of eight to ten weeks on timed papers is where most late grade movement comes from, so plan both.

faqs.question: What does a Cambridge IGCSE tutor charge in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Judge any quote against the published market. Unitors publishes IGCSE tutoring from AED 150 an hour; TutorChase publishes AED 270; Bestimate's rate table puts specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above and budget online tutoring at the lower end, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65. Bestimate's monthly estimate for a weekly one-hour session is AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market. IB Gram publishes no rate card here; the next step is a trial lesson at no charge once a tutor is matched to the syllabus code, then a quote against the actual subject and tier.

al-ain/cambridge-igcse-tutor.closingBody: Find the document that lists your child's four-digit syllabus codes, the tier entered in each subject and the practical components, then ask the examinations officer which administrative zone the centre sits in and get that timetable. Those two pieces of paper answer more questions than any amount of general advice, and they are what any competent Cambridge tutor will ask for first. Send them to us with one marked school paper and we will match a tutor to the code rather than to the subject name. Lessons are one-to-one over live video at Gulf Standard Time; home visits are an India-only service and are not offered anywhere in the UAE.

al-ain/falaj-hazza.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are matched to a specific decision as well as a subject: securing algebra before a tier entry, converting between two boards' paper structures, and building the readiness that makes a Higher Level choice realistic rather than aspirational.

intro.heading: Four decisions, each one capping a grade before a paper is sat
paragraphs: Falaj Hazza sits west of central Al Ain, closer to the school cluster than the southern districts and denser than most of the city, with a mixture of family villas and low apartment blocks along its main streets. Journeys into school are short by Al Ain standards, which means households here have more usable evening hours than families further out. What they ask about, as a result, is rarely scheduling. It is choices.

Four of those choices matter more than anything a tutor will ever teach. At around fourteen a school decides, or a family accepts, whether a child is entered for Core or Extended tier in several IGCSE subjects, and that entry caps the grade available. At fifteen the board is fixed, which decides the paper architecture and the formula sheet. At sixteen a mathematics route is chosen that some university courses will read as a prerequisite. And at sixteen again, six subjects are assigned a level in a single afternoon of form-filling.

None of those four decisions is reversible on a comfortable timescale, and none of them is usually explained to a family in terms of what it closes. A parent is told their child has been placed in the Core group and hears a reassurance about appropriate challenge. What has actually happened is that the maximum achievable grade has been reduced, and if that was the right call the family deserves to know it was a call. If it was a default applied to a set rather than to a student, it deserves to be questioned.

This is why enquiries from this district often begin with a question that sounds administrative. Which paper is my daughter sitting? Why does my son's past paper look different from his cousin's? Can the school change the entry now? Those are the right questions, asked slightly too late, and the tutoring that follows is usually either closing a gap fast enough to justify a tier change or making the best of a ceiling that cannot now be raised.

What follows sets each decision out with the person who makes it, the point at which it hardens, and what a parent can reasonably ask for before then. It also covers the honest version of the repair work: what can be fixed in a term, what takes a year, and what cannot be fixed at all once an entry has closed. There is no benefit in pretending otherwise, because a family planning around a false hope spends money badly.

Delivery is one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE and nobody will be sent to a Falaj Hazza address; that is an India-only service. Where this page quotes a market rate or an awarding-body date it names the source, and where a figure could not be verified it is left out, which is why no IB examination dates appear anywhere on this site.

al-ain/falaj-hazza.programmesIntro: Falaj Hazza households are mainly on the British route and the IB continuum. Each programme is described here by the decisions it forces and when they land, because that is what families in this district are actually asking about.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson International GCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined by terminal papers. Several subjects are tiered: Cambridge uses Core and Extended, Pearson uses Foundation and Higher in some subjects. A Core or Foundation entry typically caps the award at around grade 5, and the entry is made by the school months before the examination. Syllabus codes such as 0580, 0620 and 4MA1 identify exactly which version is being sat.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge runs a June series and a November series for UAE centres and allocates each centre to one of six administrative zones, stating that the correct zone timetable must be used and that it cannot take responsibility for candidates who use the wrong one. Final entries for the June series close in the spring, roughly four months before the first paper, which shows how early the decision hardens - and the date comes to you from the centre rather than from Cambridge.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three or four at Higher Level and the rest at Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internal assessment usually carries twenty to thirty per cent of a subject grade. The level decision is made on all six subjects at once, often in a single meeting, and changing one after teaching begins has knock-on effects on the timetable.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain the number of Diploma campuses is small, so some Higher Level combinations exist in a single set at a single school. A level change that would be routine in a large city can be impossible here simply because the set is full or the subject is timetabled against another one the student needs.

programmes.name: International AS and A Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects studied in depth, assessed by papers, modular with Pearson and stageable with Cambridge. Fewer subjects means an earlier and narrower commitment than the Diploma, and a wrong subject choice is more costly because there is less to compensate with.
programmes.countryNote: Several Al Ain campuses run A Level rather than the Diploma, which makes the choice at sixteen a genuine fork rather than a preference. Families switching campus to get one or the other should confirm which boards and which subject combinations are actually timetabled before accepting a place.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject marked out of eight, converted to a 1-7 grade, with a Personal Project at the end. There is no tiering, but set placement within a subject frequently predicts the tier or level a student will later be offered, which makes Year 9 performance quietly consequential.
programmes.countryNote: The decision that matters in the middle years is mathematics set placement, because in most schools the upper sets lead to Extended tier and Higher Level and the lower ones do not. That link is rarely spelled out to families, and Year 9 is the last comfortable moment to change the trajectory.

al-ain/falaj-hazza.subjectsIntro: Requests from Falaj Hazza tend to be tied to a decision: securing a subject enough to justify a tier change, or bridging between two boards. Each entry names the subject and the decision it interacts with.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580)
subjects.description: The most consequential tier decision in the curriculum, because mathematics gates science routes, Higher Level options and several university courses. Extended entry assumes fluent algebra, so securing algebra in Year 9 or early Year 10 is what makes a tier change arguable.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Same subject, different paper architecture, different formula sheet and a different question escalation pattern. Higher tier questions escalate within a single question, so a student trained on Cambridge papers can lose accessible marks simply through unfamiliarity.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: The clearest available signal of readiness for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. A student who copes with it comfortably is a credible candidate for that route; a student who struggles is better served by Applications and Interpretation, and knowing that at sixteen is worth a great deal.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 and Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: A Core entry removes the content a Diploma or A Level chemistry course assumes, so the tier decision here is also a decision about sixth-form options. Moles and electrolysis carry the marks and are the usual evidence used to argue for an Extended entry.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: Mathematical confidence is the real gate rather than physical intuition, which is why a weak mathematics set placement often drags a physics tier down with it. The practical or alternative-to-practical component is also chosen by the school and is worth asking about.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 and Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: The science where an Extended entry is most often achievable with focused work, because the content is volume rather than abstraction. Command terms decide this paper more than any other at the level, which makes it responsive to technique work.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof and calculus, and the route some engineering, physics, mathematics and economics courses expect. Higher Level assumes manipulation happens without hesitation, which is why the Additional Mathematics signal at sixteen is so useful.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and technology, and an entirely respectable route that is not interchangeable with Analysis and Approaches for admissions purposes. Check the specific requirement of the specific course rather than relying on a general impression.

subjects.name: Chemistry at Diploma level
subjects.description: Higher Level adds substantial content and a harder paper, and the level decision interacts with medicine and engineering requirements. Students arriving from a Core IGCSE entry face a genuine content gap that needs planned work rather than optimism.

subjects.name: Physics at Diploma level
subjects.description: Higher Level demands comfort with algebraic rearrangement under time. The honest readiness test is not interest in physics but how a student copes with multi-step algebra when nothing is given in a convenient form.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Higher Level adds quantitative content and a third paper. Students choose it expecting essays and meet calculation, which is a level-decision problem rather than a teaching problem and is best caught before the form is signed.

subjects.name: English A and English B
subjects.levels: HL, SL and Language B routes
subjects.description: Placement between English A and English B is a decision with university consequences, because some institutions read them differently as evidence of language proficiency. It is worth asking the school explicitly which one a child is being placed in and why.

sections.heading: Who lives in Falaj Hazza, and when each household meets its first decision
paragraphs: This is a settled district with short school runs, which produces a particular kind of enquiry. Families here are not usually struggling to find an hour; they have the hour. What they want to know is whether a decision made about their child was the right one, and whether it can still be changed. That is a better question than most families ask and it arrives, almost always, between six and eighteen months later than it should.

The households split roughly three ways. Long-settled families with children who have been at one campus since primary, who know the school well and have usually accepted its set placements without examining them. Families who moved into the city in the last few years, often from elsewhere in the Gulf or from an Indian-board school, whose child met the tier decision shortly after arriving. And bilingual households managing the Arabic stream decision alongside everything else on this page.

Each meets its first hard decision at a different point. A long-settled family typically meets it at the Year 9 mathematics set review, which most of them do not realise is a decision at all. A recently arrived family meets it immediately, because a new school places a child on limited evidence. A bilingual household meets the language placement decision earliest of all, sometimes in primary, and almost never revisits it.

The table sets out those household types with the decision each one meets first, the year it typically lands and what it costs to get wrong. The purpose is to let a parent locate their own position in the sequence, because the appropriate action is entirely different depending on whether a decision is six months away or already fixed.

sections.heading: Core or Extended: the tier that sets the ceiling
paragraphs: In several IGCSE subjects a school enters a student for one of two tiers. Cambridge calls them Core and Extended; Pearson uses Foundation and Higher in some subjects. The two tiers sit on the same syllabus but assess different portions of it, with different papers, and the lower tier carries a maximum award. In practice a Core or Foundation entry usually caps the result at around grade 5, and no amount of excellent performance on that paper can produce a higher grade.

That is the fact most worth knowing on this page, and it is the one least often stated to families. A parent told their child is in the Core group hears a reassurance about appropriate challenge. What has happened is that the top of the grade range has been removed. Sometimes that is the right decision, because entering a student for a paper they cannot access produces a worse outcome than a secure result at the lower tier. But it is a decision, and it should be visible as one.

The consequences run forward. A Core chemistry entry removes content that a Diploma or A Level chemistry course assumes, so the tier decision at fourteen quietly shapes what is available at sixteen. A Foundation mathematics entry makes a Higher Level mathematics route unrealistic. Families who understand that chain in Year 9 behave differently from families who discover it in Year 11, and the difference in outcome is substantial.

What a parent can do is ask three questions in writing. Which tier is my child currently expected to be entered for, in each subject? What evidence would the department need in order to enter them for the higher tier? And what is the last date on which that entry can be changed? Those three answers convert a vague worry into a plan with a deadline, and the deadline is real: Cambridge closes final entries for the June series in the spring, months before the first paper, and the centre is the only party that knows the exact day.

sections.heading: Cambridge or Pearson: one subject, two different examinations
paragraphs: Parents in this district regularly discover that their child's cousin at another Al Ain campus is sitting a different examination in the same subject. Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel both offer International GCSE qualifications, both are widely accepted, and they are not the same assessment. The syllabus codes differ, the paper structures differ, the formula sheets differ and the practical arrangements differ. Revising from the wrong board's past papers is a genuine and common waste of a term.

The differences that affect a student most are structural rather than academic. Pearson's modular approach in some subjects allows units to be resat; Cambridge's International A Level can be staged across series. Question escalation differs: in some Pearson papers difficulty rises inside a single question, so a student who abandons a question at the first unfamiliar part loses the accessible marks that follow. Cambridge's zone system means the timetable itself differs by region, and the board states plainly that the correct zone version must be used.

The series calendars also differ. Cambridge runs June and November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Pearson runs International GCSE examinations in May or June and in November, with the November 2026 final timetable running from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026.

The practical instruction for a family is short. Find out the syllabus code, not the subject name: 0580 and 4MA1 are both mathematics and they are not interchangeable. Get it from the school in writing. Then make sure every past paper, revision guide and tutor matches that code. A tutor who cannot tell you which code they are teaching is not teaching your child's examination.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation
paragraphs: At sixteen a Diploma student chooses between two mathematics courses that are not interchangeable in the eyes of every university. Analysis and Approaches is the proof and calculus route. Applications and Interpretation is the statistics, modelling and technology route. Both are respectable, both are demanding at Higher Level, and both are routinely chosen for the wrong reason, which is a belief that one is easier.

The honest readiness test is not interest and not current grade. It is how a student copes with multi-step algebraic manipulation when nothing is presented in a convenient form. A student who has taken Additional Mathematics and coped comfortably is a credible candidate for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. A student who finds algebra effortful under time will be more successful, and happier, on Applications and Interpretation, and will not be penalised for it by most courses.

The exception is the set of courses that specify the route. Engineering, physics, mathematics and some economics programmes at some institutions ask for Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, and a student who chose the other route cannot usually substitute. That is not universal and it changes between institutions and years, which is why the only safe approach is to read the specific requirement for the specific course on the institution's own admissions pages before the form is signed.

What should not happen is the common sequence: choose on a general impression, discover the requirement in Year 13, and then attempt a late switch that the timetable cannot accommodate. In Al Ain this is sharper than elsewhere because a school may run only one set in each course, so a switch depends on a place existing in the other one. Checking the requirement at sixteen costs an evening of reading and saves an entire application strategy.

sections.heading: Higher or Standard Level, decided on six subjects in one afternoon
paragraphs: The Diploma level decision has a strange quality: it is six decisions made simultaneously, usually in one meeting, with incomplete information, and it determines the shape of two years. Higher Level means more content, an extra paper in several subjects, and a greater internal assessment burden. Standard Level means less of each. Students typically take three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, and the distribution matters as much as the individual choices.

The mistake that recurs is choosing Higher Level by interest and then discovering the workload interaction. Three Higher Level subjects with heavy coursework, taken together, produce a term in which three substantial pieces of work are due in the same fortnight. Two heavy Higher Levels and one lighter one is a far more survivable combination, and nobody points this out during the form-filling because each subject is discussed on its own.

The second mistake is treating a level as a judgement of ability. A student who takes a subject at Standard Level and scores highly has done better, by any measure that matters, than a student who took it at Higher Level and scraped through. University requirements are specific about which subjects they want at Higher Level, and for everything outside that list a strong Standard Level result is worth more than a weak Higher Level one.

What a family can reasonably ask is which Higher Level sets the school actually runs, how large they are and who teaches them. In a city with few Diploma campuses a Higher Level set may be one group taught by one teacher who also carries Standard Level, and that is relevant information. It is not a criticism of the school; it is the context in which a level decision is being made, and it is better known than discovered.

sections.heading: Diploma or A Level at sixteen, in a city with few campuses
paragraphs: The choice between the Diploma and A Level is usually presented as a philosophical one: breadth against depth. That framing is true and not very useful, because in Al Ain the decision is frequently settled by what is timetabled where. A student wanting three specific A Level subjects, or a particular Higher Level combination, may find that only one campus in the city offers it, which converts a curriculum decision into a logistical one.

Taken on the merits, the differences are real. The Diploma requires six subjects plus three core components, which suits a student who is broadly capable and organised enough to manage several independent deadlines. A Level concentrates on three or four subjects, which suits a student with clear strengths and a settled direction, and it produces a lighter coursework load with heavier paper weighting.

The practical risks differ too. A Diploma student who is weak in one subject carries it for two years as part of a points total. An A Level student who chose the wrong third subject has less to compensate with, because the three results are read individually. Neither structure is safer in the abstract; what matters is the match between the structure and the particular student, and that is a conversation worth having with evidence rather than with preference.

The one piece of advice that applies to both is to confirm the offer before committing. Ask which subjects at which levels are actually running next year, how large the sets are, and whether the combination you want is timetabled against itself. Schools answer that question readily when asked in writing, and the answer occasionally changes a decision entirely.

sections.heading: Who actually decides, and what a parent may ask for
paragraphs: A recurring source of frustration in this district is uncertainty about who holds each decision. The short version is that the school holds nearly all of them. Set placement is a departmental decision. Tier entry is made by the school and submitted to the awarding body. Level offers at Diploma are made by the school within the constraints of its own timetable. A parent cannot overrule any of these, and a tutor certainly cannot.

What a parent can do is ask specific questions and ask for answers in writing, which changes the quality of the response. Vague concern produces vague reassurance. A written question about which tier a child is intended for, what evidence would change it and when the entry closes produces a dated answer from somebody accountable. That is the single most effective action available to a parent in this situation, and it costs nothing.

The second thing a parent can do is supply evidence. Departments move students between tiers and sets on evidence, not on enthusiasm, and the evidence they find persuasive is performance on the higher tier's own material. That is what makes a bounded piece of preparatory work worth buying: not to argue with the school, but to produce the thing the school needs in order to say yes. It also means the work has a deadline attached, which is the entry date.

The third is to accept a no gracefully when it comes with a reason. Sometimes a department's judgement is correct and an entry at the higher tier would produce a worse result than a secure one at the lower. A family that understands why can plan around the ceiling: choose sixth-form subjects that the entry supports, or plan a resit in a later series. That is a real plan, and it beats a year of resentment aimed at a classroom.

sections.heading: What it costs to repair a decision late
paragraphs: Market rates first, with sources. EdFlik publishes online tutoring from AED 45 to 65 an hour, Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52, Unitors lists IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, TutorChase shows AED 270, the Bestimate survey puts specialist IB and IGCSE work at AED 200 to 450 and above with in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350, and BartyED publishes AED 650. None of these is an IB Gram price, and a quote here comes from a conversation.

The more interesting cost on this page is the one measured in time rather than money. A tier decision questioned in Year 9 can be changed with a term of secure algebra work. The same decision questioned in February of Year 11 cannot be changed at all, because the entry has closed, and the only remaining options are a resit in a later series or a sixth-form plan built around the ceiling. The money is similar in both cases. The outcome is not.

That asymmetry is the reason this page exists in the shape it does. The highest-value tutoring in this district is early and cheap: a readiness assessment before a level choice, a term of algebra before a tier entry, three sessions of board conversion when a child moves campus. The lowest-value is late and expensive: an urgent block in the final term aimed at a ceiling that was set eighteen months earlier.

The table below sets out when each decision can still be changed and what the realistic repair looks like at each point. It is deliberately honest about the cases where the answer is that nothing can be done now, because a family told the truth in February can at least plan the resit properly, while a family sold hope spends the money and keeps the ceiling.

sections.heading: Availability, delivery and the lines we do not cross
paragraphs: A page about decisions should be honest about the one it cannot influence, which is availability. In Al Ain the local specialist pool is thin for Higher Level sciences, the less common Diploma languages, Music, Design Technology and Further Mathematics, because cohorts in those subjects are small everywhere and the city has few campuses. If a request lands in one of those, the answer at the first conversation is a named match time or a clear no.

Where no UAE-based specialist is free, the fallback is a tutor based elsewhere teaching the same syllabus over live video and scheduled to Gulf Standard Time, disclosed before any booking. Several providers in this market route families to non-UAE delivery without saying so, which is a trust failure rather than a logistical one. On home visits the position is unambiguous: IB Gram sells none anywhere in the UAE, and nobody will be sent to a Falaj Hazza address; that service exists only in India.

On assessed work the boundary is fixed. A tutor may teach the skills a task needs, explain what each criterion asks for, question a draft the student has written and point out where a section fails to answer its own question. A tutor may not write, draft, complete or edit to completion an internal assessment, Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge essay or Personal Project. The student signs the authenticity declaration and the student carries any finding.

No IB examination dates appear on this site because none has been verified from the IB itself, and the Cambridge and Pearson dates used here are taken from the boards' own published material.

process.title: Ask the school three written questions
process.description: Which tier or level is my child intended for in each subject, what evidence would change it, and when does the entry close? Written questions produce dated answers from somebody accountable. Vague concern produces vague reassurance, which is why so many families discover a ceiling rather than choose one.

process.title: Get the syllabus code, not the subject name
process.description: 0580 and 4MA1 are both mathematics and are not interchangeable. The code determines the papers, the formula sheet, the question structure and which past material is useful. Confirm it with the school in writing, then make sure every revision guide and every tutor matches it.

process.title: Test readiness with the work the route actually demands
process.description: Not the current grade and not interest in the subject. For Higher Level mathematics that means multi-step algebra under time with nothing given in convenient form. One honest session here is cheaper than two years spent in the wrong course, and the honest recommendation sometimes points at the other route.

process.title: Build the evidence a department can act on
process.description: Schools move students between tiers and sets on performance against the higher tier's own material. A bounded block of work aimed at producing that evidence, finished before the entry deadline, is the practical route to a change. Arguing without evidence rarely moves anything.

process.title: Plan around a ceiling you cannot now move
process.description: When an entry has closed, say so and plan properly: sixth-form subjects the entry supports, or a resit in a later series with the deadlines mapped. A family told the truth in February can still plan. A family sold hope spends the money and keeps the ceiling anyway.

whyPoints.title: The decisions are named, with their deadlines
whyPoints.description: Tier, board, route and level each cap what a student can be awarded, and each hardens on a date. Setting them out with the person who decides and the last point of change is more useful to a Falaj Hazza family than another page about study skills, because this is the part nobody explains until it is fixed.

whyPoints.title: Tier entry is described as a ceiling, not a comfort
whyPoints.description: A Core or Foundation entry commonly caps the award at around grade 5 and removes content that sixth-form courses assume. That may still be the right call, but it is a call. Saying it plainly is how a parent gets to participate in the decision rather than receive its consequences.

whyPoints.title: Board differences are treated as practical, not academic
whyPoints.description: Paper architecture, formula sheets, question escalation and zone timetables differ between Cambridge and Pearson, and revising from the wrong one wastes a term. Work starts from the confirmed syllabus code, which also means a tutor can say exactly which examination they are preparing a student for.

whyPoints.title: Readiness is tested on the real demand
whyPoints.description: A mathematics route choice is assessed by how a student handles multi-step algebra under time, not by their current grade or their interest. Where the honest answer is the other route, that is the recommendation given, including when it means recommending less work for us rather than more.

whyPoints.title: Late is said to be late
whyPoints.description: When an entry has closed, there is no version of tutoring that raises the ceiling, and pretending otherwise sells a family hope at full price. The alternative offered is a real plan: a sixth-form combination the entry supports, or a resit in a later series with the dates mapped backwards.

whyPoints.title: Availability and delivery are disclosed up front
whyPoints.description: Higher Level sciences and uncommon languages are thin in this city, so the first conversation gives a named match time or a clear no. Where a tutor would be based outside the UAE that is said before booking. No home visits are sold anywhere in the Emirates, and no regulator approval is claimed.

faqs.question: What does a Core tier entry actually mean for my child's grade?
faqs.answer: It caps it. Core and Extended sit on the same syllabus but assess different portions of it with different papers, and a Core or Foundation entry commonly limits the award to around grade 5 regardless of how well your child performs. A parent told their child is in the Core group usually hears a reassurance about appropriate challenge rather than a statement about the ceiling. Sometimes the lower tier is genuinely the right call, because an inaccessible paper produces a worse result than a secure one, but it is a decision and you are entitled to see it as one.

faqs.question: Can a tier entry still be changed in Year 11?
faqs.answer: Only before the entry deadline, which sits months before the examination. Cambridge closes final entries for the June series in the spring, roughly four months ahead of the first paper, and the date reaches you on your child's statement of entry rather than from the board. After it the entry is fixed and no amount of tutoring changes the ceiling for that sitting; what remains is the November series, which takes its own entry on its own deadline. Ask the school in writing which tier is intended, what evidence would change it, and the last date a change is possible. Those three answers turn a worry into a plan with a real deadline attached to it.

faqs.question: How do I find out which exam board my child actually sits?
faqs.answer: Ask the school for the syllabus code in writing, not the subject name. Cambridge uses four-digit codes such as 0580 for mathematics, 0620 for chemistry and 0625 for physics; Pearson uses forms like 4MA1, 4CH1 and 4PH1. Both are International GCSE qualifications and they are different examinations with different papers, formula sheets and question structures. Once you have the code, every past paper, revision guide and tutor should match it. A tutor who cannot tell you which code they teach is not preparing your child's examination.

faqs.question: My nephew at another Al Ain school has different past papers. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly a different board, and occasionally a different Cambridge zone. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and the timetable differs between them; the board states that using the correct zone version is essential and that it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who misses a paper after using the wrong one. Pearson publishes its own series timetables, including provisional versions ahead of each series. So two cousins in the same city can legitimately be sitting different papers on different days in the same subject.

faqs.question: Which Diploma mathematics route should my child take?
faqs.answer: Decide on how they handle multi-step algebra under time with nothing given in a convenient form, not on which course sounds easier. Analysis and Approaches is the proof and calculus route; Applications and Interpretation is statistics, modelling and technology. A student who coped comfortably with Additional Mathematics is a credible Higher Level Analysis and Approaches candidate. A student who finds hand algebra effortful will do better and be happier on the other route, and most courses will not penalise them for it.

faqs.question: Will Applications and Interpretation close any university doors?
faqs.answer: For some named courses, yes. Engineering, physics, mathematics and certain economics programmes at some institutions specify Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, and a student on the other route generally cannot substitute. That is not universal and it changes between institutions and intake years, so the only safe method is to read the specific requirement for the specific course on the institution's own admissions pages before the option form is signed. One evening of reading at sixteen protects an entire application strategy.

faqs.question: Is Standard Level a lesser result than Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Not in any way that matters outside a named prerequisite. A student who takes a subject at Standard Level and scores highly has done better than one who took it at Higher Level and scraped through, by every measure an admissions officer applies. Universities are specific about which subjects they want at Higher Level, and for everything outside that list a strong Standard Level result is worth more than a weak Higher Level one. Treating the level as a verdict on ability is how families end up with unsustainable combinations.

faqs.question: How many Higher Level subjects with heavy coursework can one student manage?
faqs.answer: Two heavy ones plus a lighter third is survivable; three heavy ones produce a fortnight in which three substantial pieces of work are all due. The reason this goes wrong is that each subject is discussed on its own during option choices, so nobody looks at the combination. Before signing the form, ask when each subject's internal assessment deadline typically falls at that school. If two or three land in the same weeks, change one of the choices rather than planning to work harder.

faqs.question: Does my child's Year 9 maths set really matter?
faqs.answer: More than almost anything else at that age, and it is rarely presented as a decision. In most schools the upper sets lead to Extended or Higher tier entry and the lower ones do not, so a set placement at thirteen influences a tier at fourteen, which influences the sixth-form options at sixteen. Each step is small and the accumulation is not. The end of Year 9 is the last comfortable point to change the trajectory, and the lever is secure algebra plus evidence the department can act on.

faqs.question: Can I ask the school to move my child up a tier?
faqs.answer: You can ask, and the useful form of the question is about evidence rather than about fairness. Departments move students on performance against the higher tier's own material, so the productive request is: what would my child need to demonstrate, and by when? Then produce it. That is what a bounded block of preparatory work is for, and it comes with a real deadline because the entry closes on a date. Arguing without evidence seldom changes a departmental judgement, and it damages the relationship you will need later.

faqs.question: What if the school says no and gives a reason?
faqs.answer: Take the reason seriously and plan around the ceiling. Sometimes a department is right, and entering a student for a paper they cannot access produces a worse outcome than a secure result at the lower tier. A family that understands why can choose sixth-form subjects the entry supports, or plan a resit in a later series with the deadlines mapped. That is a genuine plan. A year spent resenting a classroom is not, and it costs the student more than the original decision did.

faqs.question: We are choosing between the Diploma and A Level. How should we decide?
faqs.answer: Partly on the student and partly on what is actually timetabled, which in Al Ain is often the deciding factor. The Diploma suits a broadly capable student who can manage several independent deadlines; A Level suits a student with clear strengths and a settled direction, with a lighter coursework load and heavier paper weighting. The risk differs too: a Diploma student carries a weak subject for two years inside a points total, while an A Level student has less to compensate with. Confirm in writing which subjects and sets are running before accepting a place.

faqs.question: My child changed campus and now revises from the wrong material. How bad is that?
faqs.answer: Recoverable, and worth fixing immediately rather than at the end of term. Paper structure, formula sheet, question escalation and practical arrangements all differ between boards, and a student revising from the wrong board's papers is practising the wrong examination. It is usually three to five sessions of conversion work: establish the correct syllabus code with the school, learn the new paper architecture, then identify the two or three content differences between the specifications. The content knowledge transfers; the examination habits do not.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting tutoring if the entry has already closed?
faqs.answer: It depends what you are buying. If the hope is a higher grade than the tier permits, no, and anyone who takes the money for that is selling you something they cannot deliver. If the goal is the best available result within the ceiling, or preparation for a resit in a later series, or readiness for a sixth-form course the entry still supports, then yes and the work is straightforward. The distinction matters, which is why we would rather have that conversation in February than take a booking.

faqs.question: Are there enough Higher Level specialists available in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Locally, for in-person tutoring, often not. The city has few campuses, so there are few resident teachers of any given subject, and Higher Level sciences, the less common Diploma languages, Music, Design Technology and Further Mathematics are thin everywhere. For online delivery the pool is not geographic, which is the practical argument for the format here. Where no UAE-based specialist is free, the fallback is a tutor elsewhere teaching the same syllabus on Gulf Standard Time, and that is disclosed before a booking rather than after.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram hold any approval from an exam board or a regulator?
faqs.answer: No, and the question deserves a direct answer because the market is full of implied approvals. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the labour ministry, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, operates no office or centre in the UAE, and publishes no self-assessed rating or success figure. Awarding-body documents are cited and linked rather than reproduced. Any provider describing itself as approved for tutoring should be asked to produce the permit or centre number behind the claim.

al-ain/falaj-hazza.closingHeading: Tell us the decision, and how long is left
al-ain/falaj-hazza.closingBody: For a Falaj Hazza family the useful opening message is the decision you are facing and the date it closes: a tier entry in November, an option form next month, a set review at the end of Year 9, or a board that has just changed. With the syllabus code and the last two pieces of marked work we can tell you whether the decision is still movable, what evidence the department would need, and what the honest repair looks like if it is not. Where the answer is that nothing can now raise the ceiling, we will say so and plan the alternative. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, no UAE home visits are sold, and we hold no regulator approval.

al-ain/hili.tutorsIntro: The tutors here work on examination technique inside a named subject rather than on general study skills. Most Hili requests are for Diploma mathematics and sciences, IGCSE sciences at Extended tier, and the written subjects where answer structure rather than knowledge is costing the marks.

intro.heading: A class hour is not a study hour, and the difference is the whole problem
paragraphs: Hili sits at the northern edge of Al Ain, around the archaeological park that forms part of the city's recognised cultural sites, with Hili Fun City nearby and the Buraimi crossing a short drive further on. It is a quieter district than the central school belt, with villa plots, farm land at the fringes and a mixture of long-settled Emirati households and expatriate families who chose space over proximity. Children here travel into the central cluster for school, which puts them in the same classrooms as the rest of the city.

Those classrooms are the subject of this page. The complaint parents in Hili bring most often is not that teaching is poor. It is that their child seems to understand the material in class and then underperforms in examinations, and nobody can explain the contradiction. The explanation is usually structural rather than personal. A teacher has a syllabus to deliver, a set of twenty or more students, and a fixed number of lessons. Content gets covered. Technique gets mentioned.

Technique is where the marks are. An examiner awards credit against command terms and against a tariff: a four-mark question expects roughly four distinct creditable points, and a student who writes a fluent paragraph containing two of them scores two. That is not a knowledge deficit and it will not improve by reading the textbook again. It improves by answering questions, having them marked against the published scheme, and seeing precisely where credit was and was not given.

The second half of the gap is independent study, which schools set and rarely teach. A Diploma student needs a working week outside lessons, and a Year 11 student in an examination year needs a meaningful share of their evenings, but almost nobody tells a fifteen-year-old how to spend those hours. Left to themselves, students reread notes, which feels productive and changes very little. The difference between rereading and retrieval practice is worth more than any amount of extra content.

This page therefore does arithmetic rather than reassurance. It counts what a class hour can deliver and what it cannot, shows how command terms and mark tariffs decide grades, budgets independent study by year group, and explains why past papers are a skill rather than a resource. It then covers what support costs in this market and what the limits are on what a tutor may touch, because a page that answers the first question and dodges the second is not much use.

Delivery is one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE and nobody will be sent to a Hili address; home visiting is an India-only service. On the northern edge of a city with a small teaching pool, the practical consequence of the online format is that your child is matched to someone who teaches their exact syllabus rather than to whoever is willing to drive out here at five in the afternoon.
bullets: Understanding content and scoring marks are two different skills
A mark tariff tells you how many separate points an answer needs
Rereading notes is the least effective common revision method
Independent study hours should be budgeted, not assumed

al-ain/hili.programmesIntro: Hili families sit mainly on the British route and the IB continuum, with a smaller group on the Indian boards. What follows is each programme described by how much of its assessment lands outside the classroom, because that is the number this page is about.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across two levels with Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS alongside. Internal assessment is marked by the teacher against published criteria and externally moderated, generally carrying twenty to thirty per cent of a subject grade. The remainder sits in terminal papers whose questions are written around command terms rather than around topics.
programmes.countryNote: A Diploma student travelling into central Al Ain from Hili has a long day before any independent work begins, and the programme assumes a substantial working week outside lessons. The three core components in particular have no timetabled teaching hour attached to them at most campuses, which is why they are the first thing to slip.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson International GCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined by terminal papers, tiered in many subjects. Every mark on every paper is allocated against a published scheme, and the scheme is specific: it names the points that earn credit and frequently names the ones that do not. A student who has never read one is working blind in the only assessment that counts.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge runs a June and a November series and allocates each centre to one of six administrative zones, stating that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the zone. For a family in Al Ain that means working only from the document the school provides, because timetables differ between zones and the board says it cannot take responsibility for a candidate who uses the wrong one.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight and converted to a 1-7 grade. The criteria assess skills, so a low score on one of them points at a process rather than at missing content. This is the stage where a student can learn to read a rubric, which pays off for the following six years.
programmes.countryNote: Middle years students in Al Ain often reach Year 11 without ever having compared their own answer against a published descriptor. Doing it once, properly, changes how they revise. It is also the cheapest intervention available at this stage, because it needs an hour and a rubric rather than a term of teaching.

programmes.name: International AS and A Level
programmes.description: Assessed by papers with the weight concentrated in the final series, modular with Pearson and stageable with Cambridge. Mark schemes at this level are more granular still, and the step up from IGCSE is mainly in how much of an answer has to be constructed rather than recalled.
programmes.countryNote: Several Al Ain campuses run A Level rather than the Diploma, and the independent-study expectation is similar in size but different in shape: fewer components, longer papers, and a heavier reliance on the student's own question practice through the two years.

al-ain/hili.subjectsIntro: Requests from Hili concentrate on subjects where marks are lost to technique rather than to content. Each entry names the assessment, the characteristic technical failure and the first thing that moves the mark.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Method marks are awarded for visible, justified steps, and students who work mentally and write only the answer lose them routinely. The repair is written layout under timed conditions, then calculus technique. The exploration needs a topic that can be modelled, not one that reads well in a title.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics and modelling, with heavy calculator dependence. The standard loss is the final interpretation sentence: a correct test statistic followed by a conclusion that does not reference the context or the question. Three sessions on interpretation usually move more marks than ten on content.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Units, significant figures and the practical skills component take most of the recoverable marks. Explanation questions need a causal chain, and students who list facts in any order lose the sequence marks. Practice is on real result tables rather than on worked examples.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Calculations are lost to presentation as often as to method, because an unlabelled line of arithmetic earns nothing when the final answer is wrong. Organic mechanisms need the arrows drawn exactly as the scheme expects. Internal assessments founder on investigations with no genuine independent variable.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The highest-volume subject and the one where rereading is most common and least effective. Retrieval practice against past questions, marked to the scheme, is what moves the grade. Experimental design and statistics are reliably the two weakest areas on arrival.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams carry marks that prose cannot recover: correct axes, correct labels, correct shift, correct new equilibrium marked. Evaluation questions need a judgement supported by the analysis already given, and students who add a new argument in the conclusion get no credit for it.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Analysis of unseen material and a comparative essay, plus the individual oral. The common failure is observation without argument: a student notices five devices and never says what the text is doing. Structure is taught with a plan and a timer, not with more reading.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Multi-step questions escalate inside a single question, so stopping at the first unfamiliar part costs the accessible marks that follow. Working through whole papers rather than topic sheets is what trains a student to keep going.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: The alternative-to-practical paper is coachable without a laboratory and is where Hili students most often lose a grade. It tests reading apparatus, identifying variables and handling real data, all of which can be practised on paper with marked feedback.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 and Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and qualitative analysis dominate the mark allocation. Students who can define a term but not lay out a calculation bleed marks across both papers, and structured working fixes it faster than more revision does.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 and Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: Command terms decide this paper more than any other science at this level. Describe, explain, suggest and compare each want a different answer shape, and the difference between them is worth whole grades across a full paper.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics at IGCSE
subjects.description: Mark tariffs are explicit and generous to a student who answers in the structure the scheme expects. Six-mark questions need application to the case material supplied, and generic textbook answers are the single most common reason for a middling grade here.

al-ain/hili.regionsIntro: Hili children travel into the central school cluster, and families here compare campuses across the city. These are the districts that recur in enquiries from this part of Al Ain, with what each means in practice.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: The main destination for school buses out of Hili, and the city's densest private-school concentration. The run is longer than from the central districts, which is the main reason study plans here start later in the afternoon.

regions.name: Al Khabisi
regions.note: Central and often on the same bus route. Families from the two districts compare campuses constantly, and the subject gaps they report are identical because the classrooms are the same.

regions.name: Al Towayya
regions.note: Between here and the centre, beside the main hospital campus. A frequent pick-up point on northern routes, which adds minutes to a Hili child's journey in both directions.

regions.name: Al Foah
regions.note: The north-eastern fringe, with large plots and few amenities. Households there face a longer version of the same journey and the same classroom gap at the other end of it.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: Towards the oasis and the city hospital, older and more settled. Diploma coursework enquiries from there outnumber transition enquiries, which is the reverse of the pattern in the newer districts.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji
regions.note: West of the centre with a long-established school set. Bilingual households there carry a heavier weekly load, which changes how much independent study time is genuinely available.

regions.name: Asharej
regions.note: East of the centre and close to the university. Older siblings studying locally are a real asset to a Year 11 student's study week, and families there use them well.

regions.name: Buraimi, across the border
regions.note: A short drive from Hili and a factor for the households whose week spans two countries. The scheduling effect is real; the academic one is not, because the papers and the syllabus codes do not change.

modes.title: Marked question practice, every week
modes.description: The standing arrangement for a student who understands the content and loses marks anyway. The student answers questions under time, the tutor marks against the published scheme in front of them, and they argue about the difference. It is unglamorous and it is the single most reliable way to convert understanding into a grade.

Most students discover they are spending the majority of their time on the least effective activity available. The output is a weekly plan with hours attached, not a motivational talk.

modes.description: Longer blocks in which a complete paper is sat under proper conditions and then reviewed immediately while the student still remembers what they were thinking. This is the pattern for the weeks between mocks and the series, and it needs ninety minutes without a hard stop at the end of it.

sections.heading: The arithmetic of a taught hour
paragraphs: Take any secondary subject and list what has to happen for a student to score well. Content has to be delivered. It has to be understood. It has to be practised until it is fluent. The student has to learn the examination's conventions, which differ by board and by paper. They have to answer questions under time, get them marked, and act on the marking. And in most programmes there is a piece of coursework with its own criteria to be planned, drafted and revised.

Now count what a class period can hold. A teacher with a full specification and a set of twenty-plus students can deliver content, check understanding across the group, and set practice. What a class cannot do at scale is mark every student's work closely enough for them to see which creditable point they missed and why, and then watch them attempt a similar question with that in mind. That is individual work. It is not a failing of the school; it is an arithmetic constraint on one adult and twenty-five students.

The result is a predictable division of labour. The school takes the content, the student takes the technique, and nobody tells the student that is the deal. Parents in Hili describe the symptom accurately every time: my child understands it when the teacher explains it and then does badly in the test. That sentence is a description of a technique gap, and it is the single most common reason a family in this district looks for a tutor.

The table below sets that division out explicitly, which is worth doing because it reframes the decision. The question is not whether the school is good enough. It is which of the rows in that table your child is currently doing alone and without feedback, and whether one hour a week of individual marking would change the outcome. For most students who understand the material, it does.

sections.heading: Command terms, and the marks they quietly decide
paragraphs: Every examination board writes questions around a small vocabulary of instructions, and each instruction has a defined meaning that the mark scheme enforces. State wants a fact with no reasoning. Describe wants the features without causes. Explain wants a causal chain in order. Compare wants both things in the same sentence. Evaluate wants a judgement supported by the analysis already offered. These are not synonyms, and a student who treats them as interchangeable loses marks in every paper they sit.

The commonest single error is answering explain as describe. A student writes what happens, accurately and in detail, and never says why, and receives roughly half the available credit. They then conclude they are bad at the subject. They are not; they answered a different question from the one asked, and nobody has shown them the difference in a way that stuck. Showing it takes one session with four questions and a mark scheme.

The second commonest is adding new material in a conclusion. Evaluation marks are awarded for a judgement that follows from the analysis in the answer. A student who introduces a fresh argument in the final sentence gets no credit for it, because there is no analysis behind it. That is a structural habit, learned quickly once it is named, and it recurs across economics, business, biology and every essay-based subject.

The table lists the terms that cost the most marks in Al Ain classrooms, with what students write instead. It is worth reading with your child rather than at them, because the fastest version of this intervention is a student recognising their own habit on the page. From that point, question practice has a target, which is the difference between practice and repetition.
