sections.heading: The Higher Level case study, and why late is fatal here
paragraphs: Higher Level students sit an additional paper built on a case study that the IB publishes in advance of the session. The case study introduces a scenario and a body of specialist terminology, and the paper expects the student to apply course concepts to that scenario in extended written answers. Because the material is released early, the paper is not a test of recall under surprise. It is a test of how many months the student spent reading around it.

This is the component where Al Ain's small cohorts show up most clearly. In a large school the case study becomes a running thread through DP2: a reading list, a glossary built collectively, guest discussion, practice essays marked and returned. In a cohort of six with one teacher covering two levels, it frequently becomes three lessons in March. A student who meets the specialist vocabulary for the first time a fortnight before the paper will write generally where the examiner wanted specifics.

The work itself is unglamorous and perfectly suited to weekly one-to-one time. Build a glossary of every term in the released material and be able to define each one without notes. Map each concept in the case study back to the part of the syllabus it comes from. Write and mark practice responses that use the scenario's own vocabulary rather than generic examples. Read the secondary material the case study points at, a little each week, from the term it is released.

If your child is Higher Level, ask the school in the first term of DP2 what the plan for the case study is and when the released material will be handed out. If the answer is vague, that is the gap worth buying tuition for, because it is finite, it is known in advance, and it is worth a fifth of the Higher Level grade in a component nobody can revise in a weekend.

sections.heading: What Computer Science tuition costs at Al Ain market rates
paragraphs: Nobody in this market publishes figures, which is why parents ring four providers and get four non-answers. The bands below come from UAE provider rate cards and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table, read in October 2026. They describe what the market charges, not what IB Gram charges. Al Ain sits inside the Abu Dhabi emirate's pricing rather than Dubai's, and in-home rates here carry more travel loading than the capital because the city is spread out and tutors are fewer.

Read the table as a budget tool. A single weekly 60-minute session with a qualified online subject tutor at the middle of the band is a predictable monthly figure, and families generally find that easier to commit to than an intensive block bought in panic three weeks before a paper. Monthly packages advertised in the UAE have included roughly AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and roughly AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions, which is the cleanest illustration of what travel time costs when someone has to drive.

Two cost traps are specific to a subject like this one. The first is paying specialist rates for general help: a mathematics tutor can support the algorithmic thinking but cannot mark Internal Assessment documentation against Computer Science criteria, and families often discover this in month three. The second is buying hours instead of buying a plan, which produces a pleasant tutor, a satisfied student and an unchanged grade.

Whatever you pay, the figure should be attached to a named plan with dates in it. Ask what the next six sessions will cover, what will be different at the end of them, and how you will know. A provider that cannot answer that is selling hours.

sections.heading: Online, in-home, or the drive to Abu Dhabi: the honest comparison
paragraphs: Al Ain families weighing a Computer Science tutor have three real options and a fourth that is usually a fantasy. The three are an online one-to-one specialist, a local in-home tutor who can travel to the district, and a weekly drive to the capital for a face-to-face specialist. The fantasy is a local in-home tutor who is also a Higher Level Computer Science specialist with recent case-study experience, because in a city this size that person usually does not exist and waiting for them costs a term.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video, with a shared screen; home visits are a service we run only in India. We say that before the comparison rather than after it, because a parent who wants someone at the door should know immediately. What we would argue is that for this particular subject the online format is not the second-best version. A tutor who can take the keyboard, set a breakpoint and step through the student's own failing program is doing something that cannot be done over a printout.

The arithmetic on the capital drive is worth doing once. Al Ain to Abu Dhabi island is around 130 kilometres each way; a weekly session there costs roughly three hours of travel on top of the lesson, on a school night, for a student who still has homework. Over a two-year Diploma that is a large number of hours spent in a car, and the sessions get cancelled first whenever anything else goes wrong.
The table sets out what each option genuinely costs in money, time and tutor pool, so the decision can be made on the numbers rather than on a feeling about screens.

sections.heading: Academic honesty, and the line this subject makes tempting
paragraphs: Computer Science is the Diploma subject where the boundary between help and malpractice is easiest to cross by accident, because code can be copied invisibly and because a parent who writes software professionally is sitting right there. The IB's position is that assessed work must be the student's own. Support may teach, explain, question and give feedback. It may not produce the artefact.

In practice that means a tutor may explain how a hash map works, may ask why a particular data structure was chosen, may teach a method for isolating a bug, and may read documentation and say that a design decision has not been evidenced. A tutor may not supply working code for the solution, restructure the program on the student's behalf, or rewrite the documentation into something the student could not have produced. We say no to those requests, and we would rather lose the booking than put a diploma at risk.

The same line applies to anything found online. Code taken from a forum or generated by a tool and submitted without acknowledgement is a malpractice issue, and the student is the one who faces the consequence. The defensible habit is to record the source of every fragment that did not originate with the student and to be able to explain line by line what each one does. A student who can do that is also a student who will survive the written papers.

This is also why we never offer to supply past papers, mark schemes, subject guides or grade-boundary tables as downloads. Those documents belong to the IB and to the examination boards. We reference them, point at the official source, and expect the school's coordinator to be the route to anything your child's cohort is entitled to see.

process.title: Tell us the level and the deadline
process.description: Two facts decide the match: Standard or Higher Level, and the date of the next thing that matters — an internal Internal Assessment deadline, a mock, or the May papers. Everything else can be worked out in the first session, but those two determine which tutor is the right one to start with.

process.title: A free first session with the actual tutor
process.description: Not a sales call and not a generic diagnostic. The tutor works on your child's current topic, with your child's own code or last assessment open on the shared screen, so you can hear how they explain something your child has already failed to understand once.

process.title: A written plan with dates
process.description: After the trial you get a short plan naming what the next six sessions cover and what should be different at the end of them. If the plan does not say anything specific, that is a reason to say no, and we would rather you asked for it than paid without it.

process.title: A fixed weekly slot on Gulf Standard Time
process.description: Scheduled around the Al Ain school run and kept the same every week, because a recurring time that never moves is what keeps a weekly booking alive through a full term. Ramadan and travel weeks are planned around rather than cancelled into.

process.title: Review against the plan, not against a feeling
process.description: Every few weeks we check the plan against what has actually happened: marks on timed questions, Internal Assessment milestones hit or missed, topics closed. If the plan is not working we change the plan or the tutor, and that conversation starts with us rather than with you.

whyPoints.title: Matched on level, not on postcode
whyPoints.description: A Higher Level student with a case study to prepare needs someone who has taught that paper, and in Al Ain that person is unlikely to live within driving distance. Online delivery means the filter is subject and level rather than geography, which is the whole argument for the format in a city this size.

whyPoints.title: Shared-screen work on the student's own code
whyPoints.description: The tutor takes the editor, sets a breakpoint and steps through the program your child wrote, with your child watching the variables change. That is the single most useful hour available in this subject and it is easier to do over a shared screen than across a table.

whyPoints.title: The Internal Assessment treated as the student's work
whyPoints.description: We coach the process, question the scope and review drafts against the published criteria. We do not produce solutions or documentation. Saying this plainly costs us some enquiries and it is the only position compatible with your child keeping their diploma.

whyPoints.title: Al Ain's calendar, not a generic UAE one
whyPoints.description: Sessions are planned around the September-to-June Al Ain year, the long summer that is the real Internal Assessment window, Ramadan timings and the school's own internal deadlines rather than the IB's published ones.

whyPoints.title: Figures with their source attached
whyPoints.description: Every AED band on this page names where it came from and when it was read. We do not publish an invented price list, a satisfaction percentage or a star rating, because a number without its method behind it is worth nothing to a parent making a decision.

whyPoints.title: An honest no when the timeline is too short
whyPoints.description: There is a point in the final term where a subject that has been neglected for two years cannot be rebuilt, and the right advice is to protect the components still in reach. We will say so rather than sell twenty sessions into a wall.

faqs.question: My child has a 4 in DP1 Computer Science. Is a 6 realistic by the May papers?
faqs.answer: Often yes, if the 4 is a technique problem rather than a content void. Ask the teacher which components the 4 came from. If it is written-paper marks lost on describing instead of explaining, and on tracing done mentally rather than on paper, that is perhaps two terms of weekly one-to-one work and it moves reliably. If the 4 reflects a student who cannot yet get a program to compile and has no approved Internal Assessment problem, the realistic target is a 5 and the priority is the coursework, because that mark is still fully recoverable while paper technique is not.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether my child's problem is coding or exam writing?
faqs.answer: Set two tasks at the kitchen table. First, ask them to complete a trace table for a short loop on paper, with every variable written at every iteration. Second, ask them to write a five-line answer to a past-paper question that begins with the command term explain. A student who manages the trace but writes a description has an examination-writing problem. A student who writes well but cannot trace has a programming-fluency problem. Most struggling students fail both tasks, and the order of repair is tracing first, because it is mechanical and it unblocks marks across several questions on the same paper.

faqs.question: Does my child need to know Java before starting the Diploma Computer Science course?
faqs.answer: No, the course teaches it, but arriving with no text-based programming experience makes the first term harder than it needs to be. Students coming out of MYP Design having used block-based tools typically spend their first weeks fighting syntax rather than learning concepts, and that is where confidence in the subject is usually lost. A few hours of structured work on syntax, compiler errors and basic control flow before DP1 begins is the cheapest intervention available in this subject, and the August before DP1 is the natural window for it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Computer Science Internal Assessment without breaking IB rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within clear limits. A tutor may explain the published assessment criteria, challenge whether a success criterion is testable, teach a method for isolating bugs, and read a draft and say where a design decision has not been evidenced. A tutor may not supply the solution code, restructure the program on the student's behalf or rewrite the documentation. The Internal Assessment is assessed as the student's own work and anything else is a malpractice risk that falls on the student, not the tutor. We state that limit at the first session rather than after a booking.

faqs.question: When should an Al Ain student start the Computer Science Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: The client conversation and the problem scope should happen inside DP1, with the build running across the DP1 summer. Count backwards from the school's internal submission date rather than forwards from today: subtract two weeks for the student's own final checking, then the development, design and scoping windows, and you usually land somewhere in the middle of DP1. Families who spend July and August travelling without a scoped problem lose the single largest uninterrupted block of coursework time the two years contain, and DP2 has no spare space to give it back.

faqs.question: Which schools in Al Ain actually offer Diploma Computer Science?
faqs.answer: Provision is patchy and changes year to year, so the only reliable answer is the one you get from the school. Several Al Ain campuses offer the subject at Standard Level only, some run a combined Standard and Higher Level class, and a few do not offer it at all. Ask the Diploma coordinator three questions: is the subject running for your child's cohort, at which levels, and how many contact hours a week the Higher Level extension topics receive. The answer to the third question is the one that predicts whether outside support will be needed.

faqs.question: What happens in the Higher Level case study paper and when should preparation start?
faqs.answer: The IB releases a case study ahead of the session, introducing a scenario and a body of specialist terminology, and the paper asks the student to apply course concepts to it in extended answers. Because the material is published early, the paper rewards months of reading rather than last-minute revision. Preparation should start in the term the material is handed out: build a glossary of every term, map each concept back to the syllabus, and write practice responses using the scenario's own vocabulary. Three lessons in March is the commonest version of this going wrong.

faqs.question: Is it worth driving from Al Ain to Abu Dhabi for a face-to-face Computer Science specialist?
faqs.answer: Rarely, once the arithmetic is done. Al Ain to Abu Dhabi island is around 130 kilometres each way, so a weekly session costs roughly three hours of travel on a school night on top of the lesson itself. Over a two-year Diploma that is a very large number of hours, and the sessions get cancelled first whenever anything else in the week goes wrong. For a subject where the work happens on a screen anyway, a live video session with a shared editor gets you a wider pool of Higher Level specialists and no travel at all.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to our villa in Zakher or Hili?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. Tutoring for Al Ain families is delivered one-to-one over live video with a shared screen, on Gulf Standard Time. For Computer Science specifically this is a genuine advantage rather than a compromise, because the tutor can take control of the editor and step through your child's own failing program line by line. We say this before quoting anything, so a family who wants someone physically present knows immediately.

faqs.question: What does weekly Computer Science tuition cost for an Al Ain family?
faqs.answer: Market rates in the UAE for a qualified subject tutor working online run roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, and for an IB specialist roughly AED 200 to 450 and upwards, according to provider rate cards and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table read in October 2026. In-home rates sit higher, around AED 180 to 500, because travel is priced in, and in a spread-out city that loading is heavier than in the capital. Those are market bands rather than our price list. The first session with us is free and you hear the tutor teach before any figure is discussed.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does a Diploma Computer Science student usually need?
faqs.answer: One weekly session of 60 or 90 minutes covers most term-time cases, with short additional blocks around the Internal Assessment and in the final twelve weeks. Two sessions a week makes sense only when there is a specific backlog with a deadline attached, such as an unbuilt Internal Assessment with three months left. More than two is generally a sign that the problem is work habits rather than subject knowledge, and that is slow and expensive to fix with paid hours rather than with a different routine at home.

faqs.question: Can the same tutor cover Computer Science and Mathematics for one student?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking because two subjects with one tutor is easier to schedule than two tutors with one slot each. The overlap is real at the algorithmic end: sequences, logic and the discipline of working a problem by hand. The overlap stops at coursework. A mathematics specialist cannot mark Computer Science Internal Assessment documentation against its published criteria, and a Computer Science specialist should not be your only support for the non-calculator Analysis and Approaches Paper 1. Where both are needed properly, two matched tutors is the honest answer.

faqs.question: My child is the only Higher Level Computer Science student in their Al Ain class. Does that matter?
faqs.answer: It matters for two specific things. The extension topics — abstract data structures, resource management and control — tend to get fewer contact hours when one teacher is covering both levels, and the case study often becomes a short unit rather than a running thread. Neither is a reflection on the school; it is arithmetic. Both are also well suited to one-to-one work, because the material is self-contained and does not need a class to function. Ask the coordinator how many weekly hours the extension content gets, and plan outside support around the gap that answer reveals.

faqs.question: Will sessions still run during Ramadan and the long Al Ain summer?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the timing changed rather than the frequency. During Ramadan most families move the weekly slot later, after Iftar, and shorten it; a 60-minute session at 21:00 works better than a 90-minute one at 17:00. The summer is different in kind: July and August are the largest uninterrupted Internal Assessment window the Diploma offers, and a short block of sessions across it is usually worth more than the same hours bought in a panic in February. Travel weeks are planned around in advance rather than cancelled at short notice.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in Al Ain need a permit, and how can I check?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit: the private tuition work permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through MoHRE, free of charge, for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone offering private tutoring without a permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Ask any tutor directly whether they hold one, and check the current rules on mohre.gov.ae rather than taking a provider's word for it.

faqs.question: It is six weeks before the papers and nothing has been done. What is actually recoverable?
faqs.answer: Paper technique, and not much else. In six weeks a student can be drilled on trace tables, on the command terms and on timed past-paper answers, and that alone is often worth a grade because the losses are systematic rather than scattered. Content taught from scratch across a two-year course is not recoverable in six weeks, and an unbuilt Internal Assessment at that point is a conversation with the school rather than with a tutor. We will say that plainly, and we would rather protect the marks still in reach than sell hours into a deadline that has already passed.

al-ain/ib-dp-computer-science-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the free session, then decide
al-ain/ib-dp-computer-science-tutor.closingBody: The useful next step is small. Tell us whether your child is at Standard or Higher Level and what the next real deadline is — an internal Internal Assessment date, a mock, or the May papers. We match a Diploma Computer Science tutor on level rather than on location, and the first session is free: your child's own code or last assessment open on a shared screen, with the tutor working on the thing that is actually stuck. Afterwards you get a short written plan with dates in it, and you decide whether the plan is worth paying for. If six weeks is too few, we will tell you that instead.

al-ain/ib-dp-economics-hl-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Diploma Economics at Higher Level for Al Ain students. Matching is by component - the extended-response paper, the data-response paper, the Higher Level policy paper, or the commentary portfolio - because those four jobs reward noticeably different teaching.

intro.heading: The emirate decides more about this plan than the syllabus does
paragraphs: Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, which means its private schools fall under ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, the body that supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. That is not a detail. It determines whose published guidance applies to your child's week, who approves a fee increase at the campus, and which inspection framework a report refers to. Most UAE tutoring pages are written about Dubai, name KHDA, and are simply about a different jurisdiction.

The second fact that shapes an Economics plan here is scale. Published figures for Dubai's private school sector in 2024-25 give a sense of how small the International Baccalaureate population is even in the country's largest market: 387,441 students across 227 private schools offering seventeen different curricula, with UK curriculum schools taking 37 per cent of enrolment, Indian 26 per cent, American 14 per cent and the IB 7 per cent. Dubai is also adding seven new private schools for 2026-27, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places. Al Ain's school set is not growing that way, so a Higher Level Economics group inland is often a handful of students taught by the campus's only economics specialist.

That has direct consequences a plan should name. A small group means fewer past-paper sets marked, less differentiation between the Higher Level and Standard Level halves of a shared class, and a single teacher supervising every commentary in the cohort - which affects how quickly draft feedback comes back and when a family should look outside the school for a second read. It also means the option block is tight: Economics, Business Management and Geography frequently compete for the same slot, and in a small cohort the timetable decides rather than the student.

The third fact is the calendar, and for Economics it is unusually demanding. The internal assessment is a portfolio of three commentaries, each based on a different published news article, each covering a different unit of the course and a different key concept. That means the student has to be reading the economic news across both years rather than hunting for three articles in one week, and it means the writing has to be scheduled into gaps the school has already spoken for. We have seen more Economics marks lost to a bad calendar than to a misunderstood diagram.

So the structure of this page follows the system rather than the textbook. What the Abu Dhabi school environment decides. How Higher Level differs from Standard Level in weighting and hours. What Paper 3 actually asks. How the portfolio is marked, criterion by criterion. Which key concept pays in which paper. What a realistic two-year Al Ain calendar looks like. Where the marks go missing. What it all costs in context. And how lessons are delivered, stated plainly.

al-ain/ib-dp-economics-hl-tutor.programmesIntro: Economics arrives late in a student's schooling - most meet it for the first time in DP1 - so the route in matters less for content than for habits. Each stage below is described by the habit it leaves behind.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Economics is taken in the individuals and societies group at Standard or Higher Level, built from four units: introduction to economics, microeconomics, macroeconomics and the global economy. Nine key concepts run through all of them. Higher Level carries 240 teaching hours, an extra examination in the form of the policy paper, and a different weighting across the components, while the commentary portfolio is common to both levels.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain the Higher Level and Standard Level groups are frequently taught together for much of the week, with the Higher Level extension content covered separately. Families should ask which Higher Level-only material has actually been taught by the end of DP1, because that answer varies by campus and determines what the first term of DP2 has to recover.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP individuals and societies builds the habit this course needs most: using evidence from a source to support an argument and then evaluating it. Students from that route tend to write better commentaries, because the portfolio is essentially a short piece of evidence-led analysis with a diagram in it, and they have been marked on that shape for years.
programmes.countryNote: MYP through to Year 11 is the minority route in Al Ain, where IGCSE is more common. Where it exists, the gain shows up in criterion E - evaluation - which is the hardest of the commentary criteria to teach from scratch in DP2.

programmes.name: IGCSE Economics and Business Studies
programmes.description: Cambridge Economics 0455 or Business Studies 0450 gives a student the vocabulary and the basic diagrams, which is a real head start. What neither builds is the evaluative habit: IGCSE rewards accurate explanation, and the Diploma pays for weighing a policy against its costs, its assumptions and the context it is applied in. A strong IGCSE grade predicts a comfortable DP1 and says nothing about Paper 3.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain students sit Cambridge in the June and November series and Pearson in May/June and November, so sibling examination seasons regularly overlap a Diploma student's commentary deadlines. That collision is predictable and should be on the calendar from the start of DP1.

programmes.name: The portfolio and the diploma core
programmes.description: The three commentaries sit alongside the Theory of Knowledge essay and the Extended Essay, and all three want sustained independent writing in the same months of DP2. Economics is also one of the most popular Extended Essay subjects, and a student doing both needs the commentary topics and the essay question kept clearly apart to avoid overlapping work.
programmes.countryNote: Internal commentary deadlines vary widely between Al Ain campuses - some schools space them one per term from DP1, others collect all three late in DP2. Which pattern your school uses changes the plan completely, so it is the first thing we ask for.

al-ain/ib-dp-economics-hl-tutor.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are the ones Al Ain Economics students most often carry alongside, and in a small cohort the combination is usually decided by the option block. Each note says where the overlap genuinely helps.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Four units and nine key concepts, assessed through extended response, data response, a Higher Level policy paper and a three-commentary portfolio. Marks are most often lost on evaluation and on diagrams that are drawn correctly but never used in the argument.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The most common alternative in the same option block, and frequently the one a student should have taken instead. It rewards applied decision-making over theoretical modelling, so a student who dislikes diagrams but likes cases often belongs here - a conversation worth having in DP1, not DP2.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: Shares the global economy unit's territory from the other side: trade blocs, sovereignty, development. Students taking both can usually reuse the same reading, and the political-economy framing improves evaluation in Economics answers noticeably.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Overlaps on development, resource use and sustainability, one of the nine key concepts. Fieldwork statistics also transfer to the data-response paper, where reading a table under time pressure is half the task.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: The strongest companion for essay technique. A student who can sustain an argument under evidence in a History Paper 2 essay has most of what the Economics extended-response paper wants, and the transfer works in both directions.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The applied statistics here map directly onto the quantitative half of the Higher Level policy paper and onto data response generally. Students taking both should be getting double value from one set of lessons on correlation, error and interpretation.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Less directly transferable, but relevant to the workload question: a student carrying Higher Level Economics, Higher Level Analysis and a Higher Level science has very little slack for three commentaries and two core components in the same year.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Behavioural insights sit close to the intervention and choice concepts, and the research-methods content sharpens evaluation. Useful signal: if evaluation is weak in both subjects, the problem is the skill, not the content.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Both compete with the commentaries for DP2 weeks, and Economics is a popular Extended Essay subject. Where a student does both in Economics, the research question and the commentary topics must be distinct, and the school's supervisor should confirm that early.

Usually five to eight sessions, timed to follow the school's mocks

sections.heading: What the Abu Dhabi school environment decides about an Economics plan
paragraphs: Start with the regulator, because it tells you which published guidance is actually about your child. ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, Al Ain included. KHDA, whose announcements dominate UAE education coverage, is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai. When KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in the emirate for 2026-27, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total, that was a Dubai decision. It is a useful reference point for what school fees do to a household budget, and it is not a statement about an Al Ain campus.

Then look at scale, because it explains the staffing reality behind a small Higher Level Economics group. Dubai's private sector in 2024-25 enrolled 387,441 students across 227 schools offering seventeen curricula, with UK curriculum schools taking 37 per cent of enrolment, Indian 26 per cent, American 14 per cent and the International Baccalaureate 7 per cent. Seven new private schools are opening there for 2026-27 - four UK curriculum, three IB - creating 16,846 places, after six opened during 2025-26 and enrolment rose six per cent. Al Ain is not on that growth curve. Its private-school set is much smaller than Abu Dhabi island's, and the IB share of a smaller market is a smaller number again.

The practical consequences for Economics are three. The Higher Level group may be small enough to be taught alongside Standard Level for much of the week, which means the Higher Level-only content needs tracking explicitly rather than trusting the published order. One teacher usually supervises every commentary in the year group, which slows draft turnaround at exactly the point a student needs it fast. And the option block is tight, so Economics, Business Management and Geography often compete for one slot and the timetable decides.

None of that is a criticism of Al Ain schools, which are working with the cohort sizes an inland city produces. It is an argument for asking three specific questions early: how many students are in the Higher Level half of the class, which Higher Level extension topics have been taught by the end of DP1, and what the school's commentary deadline pattern is. Those answers shape a plan more than any syllabus summary does.

The Dubai fee freeze of 22 May 2026 is Dubai-only and is context, not a local rule
The IB is a small share even of Dubai's 387,441 private-school students

sections.heading: Higher Level against Standard Level: the extra paper and the extra hours
paragraphs: The two levels share four units - introduction to economics, microeconomics, macroeconomics and the global economy - and the same nine key concepts. Higher Level runs to 240 teaching hours against 150, carries additional content inside each unit, and adds a third examination. The portfolio of three commentaries is common to both.

The weightings differ in a way that changes revision priorities completely. At Standard Level the paper work splits between an extended-response paper at thirty per cent and a data-response paper at forty, with the portfolio at thirty. At Higher Level the extended-response paper falls to twenty per cent, data response to thirty, the portfolio to twenty, and the policy paper takes thirty. So a Higher Level student has nearly a third of their grade sitting on a component a Standard Level student never sees, and a correspondingly smaller share on the essay paper that most revision time instinctively goes to.

That reweighting is the single most useful fact on this page for a family deciding where hours should go. A Higher Level student spending every session on essay technique is optimising the smallest of their three examination components. Paper 3 and data response together are sixty per cent of the Higher Level grade, and both reward quantitative handling and structured policy reasoning rather than fluent prose.

Component durations, mark totals and weightings are published in the subject guide your child's school teaches from and are revised between guides. Confirm them with the school before using the table below to set priorities, and ask specifically which Higher Level extension topics in each unit have been covered.

sections.heading: Paper 3, and where Higher Level grades actually separate
paragraphs: Paper 3 is the Higher Level policy paper: one hour forty-five minutes of compulsory questions that mix quantitative work with a requirement to recommend and justify a policy. It carries thirty per cent of the grade - more than the extended-response paper and the portfolio individually - and most students do not meet it properly until a mock examination in DP2.

It fails in predictable ways. The first is arithmetic under time: the quantitative parts are not difficult mathematics, but a student who has to think about every calculation loses minutes they needed for the written sections. Drilling the routines until they are automatic is two or three sessions of work and it pays for itself immediately. The second is the recommendation itself. Students write what a policy does rather than why this policy, in this context, with these trade-offs, given what the data shows. The marks are in the justification and the acknowledgement of what might go wrong.

The third failure is structural. Paper 3's questions build, so a student who abandons a part they cannot complete loses the parts that follow it. Teaching the behaviour - state the assumption, make the calculation, carry it forward, say what it implies - is more valuable than teaching more content, because by DP2 the content is usually there and the handling is not.

Timing matters as much as technique. Paper 3 work placed too early is wasted, because policy reasoning needs the macroeconomics and global economy content behind it; placed too late it competes with whole-paper revision. After the mocks and before the final stretch is the window, which in practice means a block of five to eight sessions in the second half of DP2. Confirm the paper's duration and weighting with the school, since both have changed between guides.

sections.heading: The portfolio: three commentaries, nine key concepts, 45 marks
paragraphs: The internal assessment is a portfolio of three commentaries, each based on a different published news article, each no longer than 800 words. Between them they must cover three different units of the course and three different key concepts, and each is marked against criteria carrying fourteen marks, with a further three marks for the portfolio meeting the rubric requirements - forty-five marks in total.

The criterion that costs most is the diagram one, and not for the reason parents expect. Students draw accurate diagrams and then fail to use them: the diagram sits in the middle of the page while the prose makes an unrelated point. The marks are for a diagram that is correctly drawn, fully labelled, referred to explicitly in the analysis and actually necessary to the argument. The second expensive criterion is evaluation, where a student lists advantages and disadvantages instead of weighing them against stated assumptions, the short and long run, or who bears the cost.

Article choice decides most of this before any writing happens. An article has to be recent, has to be about an identifiable economic event rather than general commentary, and has to allow a diagram that genuinely explains something. News opinion pieces are the commonest bad choice, because they argue rather than report, and a student then ends up evaluating the columnist instead of the economics. Testing three candidate articles against those conditions takes twenty minutes and saves a commentary.

The portfolio's three-way spread is the other planning trap. Because the commentaries must cover different units and different key concepts, choosing all three in the first available window usually produces two good ones and one forced. Spacing them - one in each of the first three available terms - lets the student pick an article that suits the unit they have just studied. Confirm the word limit, the criteria and the rubric requirements against your cohort's subject guide.

sections.heading: The nine key concepts, and which component each one pays in
paragraphs: Scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, economic well-being, sustainability, change, interdependence and intervention. Students learn the list in the first weeks of DP1 and then treat it as decoration, which is a mistake with a measurable cost: one commentary criterion is specifically about integrating a key concept, and examiners reward the same integration in extended response and in the policy paper.

The practical use of the list is as a planning tool. The portfolio needs three different concepts, so choosing them deliberately - rather than discovering in week three of DP2 that two commentaries both lean on efficiency - saves a rewrite. And in the examination, a concept is the fastest route to evaluation: a student asked whether a subsidy is justified can reach a real judgement by asking what it does to equity and to sustainability, rather than listing effects.

Some concepts are also far easier to evidence than others in a UAE context, which is worth saying because article choice is a local decision. Interdependence and change are straightforward to find in regional trade and energy coverage. Sustainability and equity appear constantly in Gulf development and diversification reporting. Intervention is the easiest of all, because almost any subsidy, tariff or price control story supplies it directly.

sections.heading: An Al Ain Economics calendar: when the commentaries actually have to be written
paragraphs: Every Economics plan in this city lives or dies on the calendar, because the portfolio is the one component a student controls and therefore the one that gets postponed. The table below is the pattern we work to for a student starting at the beginning of DP1, with the caution that the internal dates belong to the school and vary widely between Al Ain campuses.

The logic is to attach each commentary to the unit just taught, so the student writes about microeconomics while microeconomics is fresh and has a reason to be reading the relevant news. That also spreads the writing across three terms instead of three weeks, which protects the evaluation criterion - the one that collapses first under time pressure. The Higher Level policy paper block then sits in the second half of DP2, after the mocks, where it does not compete with the commentaries.

Two local fixtures go on the calendar before anything else. Ramadan moves the evening, and most of our Al Ain families switch to post-iftar sessions with shorter running times, which suits commentary discussion better than timed paper work. The long inland summer is when families travel, so a reduced cross-time-zone schedule is normal, and it is a good window for article collection because reading the news does not require a tutor.

On dates set by awarding bodies rather than by the school: Cambridge and Pearson publish their timetables, and for sibling examinations in the household those matter. A UAE candidate sits one of two Cambridge series, June or November, and the planning work is in counting backwards from whichever one the school has entered them for: entries close months ahead of the first paper, in the spring for a June series and around the start of the autumn term for November, and the binding date sits on the centre's statement of entry rather than on any page like this one. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, so the only timetable worth printing on a revision plan is the zone version the school itself uses. For the IB Diploma itself we publish no session or results dates here, because none in this project's research is confirmed from the IB directly - your school's Diploma coordinator holds the windows and the internal upload dates, and that is the source to use.

sections.heading: Where Higher Level Economics marks are actually lost
paragraphs: Four patterns account for most of the gap between a 4 and a 6, and only one of them is about knowing less economics. The first is the unused diagram. Students draw correctly and then write prose that does not refer to the diagram, which forfeits marks in both the commentary and the extended-response paper. The fix is mechanical: every diagram gets a sentence that names it, points at the specific movement on it, and says what that movement means for the argument.

The second is listed evaluation. Asked to evaluate, a student produces a column of advantages and a column of disadvantages and stops, which reads as balanced and scores in the middle. Real evaluation weighs: against stated assumptions, over the short run and the long run, and by asking who bears the cost. Teaching it means forcing a judgement at the end of every answer, in one sentence, with a reason attached.

The third is the definition-and-calculation marks on data response. Paper 2 hands out marks for defining terms accurately and for correct calculation with units, and students in a hurry skip both to get to the analysis they find interesting. Those are the cheapest marks in the whole course and the most commonly abandoned. An audit of one marked data-response paper usually finds four or five of them left on the table.

The fourth is the Higher Level content gap created by a shared class. Where Higher Level and Standard Level are taught together for much of the week in a small Al Ain cohort, the Higher Level extension material is covered in separate sessions that are easier to lose to a school event or an absence. The signature is a student who is fine on Papers 1 and 2 and lost on Paper 3, and the remedy is to list the extension topics and check them off rather than assume coverage.

sections.heading: What Economics support costs in context for an Al Ain family
paragraphs: Tutoring is the small line in an education budget and the only one a family can aim precisely, which is why it is worth costing by the job. The table below prices the actual jobs in Economics - a commentary, a Paper 3 block, a term of weekly work - against the bands providers publish, so the comparison is with the alternatives rather than with an abstraction.

The bands themselves, for completeness and with their sources. Budget online tuition and university-student tutors advertise AED 45 to 150 an hour, EdFlik listing from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. Qualified subject tutors working online publish AED 150 to 300, Unitors showing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one visits including travel are quoted at AED 180 to 500, with Bestimate's Dubai table at AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors at AED 200 to 500. IB and IGCSE specialists sit at AED 200 to 450 and above, TutorChase published at AED 270. Premium named or examiner-level provision reaches AED 500 to 650 and beyond, BartyED at AED 650. Monthly packages advertised in this market include AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions, and Bestimate's monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions run AED 240 to 600 for budget, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support.

All of those figures were published by the providers named and read in October 2026. None is an IB Gram price list. We quote after a free trial lesson produces a diagnosis, because the honest variable in Economics is which component needs the hours, and that is not knowable from a report card. The bands do let you interrogate a quote: ask whether marked written work is included, whether the tutor has taught Paper 3 specifically, and whether travel sits inside the number.

For the larger context, school fees are the dominant education cost in any UAE household, and the clearest recent published marker is KHDA's confirmation on 22 May 2026 that Dubai private school fees would not rise for 2026-27 under the emirate's second economic incentives package. Al Ain campuses sit under ADEK rather than KHDA, so that specific decision does not apply here - but it frames the proportion: the tutoring decision is a fraction of the fee decision, and it is the one that can be pointed at a single component.

sections.heading: How lessons are delivered, and the home-tutor question answered plainly
paragraphs: Families in Al Ain searching for Economics help often mean someone at the table, so the position without hedging: IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. In-home tutoring is a service we run only in India, and we hold no office, centre or branch anywhere in the Emirates. Al Ain sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with articles and data shared on screen, diagrams drawn on a shared whiteboard, and marked work returned in writing.

For this subject the online format has advantages that are not generic. The commentary depends on live published articles, and a session where tutor and student open the same article together, scroll the same data table and annotate the same paragraph is closer to how the work is actually done than a conversation about an article one person has printed. Diagrams are drawn and redrawn on a shared canvas and the file survives the session, so a student revising in April has the version built in November. And a recorded explanation of a Paper 3 calculation can be rewatched, which is more useful than a remembered one.

The supply argument is the stronger one, though. The pool of tutors who can reach an Al Ain address on a weekday evening and who have taught the Higher Level policy paper is extremely small - the city's inland position is exactly why. A specialist travelling from Abu Dhabi is roughly 130 kilometres each way, which is rarely sustainable weekly for a whole academic year. Online, the constraint disappears and the match is made on the component rather than on the commute.

One honest limit: online delivery does not make a student read the news, and this course rewards students who do. We set the reading expectation explicitly, ask for article candidates rather than supplying them, and if after six weeks nothing has been read between sessions we say so plainly rather than selling another term.

process.title: Send the school's commentary pattern
process.description: Whether your child's campus spaces the three commentaries across terms or collects them late in DP2, and the dates it has set. That single answer changes the whole shape of an Economics plan and it differs between Al Ain campuses.

process.title: Send a marked data-response paper
process.description: Not an essay - a marked Paper 2 attempt. It shows whether definition and calculation marks are being abandoned, whether diagrams are being used, and whether evaluation is listed or weighed. Those three faults cover most of what goes wrong.

process.title: A free trial lesson with the tutor who would mark the work
process.description: Sixty minutes spent on a data-response question and an article test, not on introductions. You receive a written diagnosis naming which component the hours should go to, including when the answer is the school's own clinics.

process.title: Check the Higher Level extension topics
process.description: In a shared Higher Level and Standard Level class the extension content is the part most easily lost. We list the topics and confirm what has actually been taught before planning Paper 3 work, rather than assuming the published order.

process.title: Fix the slot and review against marked work
process.description: A weekly slot held for the term around the Al Ain school run and Ramadan timings, with marked work compared against the baseline every few weeks. Two reviews without movement means changing the approach or the tutor.

whyPoints.title: The right regulator, and no borrowed authority
whyPoints.description: Al Ain sits under ADEK, and we say what that body actually does. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and we will not imply otherwise.

whyPoints.title: Weighted towards the components that carry the grade
whyPoints.description: Paper 3 and data response are sixty per cent of a Higher Level Economics grade. A plan that spends every session on essay technique is optimising the smallest examination component, and we say so in the first conversation.

whyPoints.title: Commentaries spaced, not clustered
whyPoints.description: Each commentary is attached to the unit just taught, which gives the student a reason to be reading the relevant news and protects the evaluation criterion. Three commentaries written in one fortnight is a predictable loss of marks.

whyPoints.title: Diagrams judged on use, not on accuracy
whyPoints.description: Marks go to a diagram that is named, pointed at and necessary to the argument. Correctly drawn and never mentioned is the commonest avoidable loss in this subject, in the portfolio and in the examination alike.

whyPoints.title: The shared-class gap checked explicitly
whyPoints.description: Where a small Al Ain cohort means Higher and Standard Level are taught together, the Higher Level extension content is the part that slips. We list it and confirm coverage rather than discovering the gap in a mock.

whyPoints.title: Figures attributed and dated
whyPoints.description: Every AED band here is attached to the provider that published it and the month it was read, and every job is costed rather than left as a rate. We quote our own fee after a diagnosis, never before one.

faqs.question: Which authority oversees my child's school in Al Ain, and does it set tutoring rules?
faqs.answer: ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools across the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, which includes Al Ain. It does not regulate private tutoring, which runs through a MoHRE work permit instead, and it does not set what a tutor may charge. KHDA, which features in most UAE education news, is responsible for private education in Dubai, so its fee and inspection announcements are not statements about an Al Ain campus. Any provider claiming regulator approval for its tutoring should be asked to evidence it.

faqs.question: How is Higher Level Economics weighted differently from Standard Level?
faqs.answer: At Standard Level the extended-response paper carries thirty per cent, data response forty and the portfolio thirty. At Higher Level the extended-response paper falls to twenty, data response to thirty, the portfolio to twenty, and the policy paper takes thirty. Higher Level also runs 240 teaching hours against 150, with extension content inside each of the four units. The practical consequence is that Paper 3 and data response together are sixty per cent of a Higher Level grade. Confirm the weightings against your cohort's subject guide before planning revision around them.

faqs.question: What exactly is in Paper 3, and when should my son start preparing for it?
faqs.answer: Paper 3 is the Higher Level policy paper: one hour forty-five minutes of compulsory questions combining quantitative work with a requirement to recommend and justify a policy. It carries thirty per cent of the Higher Level grade. Preparation belongs after the school's mocks, in a block of roughly five to eight sessions, because the policy reasoning needs the macroeconomics and global economy content behind it. Started in DP1 it is wasted; left to the final fortnight it competes with whole-paper revision. Most students otherwise meet it twice: once in a mock and once for real.

faqs.question: How many commentaries does the Economics portfolio need, and how long is each one?
faqs.answer: Three, each based on a different published news article and each no longer than 800 words. Between them they must cover three different units of the course and three different key concepts, with marks awarded per commentary plus a portfolio-level allocation for meeting the rubric requirements - forty-five marks in total. Material beyond the word limit is not credited. The commonest avoidable error is two commentaries drawn from the same unit, which costs marks at portfolio level however good the individual pieces are.

faqs.question: What makes a news article suitable for a commentary?
faqs.answer: Three conditions. It should be recent, within the window the guide allows and the school confirms. It should report an identifiable economic event rather than offer general commentary, because a student needs something specific to apply theory to. And it should permit a diagram that genuinely explains part of what happened. Opinion columns are the commonest bad choice: they argue rather than report, and the student ends up evaluating the writer instead of the economics. Testing three candidates against those conditions takes twenty minutes and often saves a whole commentary.

faqs.question: Why does my daughter draw perfect diagrams and still lose marks?
faqs.answer: Because the diagram is not being used. Marks go to a diagram that is correctly drawn, fully labelled, referred to explicitly in the analysis and necessary to the argument - not to a diagram that sits accurately in the middle of the page while the prose makes an unrelated point. The repair is mechanical and quick: every diagram earns a sentence that names it, points at the specific movement on it and says what that movement means. It applies in the commentary and in the extended-response paper equally.

faqs.question: What does real evaluation look like in an Economics answer?
faqs.answer: A judgement with a reason attached. Listing advantages and then disadvantages reads as balanced and scores in the middle, because nothing has been weighed. Evaluation weighs against something: the assumptions the theory rests on, the short run against the long run, or who actually bears the cost. One sentence of judgement at the end of every answer, with a stated basis, moves more marks than extra content. The nine key concepts are the fastest route to it, since equity and sustainability both supply a criterion for judging a policy.

faqs.question: Our Al Ain school teaches Higher and Standard Level Economics together. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: It is a coverage question rather than a quality one. With small cohorts a combined class is simple arithmetic, but the Higher Level extension material is then covered in separate sessions that are easier to lose to an absence or a school event. The signature of a gap is a student who is fine on Papers 1 and 2 and lost on Paper 3. Before planning anything we list the Higher Level extension topics in each unit and confirm which have actually been taught, which usually takes one session and prevents a term of guessing.

faqs.question: Should my son be taking Business Management instead of Economics?
faqs.answer: It is worth asking in DP1 rather than DP2, and in Al Ain the two often compete for the same option slot. Economics rewards theoretical modelling, diagrams and policy reasoning; Business Management rewards applied decision-making on cases. A student who engages with company situations but resents diagrams is frequently in the wrong one of the two. The decision belongs to the school and has a deadline. If a trial lesson suggests the subject rather than the support is the problem, we will say so.

faqs.question: How many sessions does an Economics HL student in Al Ain usually need?
faqs.answer: By job rather than by term. A commentary block is three or four sessions. A Paper 3 intensive after the mocks is five to eight. A term of weekly content and marked answers is twelve to fourteen. Published specialist rates in this market run AED 200 to 450 and above per hour, with TutorChase at AED 270, so those job sizes convert straight into a budget. We quote after a free trial lesson, because which component needs the hours is not knowable from a report card.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send an Economics tutor to our home in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE - in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India - and we hold no office, centre or branch anywhere in the Emirates. Al Ain sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with articles and data opened on a shared screen and diagrams drawn on a shared whiteboard. For this subject that genuinely helps: the commentary depends on live published articles, and working through the same page together is closer to how the task is actually done.

faqs.question: Is it true that school fees are frozen, and does that affect what tutoring costs?
faqs.answer: KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. That is a Dubai decision and Al Ain campuses sit under ADEK, so it is context rather than a local rule. It has no bearing on tutoring rates, which no education regulator in the UAE sets. It is useful only as a reminder of proportion: fees are the large number and tutoring is the small, targetable one.

faqs.question: Can my child's own economics teacher tutor them privately in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: It has been reported that ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from giving paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and that teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That reporting should be checked against ADEK's current policy document before being treated as exact wording. Either way it is the arrangement most likely to create a problem for the teacher, and we would not recommend pursuing it.

faqs.question: When should we be collecting commentary articles if the deadlines are later?
faqs.answer: Continuously, from the first term of DP1. The portfolio needs three articles from three different units, so a student who reads regional economic coverage weekly ends up choosing from a collection instead of searching under pressure. The long summer is a good window for this, because reading the news needs no tutor and no timetable. Students who leave article selection to the fortnight before a deadline usually produce one strong commentary and two forced ones, and the weakness shows up in the evaluation and key-concept marks.

faqs.question: Do the commentaries keep moving forward through Ramadan and the travel months?
faqs.answer: The timing moves rather than the plan stopping. During Ramadan most Al Ain families switch to post-iftar slots and we shorten sessions, which suits commentary discussion better than timed paper work - so we usually move the writing-heavy items into those weeks and the timed papers out of them. Across the inland summer, families travelling away keep a reduced schedule across time zones, which works because nothing in a video session depends on either person being in the city. The revised schedule is agreed in advance so the calendar shifts as a set.

faqs.question: What happens if no Higher Level Economics specialist is free in our slot?
faqs.answer: We tell you instead of substituting a general individuals-and-societies tutor. The policy paper and the commentary criteria need someone who has taught them, and in peak season the early-evening Gulf Standard Time slots fill. In that case we offer the nearest available times, a different weekday, or a start a fortnight later with the calendar recalculated from the school's commentary deadline. Where the deadline makes that impossible we say so, because selling a block that cannot reach the submission date helps nobody.

al-ain/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-lite.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Diploma Programme English A: Language and Literature at both levels: unseen non-literary analysis, the comparative essay on literary works, the Individual Oral and the Higher Level essay. Al Ain students are matched on level and on the component with the nearest deadline.

intro.heading: Four components, four different clocks
paragraphs: English A: Language and Literature is the Diploma subject where the gap between a 4 and a 6 is almost never about reading more. It is about four separate assessments, each with its own clock, and a student who is behind on all four needs a different plan from one who is behind on three but has a strong Individual Oral already recorded. The first useful question is not what your child has read. It is which components are already fixed, which are in progress, and how many weeks remain on each.

That is the shape of this page, because it is the shape of the actual problem. Paper 1 and Paper 2 are sat at the end and can be improved up to the final fortnight. The Individual Oral is assessed internally, usually in DP2, and once it is recorded the mark is effectively fixed. The Higher Level essay has a submission date months before the papers. A parent who understands that ordering can direct money and attention at the component where it still changes something, instead of spreading it thinly across all four.

Al Ain adds a specific wrinkle that Dubai pages never mention. Many students here come from households where English is the language of school but not the language of home, and Language and Literature assumes a reader who can handle an unseen advertisement, political cartoon or opinion column written for an audience somewhere else entirely. A student with excellent English and no cultural footholds in the text loses marks on inference rather than on language. That is a teachable gap, but it has to be named before it can be taught, and most schools do not name it.

Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For this subject the format is genuinely well suited: the work is annotating the same text and the same marked script at the same time, which a shared screen does cleanly, and which also leaves a record of every annotated paragraph that both the student and the parent can go back to.

What follows is the honest sequence. How to read the grade you already have. The four components and which one is still movable. Paper 1 and the first twelve minutes that decide it. The Individual Oral, counted backwards from the recording date. The Higher Level essay. The learner portfolio, which is the cheapest insurance in the course. Which Language A route suits a bilingual Al Ain student. And what the Al Ain market charges, in AED, with the date and the source named. Where a UAE university place is the destination rather than a UK or US one, we also cover how the Ministry of Education equivalency route reads a Language A grade, because that is the one detail Al Ain families are most often told wrongly.

al-ain/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-lite.programmesIntro: The English grade a student leaves the Diploma with is partly decided before DP1 begins, and the route into Language and Literature matters as much as the course itself. These are the stages that shape an Al Ain student's outcome in this subject.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language and Literature is the direct feeder, and it rewards a slightly different thing from the Diploma. MYP marking credits personal response and creative engagement generously; Diploma marking credits analysis of how a text produces its effect. A student can leave MYP with a 7 for writing beautifully about how a poem made them feel and arrive in DP1 with no habit of naming a technique and explaining its function.
programmes.countryNote: Because Al Ain cohorts are small and often continuous from MYP into DP, a year group's writing habits tend to be uniform. If the MYP department prized personal response, the whole DP1 class will be writing personal responses in October and losing the same marks in the same place. That is worth knowing, because it means your child's weakness may be a house style rather than an individual gap.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme, first year
programmes.description: DP1 covers the first areas of exploration, the first literary works and the start of the learner portfolio. The global issue for the Individual Oral is often chosen late in DP1, and the extracts selected soon after. A student who reaches the end of DP1 with an empty portfolio and no idea what a global issue is has lost the year's cheapest work.
programmes.countryNote: The Al Ain school year runs roughly September to late June, with a long July and August gap. For this subject the summer is reading time rather than coursework time: the Paper 2 literary works are best read once in the summer and reread in DP2, and a student who has never read the works outside class is starting the comparative essay from nothing.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme, second year
programmes.description: DP2 completes the areas of exploration, records the Individual Oral, submits the Higher Level essay where applicable, and ends in timed practice on the two papers. The order matters: the Oral is the component that stops being movable once it is recorded, so it deserves attention before the papers do.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain students sit the May session. The Individual Oral recording window and the Higher Level essay submission date are set by the school rather than published nationally, so get both from the Diploma coordinator in writing in the first term of DP2. Families planning from the student's recollection of those dates reliably lose two to three weeks.

programmes.name: Higher Level Language and Literature
programmes.description: Higher Level sits two unseen texts in Paper 1 rather than one, which changes the paper from a careful piece of close reading into an exercise in time management. It also adds an essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words on a text or body of work studied in the course, developed from the learner portfolio and externally assessed.
programmes.countryNote: In a small Al Ain cohort the Higher Level essay is frequently the component with the least class time attached to it, because the teacher is covering shared content for both levels. It is also the component most easily rescued with one-to-one work, since it is a single piece of writing with a known deadline and a published set of criteria.

al-ain/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-lite.subjectsIntro: Language and Literature is the subject on this page. These are the Diploma subjects our tutors cover for Al Ain students, described by what the marks actually reward.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen non-literary analysis, the comparative essay on literary works, the Individual Oral and, at Higher Level, the essay. Marks are lost on feature-spotting without function, on comparative essays that run two separate essays side by side, and on Orals where the global issue is too broad to anchor an argument.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: The alternative Language A route, built entirely on literary works with no non-literary texts in the papers. It suits a confident reader who finds advertising and journalism harder to analyse than poetry, and it removes Paper 1's unseen non-literary text in favour of an unseen literary one.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: A language acquisition course rather than a Language A course, assessed on reading, writing, listening and speaking rather than on literary analysis. The right route for some students, and choosing between English B and English A Language and Literature is a conversation to have in Year 11, not in DP1.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Al Ain students frequently take an Arabic course alongside English A, and the two can support each other: analytical vocabulary transfers, and a student who understands how rhetoric works in one language sees it faster in the other. Timetabling two language subjects does compress revision time, though.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: The closest analytical cousin to this subject. Source analysis in History rewards exactly the skill Paper 1 rewards: identifying what a text is trying to do to its reader and saying how. Students strong in one usually transfer quickly to the other once the command terms are mapped.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Shares the evaluative essay structure and the need to use evidence rather than recite it. Students who learn to connect a limitation to a claim in Psychology tend to stop feature-spotting in English, because the underlying habit is the same.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Often the subject a strong English student is weakest in, and the one that drags the total. Proof, sequences and the non-calculator paper are the pressure points, and the fix is practice volume rather than insight.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: A common pairing for students heading towards digital humanities or media degrees. The Internal Assessment demands the same documentation discipline that a learner portfolio demands, which is to record decisions as they are made rather than reconstruct them later.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Language and Literature students are well placed in both, because the subject already asks how meaning is made and who decides. Support is teaching, feedback and process coaching on the student's own work only, never production of it.

sections.heading: What an Al Ain parent is usually asking by the time they search this
paragraphs: In practice the search comes at one of three moments. A DP1 report has come back with a 4 and the comment says the writing is descriptive rather than analytical. A DP2 mock Paper 1 has come back poorly and the student says they ran out of time. Or the Individual Oral recording window has been announced and nobody at home knows what a global issue is. Each of those wants a different first session, and the answer to all three is not more reading.

The practical shape of the help is a weekly one-to-one slot of 60 or 90 minutes over live video, starting after 16:30 so the school run is finished, with the hour pointed at whichever component still has time on it. Market rates in the UAE for a qualified subject tutor working online run roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, and for an IB specialist roughly AED 200 to 450 and upwards, according to provider rate cards and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table read in October 2026. Those are market bands rather than our price list, and the first session with us is free.

The reason sequencing matters so much in this subject is that the components stop being movable at different times. Once the Individual Oral is recorded, that mark is fixed. Once the Higher Level essay is submitted, so is that one. The two papers remain improvable until the final fortnight. A family that spends February on Paper 2 while the Oral recording window passes unprepared has spent money on the component that needed it least.

The rest of this page sets out each component, what it rewards, where Al Ain students specifically lose marks, and the point at which a remaining timeline is honestly too short. All of it is readable without buying anything.

sections.heading: Reading the English grade you already have
paragraphs: A 4 in English A at the end of DP1 is a far less alarming number than it looks, because reports in a two-year course are generally marked against the final standard rather than against where a DP1 student should be. What matters is the comment, and English comments are unusually informative if you know how to read them. There are really only four things a teacher can be saying, and each one has a different price attached.

A comment about writing being descriptive rather than analytical means the student names features and does not explain their function. This is the commonest comment in the subject and it is the cheapest to fix, because it is a sentence-level habit: identify the technique, then say what it does to the reader, then say why that serves the text's purpose. Students can be taught that three-part move in a handful of sessions and then practise it for months.

A comment about organisation or focus means the essays are not planned. That is a timing and planning problem rather than a reading problem, and it is fixed with a six-minute planning routine practised until it is automatic rather than with more content. A comment about expression and language means accuracy and register, which moves slowly and steadily and responds to volume of marked writing more than to explanation.

The fourth comment is the one to take seriously: not understanding the texts. If a student genuinely cannot follow what an unseen opinion column is doing, the problem is inference and cultural context rather than technique, and in a bilingual Al Ain household that is a very common and entirely fixable situation. It is also the one that needs the most lead time, so the comment is worth asking about explicitly rather than waiting for it to appear in writing.
bullets: Descriptive not analytical: a sentence-level habit, fixed fast
Organisation and focus: a planning routine, not more reading

sections.heading: The four components and which one is still movable
paragraphs: Language and Literature is assessed through two written papers, an internally assessed oral and, at Higher Level, an essay. Paper 1 is guided textual analysis of unseen non-literary material: Standard Level students work on one text, Higher Level students on two, with a guiding question attached to each. Paper 2 is a comparative essay answering one general question using two of the literary works studied in class, with no texts available in the examination room. The Individual Oral is a prepared ten-minute presentation followed by five minutes of questions. The Higher Level essay runs to 1,200 to 1,500 words.

Component weightings differ by level and are published in the subject guide your child's cohort follows, so confirm the exact percentages and durations with the school's Diploma coordinator rather than taking them from any website. What does not change is the marking architecture: the components are assessed against criteria covering knowledge, understanding and interpretation; analysis and evaluation; focus and organisation; and language. Knowing which criterion a student loses marks on is more useful than knowing the total, and most students have never been told.

The table below is the planning view. Read the final column first, because it is the one that determines where this term's money should go. A component that is already recorded or submitted cannot be improved, however much tuition is bought, and a component sat in May can be improved up to the last fortnight.

One further point parents rarely hear: Paper 2 is sat without the texts. Everything the student quotes has to come from memory, which means the revision task is partly a memory task and needs to start earlier than a student's instinct suggests. Building a small bank of quotations that can serve several possible questions is a DP2 autumn job, not an April one.
