sections.heading: Paper 1 and the first twelve minutes that decide it
paragraphs: Paper 1 is the component where good students most often underperform, and the reason is almost always the opening minutes. The paper gives an unseen non-literary text and a guiding question. A student who starts writing in minute two produces a running commentary that follows the text from top to bottom, names devices as they appear, and never develops an argument about what the text as a whole is doing. The marks for analysis and evaluation sit in that missing argument.

The alternative routine is mechanical and teachable. Read the text once for what it is and who it is for. Read the guiding question and decide what the answer to it is, in one sentence, before writing anything. Find three or four places in the text that support that sentence, including at least one that complicates it. Then write, leading with the argument and using the text as evidence rather than as a route march. That routine costs about twelve minutes and buys the whole of criterion B.

Higher Level changes the problem rather than deepening it. Two texts in one sitting means the first analysis has to be finished on time or the second one is compromised, and students who are strong readers are exactly the ones most likely to over-invest in the first text. The practice that fixes this is unpleasant and effective: timed double texts, with the first analysis stopped at the clock whether it is finished or not, repeated until the student stops needing to be stopped.

For many Al Ain students there is a prior problem, which is cultural rather than technical. Non-literary texts in this paper are frequently advertisements, political cartoons, opinion columns and public information campaigns, written for audiences with assumed knowledge. A student who has not met that assumed knowledge cannot infer the irony, and then analyses the surface. The fix is a reading diet rather than a lesson: a few unfamiliar texts a week, discussed, over months. Started in DP1 it is easy. Started in March of DP2 it is not.

sections.heading: The Individual Oral, counted backwards from the recording date
paragraphs: The Individual Oral is the component families understand least and the one with the hardest edge, because once it is recorded the mark is effectively fixed. The student presents for ten minutes on a global issue, using one literary and one non-literary extract of no more than 40 lines each, and then answers five minutes of questions from the teacher. The work that determines the mark happens weeks before the recording, in the choice of global issue and the choice of extracts.

The commonest failure is a global issue that is too large. A student who chooses something as broad as inequality or the environment has nothing specific to argue, and ten minutes of general observation scores poorly against every criterion. A narrow issue, framed as a claim rather than a topic, gives the student something to prove and gives the extracts a job to do. Narrowing that issue is usually two sessions of work and it is the single highest-value intervention available in this component.

The extracts are the second decision. They must be short enough to be read closely in the time available, rich enough to support the argument, and different enough from each other that the comparison is not trivial. A pair chosen because they are both about the same subject is usually a weaker pair than one chosen because they handle the same issue in opposing ways. The student chooses and justifies them; the tutor questions whether they will carry ten minutes.

A tutor's limits here are specific. We may teach the structure, question whether the issue is narrow enough, challenge whether an extract earns its place, and give feedback after hearing the student rehearse. We may not write the presentation, script it, or supply the argument. The Oral is assessed as the student's own work and the student has to be able to answer unprepared questions about it for five minutes, which is a test no script survives anyway.

sections.heading: The Higher Level essay, and why the learner portfolio is the real preparation
paragraphs: The Higher Level essay is a piece of 1,200 to 1,500 words on a text or body of work studied in the course, developed from the student's own learner portfolio and assessed externally. It is the most controllable component in the subject, because the deadline is known, the length is fixed and the student chooses the question. It is also the component most often left until the term it is due, which converts a manageable task into a fortnight of panic.

The portfolio is the reason the essay is manageable or not. It is a required ongoing record of the student's responses to the works and texts studied, and it is not directly assessed, which is precisely why students neglect it. A student with two years of recorded responses opens the portfolio, finds three ideas worth 1,400 words, and picks the strongest. A student with an empty portfolio has to generate an original line of argument about a text they read eighteen months ago, from memory, in a fortnight.

Choosing the question is where most of the quality is decided. A question too broad cannot be sustained with evidence inside 1,500 words; a question too narrow runs out at 800 and gets padded. The usable test is whether the student can state the answer in one sentence and then name four pieces of textual evidence that support it, with at least one that complicates it. If they cannot, the question is wrong and no amount of writing will rescue it.

Our role is feedback and teaching, within the same boundary that applies to every assessed component. We can explain the criteria, challenge a question, read a draft and say where the argument is unsupported or where the evidence is doing no work. We cannot write or restructure the essay. The practical consequence is that the useful sessions are the early ones, on the question and the plan, rather than the late ones on the prose.

sections.heading: Language A, Literature, or English B: choosing the route in a bilingual Al Ain household
paragraphs: A real question for many Al Ain families is not how to improve in Language and Literature but whether it is the right course at all. The IB offers English A: Language and Literature, English A: Literature, and English B, and they are different courses with different demands rather than three difficulty levels of the same thing. Choosing wrongly costs two years, and the decision is best made in Year 11 with the school, not in the second term of DP1.

Language and Literature splits attention between literary works and non-literary texts: advertising, journalism, speeches, cartoons, public campaigns. It suits a student interested in how language works in the world and comfortable with unfamiliar cultural reference. Literature removes the non-literary strand and works entirely with literary texts, including an unseen literary text in Paper 1. It suits a confident reader who finds a poem easier to analyse than an advertisement, which is more students than the course-selection evening suggests.

English B is a language acquisition course, not a Language A course, and the honest framing matters. It is assessed on reading, writing, listening and speaking rather than on literary analysis. For a student whose English is still developing it is the course in which they can actually demonstrate what they know, and taking it is not a concession. What does need checking, carefully and early, is how the intended university destination treats English B, because some degree routes have specific language requirements.

Whichever route is chosen, a bilingual student in Language and Literature has one gap worth naming: assumed cultural knowledge in non-literary texts. That is not a language weakness and it should not be treated as one. It is closed by reading unfamiliar texts regularly and talking about them, which is slow, cheap and entirely effective when started in DP1.

sections.heading: What English A tuition costs at Al Ain market rates
paragraphs: Very few providers in this market publish a rate, which is why four phone calls produce four deflections. The bands below come from UAE provider rate cards and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table, read in October 2026. They describe the market, not IB Gram's prices. Al Ain sits inside Abu Dhabi emirate pricing rather than Dubai's, and in-home rates here carry heavier travel loading because the city is spread out and tutors are fewer.

Read it as a budget tool. A weekly 60-minute session with a qualified online subject tutor in the middle of the band is a predictable monthly figure, and most families manage that better than an intensive block bought in panic. Monthly packages advertised in the UAE have included roughly AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and roughly AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions, which is the clearest available illustration of what travel adds to a rate.

Two traps are specific to English. The first is paying for a general essay tutor rather than a subject specialist: someone can improve a paragraph without being able to say which criterion a mark was lost on or how an Individual Oral is actually assessed. The second is buying hours in the wrong component. Money spent on Paper 2 while the Oral recording window passes unprepared buys nothing, because that mark closes.

We publish no IB Gram price list here, no satisfaction figure and no star rating, because a number without its sample, date and method is not evidence. What we will do is quote the market with its source and then let you hear a tutor teach for free before any figure is discussed.

sections.heading: How lessons run, and the home-tutor question answered plainly
paragraphs: Al Ain families weighing English A help have three real options: a local tutor who travels to the district, a weekly drive to a specialist in the capital, or an online one-to-one specialist. The local tutor's rate includes travel, which in a spread-out city pushes it towards the top of the market band. The capital drive is roughly 130 kilometres each way, or about three hours of travel on a school night on top of the lesson, which over two Diploma years is a very large number of hours.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video; home visits are a service we run only in India. We state that before making any case for the format, because a family who wants someone physically present deserves to know in the first paragraph rather than the last. The case we would make is narrow: for this subject the work is annotating a text and a marked script together, and a shared screen does that at least as well as a table does.

The practical gain is that the record survives. Every annotated paragraph, every marked draft and every criterion note stays in one place the student and the parent can both open, instead of in a notebook that disappears in March. For a subject assessed partly on a portfolio and partly on work developed over two years, having the trail intact is worth more than it sounds.

Scheduling is the last piece and in Al Ain it is the decisive one. Sessions run on Gulf Standard Time, usually between 16:30 and 21:00, built around the school run and around the homework load from the mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies lessons that sit alongside the Diploma. During Ramadan the slot moves later and shortens. The summer is reading time: the Paper 2 works read once properly in July beat the same works skimmed in April.

process.title: Tell us the level and which component is nearest
process.description: Three facts decide the match: Standard or Higher Level, which literary works the department chose for Paper 2, and whether the Individual Oral has been recorded yet. The third one determines where the next two months of effort should go, and it is the question parents least often think to ask.

process.title: A free first session with the actual tutor
process.description: Not a sales call. The tutor works from your child's last marked piece of writing on a shared screen and shows which criterion the marks were lost on. You hear the explanation of a weakness your child has already been penalised for once.

process.title: A written plan with the component order in it
process.description: After the trial you get a short plan naming the next six sessions and the order of components, because order matters more here than in most subjects. If the plan does not say which component is being protected and why, that is a reason to decline it.

process.title: A fixed weekly slot on Gulf Standard Time
process.description: Built around the Al Ain school run and the mandatory-subject homework load, and kept at the same time every week. Ramadan sessions move later and shorten; the summer is planned as reading time for the Paper 2 works rather than left empty.

process.title: Review against marked work, not impressions
process.description: Every few weeks we compare the plan with the evidence: marks on timed unseen texts, criterion scores moving, Oral rehearsals timed and improving. If the plan is not working we change the plan or the tutor, and we start that conversation rather than waiting for you to.

whyPoints.title: Component order before content
whyPoints.description: The Individual Oral and the Higher Level essay stop being improvable once they are recorded or submitted; the papers do not. We plan around that ordering, because money spent on a component whose mark has closed buys nothing at all.

whyPoints.title: Criterion-level diagnosis
whyPoints.description: Most students have never been told which criterion their marks are lost on. We start from the last marked script and name it, because knowing whether the problem is analysis, organisation or language decides what the next six sessions should contain.

whyPoints.title: Bilingual households advised honestly
whyPoints.description: Assumed cultural knowledge in non-literary texts is a real and nameable gap, not a language weakness, and the route choice between Language and Literature, Literature and English B deserves a straight answer rather than a sales answer.

whyPoints.title: The Oral and the essay stay the student's own work
whyPoints.description: We teach structure, challenge a global issue, question an extract and give feedback on the student's own draft or rehearsal. We do not script presentations or write essays. That boundary is stated before anyone pays, not after.

whyPoints.title: Sourced figures, no invented statistics
whyPoints.description: Every AED band here carries the date it was read and the source it came from. We publish no price list, no satisfaction percentage and no star rating, because an unsourced number is worth nothing to a parent making a decision.

whyPoints.title: Al Ain's week, not a generic UAE one
whyPoints.description: Slots are set around the school run from districts like Zakher and Hili, the mandatory-subject homework load, Ramadan timings and the long summer that is this subject's real reading window.

faqs.question: What is the difference between IB English A Language and Literature and English A Literature?
faqs.answer: They are different courses rather than two difficulty levels. Language and Literature splits the course between literary works and non-literary texts such as advertising, journalism, speeches and cartoons, and Paper 1 gives unseen non-literary material to analyse. Literature works entirely with literary texts and sets an unseen literary text in Paper 1 instead. A confident reader who finds a poem easier to handle than an advertisement is often better served by Literature, and that is more students than the course-selection evening suggests. The choice belongs in Year 11, with the school.

faqs.question: My child's English report says the writing is descriptive rather than analytical. What does that actually mean?
faqs.answer: It means your child names techniques without explaining their function. A descriptive answer says the writer uses a rhetorical question. An analytical one says the writer uses a rhetorical question, which forces the reader to supply the answer themselves and so makes them complicit in the argument. The repair is a three-part sentence habit: identify the technique, say what it does to the reader, say why that serves the text's purpose. It can be taught in a handful of sessions and then needs months of practice, which is why it is worth starting in DP1.

faqs.question: How many unseen texts does my child analyse in Paper 1 at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Two, each with its own guiding question, where Standard Level students analyse one. That changes the paper's main difficulty from close reading to time management, and it catches out strong readers in particular, because they over-invest in the first text and then write the second analysis in a hurry. The practice that fixes it is uncomfortable: timed double texts with the first analysis stopped at the clock whether it is finished or not, repeated until the student paces themselves without being stopped.

faqs.question: Can my child take the literary texts into the Paper 2 comparative essay?
faqs.answer: No. Paper 2 is sat without the works, so every quotation and every detail has to come from memory. That makes revision for this paper partly a memory task, and it needs to start earlier than most students expect. The efficient approach is a small bank of quotations chosen because each one can serve several possible questions, rather than a long list tied to specific themes. Building that bank is autumn work in DP2, and students who leave it to April end up paraphrasing vaguely and losing marks on evidence.

faqs.question: What is a global issue for the Individual Oral, and how narrow should it be?
faqs.answer: A global issue is a significant concern that operates across cultures and can be explored through specific texts. The commonest mistake is choosing something far too large, such as inequality or the environment, which leaves the student with nothing specific to argue across ten minutes. A workable global issue is framed as a claim rather than a topic, narrow enough that two extracts can genuinely prove or complicate it. Narrowing it is usually two sessions of work and it is the highest-value intervention available in this component.

faqs.question: How long can the extracts for the Individual Oral be?
faqs.answer: Each extract may be up to 40 lines, and your child needs one from a literary work and one from a non-literary text, both studied during the course. Shorter is frequently better: an extract the student can read closely inside the ten minutes supports more analysis than a long one skimmed. The stronger pairings are usually the ones chosen because the two texts handle the same global issue in opposing ways, rather than because they happen to be about the same subject. The student chooses and justifies them; a tutor can only question whether each one earns its place.

faqs.question: Once the Individual Oral has been recorded, can the mark be improved?
faqs.answer: Effectively no, which is why the recording date should drive your planning. The Oral is internally assessed and externally moderated, and once your child has delivered it the mark is set. This is the single most important scheduling fact in the subject, because families routinely spend the term before the recording working on Paper 2 and then discover the Oral has closed at a mark they are unhappy with. Ask the Diploma coordinator for the recording window in writing at the start of DP2 and plan backwards from it.

faqs.question: What is the learner portfolio for if it is not assessed?
faqs.answer: It is the raw material for the Higher Level essay and the memory of the whole course. The portfolio is a required ongoing record of your child's responses to the works and texts studied, and because no mark is attached to it directly, students neglect it first. The cost shows up later: a student with two years of recorded responses opens it and finds three essay-worthy ideas, while a student with an empty portfolio has to invent an original argument about a text read eighteen months earlier, from memory, in a fortnight.

faqs.question: How long is the Higher Level essay and when should it be started?
faqs.answer: It runs to 1,200 to 1,500 words on a text or body of work studied in the course, developed from the learner portfolio, and assessed externally. The submission date is set by the school and sits months before the May papers, so get it from the Diploma coordinator in the first term of DP2. The work that decides the quality is choosing the question, and the test is whether your child can state the answer in one sentence and then name four pieces of textual evidence, including one that complicates it. If not, the question is wrong.

faqs.question: My child has strong English but struggles with the unseen advertisements and cartoons. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always because of assumed cultural knowledge rather than language. Non-literary texts in this paper are written for audiences with shared reference points, and a student raised in the Gulf may read an ironic opinion column straight because the irony depends on knowledge they were never given. That is not a language weakness and treating it as one wastes time. The repair is a reading diet: a few unfamiliar texts a week, discussed rather than annotated, sustained over months. Started in DP1 it is easy; started in March of DP2 it is not.

faqs.question: What can an English tutor legitimately do with my child's Individual Oral or Higher Level essay?
faqs.answer: A tutor may explain the published criteria, challenge whether a global issue is narrow enough or an essay question sustainable, question whether an extract earns its place, listen to a rehearsal and give criterion-based feedback, and read the student's own draft and say where the argument is unsupported. A tutor may not script the presentation, supply the argument or write or restructure the essay. Both components are assessed as the student's own work, and the five minutes of unprepared questions after the Oral is a test no script survives in any case.

faqs.question: What does weekly English A tuition cost for a family in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Market rates in the UAE for a qualified subject tutor working online run roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, and for an IB specialist roughly AED 200 to 450 and upwards, according to provider rate cards and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table read in October 2026. In-home rates sit higher, around AED 180 to 500, because travel is priced in, and that loading is heavier in a spread-out city than in the capital. Those are market bands and not our price list. The first session with us is free, before any figure is discussed.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send an English tutor to our house in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. Tutoring for Al Ain families is delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and we say so before any pricing conversation so that a family wanting someone physically present knows immediately. For this subject the shared screen carries a real advantage: tutor and student annotate the same text and the same marked script together, and every annotated draft stays somewhere both the student and the parent can reopen later.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does an Al Ain English A student usually need?
faqs.answer: One weekly session of 60 or 90 minutes covers most term-time cases, with a short concentrated block before the Individual Oral recording window or the Higher Level essay deadline, and a denser run of timed practice in the final twelve weeks. Two sessions a week is worth it when a specific component has a near deadline. Beyond that, the limiting factor is usually how much marked writing the student is actually producing between sessions, and more paid hours do not fix that.

faqs.question: It is ten weeks before the May papers. What is realistically improvable in English?
faqs.answer: Paper 1 and Paper 2 technique, substantially. In ten weeks a student can learn the twelve-minute opening routine for an unseen text, build a usable quotation bank, and practise comparative planning until it is automatic, and those gains are real because the losses were systematic. What cannot be improved is a recorded Individual Oral or a submitted Higher Level essay, and reading two literary works properly from scratch in ten weeks alongside five other subjects is not realistic. We will say which of those applies rather than selling hours into a closed component.

faqs.question: Will sessions keep running through Ramadan and the long Al Ain summer?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the timing changed rather than the frequency. During Ramadan most families move the slot later, after Iftar, and shorten it, which suits this subject because feedback on one piece of writing is short concentrated work. The summer is different in kind: July and August are when the Paper 2 literary works can actually be read properly rather than skimmed, and a light run of discussion sessions across the break is usually worth more than the same hours bought in April. Travel weeks are planned around in advance.

al-ain/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-lite.closingHeading: Send the last marked script and the Oral date
al-ain/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-lite.closingBody: Two things make the first session useful: your child's most recent marked piece of English writing, and the date of the Individual Oral recording window if it has been announced. With those we can tell you which component still has time on it and which does not, and match a Diploma Language and Literature tutor who has taught and assessed this course. The first session is free and runs on the real script rather than a generic diagnostic. Afterwards you get a short written plan with the component order in it, and the decision stays yours.

al-ain/ib-dp-extended-essay-tutor.tutorsIntro: The mentors below work on the Extended Essay as a research problem: narrowing a question until it can be answered, choosing a registration subject the student can actually gather evidence in, and reading drafts the student has written against the five published criteria. Book the free session and bring whatever exists, even if it is only a title.

intro.heading: Three facts about Al Ain that change how this essay should be planned
paragraphs: The Extended Essay is the only part of the Diploma where a student is formally asked to work alone, and it is the part where families most often look outside the school for help. That instinct is reasonable and the framing is usually wrong. The essay is not a writing task that happens to require research. It is a research task whose mark is almost entirely determined before the first paragraph is written, by the question chosen, the subject it is registered in, and whether evidence exists that a seventeen-year-old in Al Ain can actually reach.

The first fact that matters here is the regulator. Al Ain sits inside the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so its private schools answer to the Department of Education and Knowledge rather than to Dubai's KHDA. That changes which inspection reports apply, which school listing is authoritative, and which professional-ethics rules bind the teachers around your child. It also means that most of the UAE tutoring advice a parent finds online, which is written for Dubai and names KHDA throughout, is describing a framework that does not govern your school.

The second fact is cohort size. Al Ain's Diploma classes are small, and a small cohort has a direct effect on the Extended Essay. A school with two Higher Level sciences and one Higher Level humanities subject has a correspondingly narrow pool of supervisors, which means students are sometimes registered in a subject because a supervisor is free rather than because the question belongs there. A question that belongs in Psychology and is registered in Business Management will be marked against Business Management criteria, and the student will spend eight months being penalised for a decision made in an administrative meeting.

The third fact is the calendar, and it is the one that actually determines outcomes. The IB sets a submission framework; the school sets the dates. An Al Ain school's internal deadlines for a title, a first draft and a final submission are typically spread across the second half of the first Diploma year and the first term of the second, and they are the only dates that matter to your child. A mentor who works to those dates is useful. A mentor who works backwards from a published examination date is working to a calendar your school does not use.

What follows from all three is a particular kind of plan. Confirm the registration subject early and challenge it if the question does not fit. Get the school's own deadline list in writing. Choose a question whose evidence is reachable from Al Ain, which is a smaller constraint here than families assume, because this city has primary-source material most students never think to use. Then do the work in the order the criteria are awarded, rather than in the order it feels natural to write.

al-ain/ib-dp-extended-essay-tutor.programmesIntro: The Extended Essay belongs to the final two years, but the habits it depends on are built earlier and the registration decision is usually taken at the end of the first Diploma year. These are the stages at which Al Ain families actually ask for help, and what is worth doing at each.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The Extended Essay sits in the Diploma core alongside Theory of Knowledge and creativity, activity, service. It is an independent research essay of up to 4,000 words, registered in a Diploma subject or taken as a World Studies essay, assessed against five criteria carrying 34 marks in total and graded from A to E. The IB recommends around 40 hours of student work and a small number of supervisor hours, including three mandatory reflection sessions.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain the practical shape of this varies more between schools than families expect. A campus with a large Diploma cohort runs a structured programme of deadlines and supervisor allocation; a campus with a dozen Diploma students runs something more informal, and the student carries more of the project-management load. Ask which of those two situations your child is in before deciding what outside help is for.

programmes.name: First Diploma year - registration and question
programmes.description: The decisive year, and the one families usually skip. The registration subject is chosen, the research question is framed, the supervisor is allocated and the first reflection session happens. Work at this stage is about narrowing: a question that starts as a topic becomes a question, then becomes a question with a stated method, then becomes a question whose evidence has been confirmed to exist before anybody writes anything.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain schools often allocate supervisors in the spring term of the first year, which means the window for challenging a mismatched registration subject is short. If a student's question is really a psychology question, the moment to say so is before allocation, not after a draft exists. Families who ask the coordinator one direct question in March avoid the most expensive mistake available in this component.

programmes.name: Second Diploma year - drafting and submission
programmes.description: Drafting, the second reflection session, the final submission and the concluding viva voce with the supervisor. This is also the term when every other internal assessment is live, so the essay competes for attention with four or five subject deadlines. The useful work here is editorial and structural: whether the argument answers the question, whether sources are being evaluated rather than cited, and whether the conclusion says something the body has earned.
programmes.countryNote: Because Al Ain schools set their own internal deadlines, a student's real submission date can sit a full term earlier than a classmate's at another campus in the same city. Two students comparing notes often conclude that one of them has months of slack. Usually one of them is reading a different school's calendar, and the only reliable fix is the written deadline list from the coordinator.

programmes.name: Year 11 into the Diploma core
programmes.description: No Extended Essay work happens here, but the two skills it depends on can be built: constructing an argument that holds across several thousand words, and evaluating a source rather than summarising it. Students arriving from IGCSE have usually written to a 600-word brief and never been asked to sustain a line of reasoning or to say why one source is more reliable than another.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain's British-curriculum schools substantially outnumber its Diploma schools, so many students cross into the Diploma from an IGCSE background at a different campus. That crossing is the natural moment to build extended-writing stamina, and a short summer block on source evaluation is worth more later than the same hours spent on subject content.

al-ain/ib-dp-extended-essay-tutor.subjectsIntro: An Extended Essay is registered in a subject, and the subject decides the criteria, the expected method and what counts as evidence. The list below covers the registrations Al Ain students most often take, with what each one actually demands and the trap attached to it.

subjects.name: World Studies
subjects.description: An essay on a contemporary global issue examined through two Diploma subjects. It is the registration most likely to produce an outstanding essay and most likely to produce a mess, because it requires genuine integration of two disciplines rather than one chapter from each. A local issue examined globally, or the reverse, is the structure that tends to work.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Demands engagement with historiography, not just events: the essay must weigh how historians have interpreted the question differently. The common failure is a narrative that is well researched and never argues. Access to sources is the practical constraint, and digitised archives have made this registration more viable from the UAE than it was a decade ago.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Requires a real organisation, a real decision and the application of course tools to it. Students who choose a multinational find only published marketing material; students who choose a reachable local business find a manager who will answer questions. The second group almost always scores higher, and the gap is entirely about evidence access.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Assessed as a review and evaluation of existing published studies rather than as original research with human participants, which is where ethical limits bite. Students routinely propose a questionnaire study of their own school and have to redesign. The strong essays interrogate methodology in the literature rather than gathering new data.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Needs a question that generates data within laboratory access the school actually has, or a well-justified fieldwork design. Al Ain's environment makes ecological questions genuinely feasible, but sampling design has to be planned properly and a single afternoon's data collection will not carry a 4,000-word essay.

subjects.name: Chemistry and Physics
subjects.description: Experimental registrations where the limiting factor is equipment and supervised laboratory time, both of which are scarcer in a small school. A theoretical or computational question, or a secondary-data analysis with a clear method, is often the realistic route and is not a lesser essay if the analysis is rigorous.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Requires economic theory applied to a specific question with data, not a general discussion of a market. The strongest UAE-based essays tend to take a narrow local market and apply a single model carefully. The usual failure is a question so broad that no amount of data could settle it.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Close textual analysis of a small number of works, or of language in a defined context. The trap is choosing three novels and producing a survey; the essays that score choose less text and go further into it. Secondary criticism must be used to argue with, not to decorate.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: The registration best served by Al Ain itself. Urban form, water use, agricultural land, tourism pressure and microclimate are all locally observable, and primary fieldwork is both feasible and distinctive. Sampling method and data presentation are where marks are won or lost rather than in the topic choice.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: A mathematical investigation with genuine mathematical content beyond the Diploma syllabus, communicated properly. Students underestimate the communication requirement: correct mathematics presented without explanation of why each step follows loses marks under the presentation and critical-thinking criteria.

subjects.name: Visual Arts and Music
subjects.description: Analytical essays about works or practice, not portfolios. These registrations suit students who can write analytically about something they also make, and they fail when the essay becomes autobiography. A defined corpus and a clear analytical frame are the whole of the planning problem.

subjects.name: Arabic and language acquisition subjects
subjects.description: An essay written in and about the target language, which for a confident Arabic speaker in Al Ain is a genuinely strong option and an under-used one. The language requirement raises the drafting load, and supervisor availability inside a small school is the practical constraint to check first.

al-ain/ib-dp-extended-essay-tutor.regionsTitle: Al Ain as a research site, district by district
al-ain/ib-dp-extended-essay-tutor.regionsIntro: The most useful thing about doing an Extended Essay in Al Ain is that the city is full of reachable primary-source material and almost nobody uses it. The notes below are about what a student in each district can actually get to and ask questions about, because evidence access is what decides this component.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: Central and close to the oasis district, the souk and several long-established schools. A student here can reach small retail and family-business owners on foot, which makes a Business Management or Economics registration with real interview evidence genuinely achievable.

regions.name: Hili
regions.note: The northern district containing Hili Archaeological Park, a UNESCO-inscribed Bronze Age site. Heritage management, tourism pressure and interpretation of archaeology are live local questions and almost unrepresented in the essays schools see each year.

regions.name: Al Qattara
regions.note: Home to the Al Qattara Arts Centre and surrounding oasis farmland. Students here have unusual access to craft practice, date cultivation and the interaction between heritage sites and residential expansion, all of which support Geography, Visual Arts or World Studies registrations.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: Established central housing near the city's older institutional buildings. Short journeys make repeated site visits practical, which matters for any question requiring data collected more than once rather than on a single afternoon.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: Southern district on the edge of agricultural land, with visible transition from farm to suburb. Land use change, irrigation and the economics of small-scale farming are observable here and support a question with genuine primary data behind it.

regions.name: Al Towayya and Al Maqam
regions.note: Districts with ready access towards Jebel Hafeet and the Green Mubazzarah area. Microclimate, altitude effects, visitor numbers and road-side vegetation all give feasible Biology and Geography fieldwork designs with repeat sampling built in.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji and Al Masoudi
regions.note: Older residential areas near the campus of United Arab Emirates University. Proximity to a university library and to researchers is the practical advantage, and a polite request for twenty minutes of an academic's time is a thing more students should try.

regions.name: Al Foah and Al Yahar
regions.note: Outer districts with date farms and newer housing. Journeys are long, which argues for a question whose data can be gathered in two or three planned visits rather than one requiring weekly access to a site.

schoolClusters.city: Central Al Ain campuses
schoolClusters.note: Private schools here are licensed and inspected by ADEK, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools across the Emirate of Abu Dhabi. For the Extended Essay the consequence is practical rather than abstract: the professional-ethics rules binding the teachers who supervise your child are Abu Dhabi's, and the inspection reports a parent should read are published by the Abu Dhabi authority rather than by Dubai's.

Al Dhafra Private Schools, Al Ain
Al Ittihad National Private School, Al Ain

schoolClusters.city: Outer campuses and the Abu Dhabi road corridor
schoolClusters.note: Corridor campuses draw from the southern and western districts and run a mix of international programmes. Supervisor allocation at these schools is often made in the spring term of the first Diploma year, and the pool of available supervisors in any one subject is small, so a student with an unusual registration should raise it early rather than hope it resolves itself.

schoolClusters.city: Research institutions within reach of an Al Ain student
schoolClusters.note: Beyond schools, the city holds institutions a determined Diploma student can actually approach for evidence: a university campus, museums, heritage sites and agricultural operations. None of these owes a student anything, and a short, specific, polite written request succeeds far more often than families expect. This is the practical content of the research advantage described above.

al-ain/ib-dp-extended-essay-tutor.modesIntro: Extended Essay support is bought in blocks rather than as an open weekly hour, because the component has three distinct moments of difficulty and nothing much happens between them. Paying for a standing weekly session across eight months is how families spend a great deal and cannot say what it bought.

modes.title: Design block, two to four sessions
modes.description: Taken before anything is written, ideally before the supervisor is allocated. The work is narrowing the question until it can be answered with evidence the student can obtain, confirming the registration subject actually fits it, and establishing a method. This is where the eventual mark is largely decided, and it is also the cheapest block to buy because it is short.
bullets: Topic narrowed to a question, then narrowed again against available evidence
Registration subject tested against the question rather than against convenience
A written method agreed before any reading begins
A list of sources confirmed to exist and to be reachable from Al Ain

modes.title: Draft review block, two to three sessions
modes.description: Taken once the student has written a full draft. The reading is criterion by criterion: whether the argument answers the stated question, whether sources are evaluated or merely cited, whether the structure allows critical thinking to appear, and whether the conclusion is earned. Feedback names the criterion and the band; the student does the rewriting.
bullets: Each criterion addressed separately with the mark band named
Paragraphs identified as carrying marks or not carrying marks
Source evaluation strengthened rather than source count increased
Word budget rebalanced towards analysis before any cutting happens

modes.title: Reflection and viva preparation
modes.description: A single session before the final reflection session with the supervisor. Reflections are assessed, and students routinely write all three in one sitting at the end, which is visible to an examiner and costs marks. Preparation is about being able to describe honestly what changed in the research and why, which is what the criterion actually rewards.
bullets: Reflections treated as a record of decisions, not a summary of content
The student able to say what they would do differently and why
Honest account of what went wrong in the research prepared, not concealed
No text supplied; the reflections must be the student's own words

modes.title: Subject-specific method support
modes.description: For registrations with a technical method - sampling design in Geography or Biology, statistical treatment in Psychology or Economics, mathematical rigour in a Mathematics essay. A short block with somebody who knows that subject's conventions prevents the single most common structural failure, which is a method that cannot support the claim the essay wants to make.
bullets: Sampling or data design checked before collection, not after
Statistical treatment matched to the data actually gathered
Subject conventions for presentation and citation applied properly
A realistic assessment of whether the planned method will produce usable evidence

sections.heading: Who governs an Extended Essay in Al Ain, and who merely administers it
paragraphs: Three different bodies have a hand in your child's Extended Essay and they do different jobs, which is worth untangling because families routinely attribute decisions to the wrong one. The International Baccalaureate sets the criteria, the word ceiling, the reflection requirement and the marking. The school sets the internal deadlines, allocates the supervisor and decides how much structure the process has. ADEK licenses and inspects the school, supervises accreditation across the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, and sets professional-ethics expectations for the staff involved. None of those three is interchangeable with the others.

The practical consequence is that complaints and questions have to be directed correctly. A deadline you think is unreasonable is a school decision, not an IB one, and the coordinator can change it. A criterion you think your child was marked harshly against is an IB matter, and the school cannot alter it. A concern about a teacher being paid to tutor their own students is an ethics matter under the Abu Dhabi framework and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct. Families who understand which door to knock on get answers; families who do not spend a term frustrated with the wrong party.

The regulator map across the country matters because UAE families move within it, often mid-Diploma. Dubai's private schools sit under KHDA, which is responsible for overseeing the quality of private education in that emirate. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain sit under ADEK. Sharjah sits under the Sharjah Private Education Authority and Ras Al Khaimah under its Department of Knowledge, both of which approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods as well as inspecting. Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah sit under the federal Ministry of Education. A student relocating from Al Ain to Sharjah in the middle of the essay changes school, supervisor, deadline set and regulator at once.

sections.heading: The five criteria and the thirty-four marks, in the order they are awarded
paragraphs: The essay is marked against five criteria and the distribution is lopsided in a way most students never internalise. Focus and method carries six marks, knowledge and understanding six, critical thinking twelve, presentation four, and engagement six. Critical thinking alone is more than a third of the total, and it is the criterion most directly damaged by a poorly framed question. A student who chooses a question that can only be answered descriptively has capped their critical thinking marks in week one, before writing anything, and no amount of later effort recovers them.

Focus and method is where the question, the topic and the methodology are assessed together. The failure mode is a question that is really a topic: anything beginning with a broad noun phrase and no verb demanding an answer. Knowledge and understanding asks whether the student has used subject-specific terminology and sources appropriate to the registration subject, which is the criterion that punishes a mismatched registration most visibly. An essay with a psychology question registered in Business Management will be read by a Business Management examiner looking for Business Management terminology, and will not find it.

Presentation is only four marks and is the cheapest to secure: consistent citation, a contents page, correct structure, legible data presentation. Students lose two or three of those four marks every year for reasons that take an afternoon to fix. Engagement, worth six, is assessed through the reflections form rather than the essay, and rewards an honest account of decisions taken and difficulties met. Reflections written as a summary of the essay's content score badly; reflections that say what the student tried, what failed and what changed score well.

The order a student should work in is not the order the criteria are listed. Question and method first, because they constrain critical thinking. Then evidence, because without it the critical thinking has nothing to be critical about. Then drafting, where knowledge and understanding and critical thinking are actually earned. Presentation last, as a checklist. Engagement runs alongside the whole thing and should be recorded as the work happens rather than reconstructed afterwards.

sections.heading: Registration subject in a small school: the decision Al Ain gets wrong most often
paragraphs: In a large Diploma cohort, a student with an unusual question finds a supervisor. In a small one, the supervisor pool is the constraint and the question gets bent to fit it. This is the structural problem with the Extended Essay in Al Ain and it is almost never discussed, because it is nobody's fault: a school with eleven Diploma students cannot keep a specialist supervisor available in every subject, and an available supervisor is better than none.

The cost of a mismatch falls on criterion B and criterion C. An examiner reads the essay as an essay in the registered subject, looking for that subject's terminology, conventions and kind of argument. A question about consumer psychology registered in Business Management will be assessed for business tools and business reasoning, and the psychological literature the student actually read will not earn the marks it would have earned under a Psychology registration. The essay is not worse. It is being marked against the wrong expectations.

There are two honest responses. The first is to challenge the registration early, which means in the spring term of the first Diploma year, before allocation hardens. A single direct question to the coordinator - which subject will this question be marked in, and does the question suit it - resolves most cases. The second is to accept the registration and reframe the question to belong there properly, which is a real piece of work and is much better done at the start than at draft stage.

What should not happen is the third option, which is proceeding with a question that belongs elsewhere and hoping the quality of the writing carries it. It does not, because criterion B is explicitly about subject fit and criterion C is assessed through that subject's lens. The table below lists the registrations Al Ain students most commonly take, how viable each is in a small school, and what a student needs to have in place for it to work.

sections.heading: The Al Ain school year, counted forward from September
paragraphs: Most Extended Essay guidance counts backwards from an examination session, which is the wrong frame for this component. The essay is submitted to the school long before any examination, on dates the school chose, and a student working to a published examination window will discover with a shock that their real deadline passed four months earlier. The only calendar that governs your child is the one the coordinator issues, and the first thing any family should do is obtain it in writing.

There is a second reason to count forward rather than backwards, and it is specific to this region. The UAE academic year carries fixtures the essay has to work around: the long winter break, the Ramadan timetable with shortened school days and shifted energy levels, Eid holidays, and the examination-term lockdown when every other internal assessment falls due at once. A plan that assumes eight months of even effort is a plan that will fail in the third month. A plan that front-loads the research into the first Diploma year survives.

The sensible structure is to put the question, the method and the evidence gathering before the winter of the first year, the full draft before the second year begins, and the second year's work entirely on revision, reflection and the viva. Students who do this find DP2 manageable. Students who carry an unwritten essay into DP2 are writing it in the same weeks as four internal assessments and their university applications, and the essay is always the thing that loses.

On examination dates themselves, a caution. Secondary sources circulate specific IB session and results dates every year and they are frequently wrong. No IB examination or results date should be taken from a tutoring page, including this one. Confirm any date with your school's Diploma coordinator or on ibo.org directly. Cambridge and Pearson publish their own timetables and are reliable for the IGCSE siblings in the household - the one published window worth planning an Extended Essay term around is Pearson's International GCSE November 2026 timetable, which runs from late October to 19 November 2026, with results reaching students the following January on the pattern the November 2025 series set when it landed on 22 January 2026. Cambridge, for its part, examines IGCSE, O Level and International A Level in the UAE in a June series and a November series only, each with an entry deadline that falls months before the first paper and is confirmed on the centre's statement of entry - but those are different qualifications and different authorities.

sections.heading: The research advantage of being in Al Ain, and why nobody uses it
paragraphs: Examiners read a very large number of Extended Essays on the same small set of topics, and the quickest route to a distinctive essay is evidence nobody else has. Al Ain supplies that unusually well and almost no student uses it. The city contains a UNESCO-inscribed archaeological landscape, working date agriculture, a national university, oasis irrigation systems still in use, a mountain with a measurable altitude gradient, and a planned urban form expanding into farmland. Each of those is a research site a student can reach in an afternoon.

What makes this an advantage rather than a decoration is that primary evidence feeds the criterion carrying twelve marks. Critical thinking requires something to be critical about, and a student with their own data has material no textbook summary can supply. An essay comparing visitor management at two heritage sites, or measuring vegetation change along a road corridor, or interviewing three date farmers about water allocation, has an analytical spine that a literature-only essay has to work much harder to build.

The constraint is not access, it is nerve. Institutions do not owe a seventeen-year-old anything, and students assume a request will be refused, so they never make it. In practice a short, specific, polite written request - naming the student, the school, the question, exactly what is being asked for and how long it will take - succeeds often enough to be worth sending five times. A research officer at a museum or an academic at the university campus in Al Muwaiji is frequently willing to give twenty minutes. The worst outcome is silence.

Two warnings. First, primary data must be designed before it is collected: a single visit yielding numbers nobody planned how to analyse is worse than no data, because it eats words and earns nothing. Second, anything involving human participants runs into ethical requirements, and in Psychology in particular the registration is built around reviewing published studies rather than running new ones. Check the registration subject's own expectations before planning to gather anything from people.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside a DP2 essay
paragraphs: A detail of UAE schooling that affects Extended Essay planning and is almost never mentioned on tutoring pages: Diploma students in UAE private schools carry mandatory national subjects alongside their IB programme. The federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. For Dubai, KHDA's guidance states that Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are mandatory in all private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with those requirements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year.

KHDA's own framework gives the detail that makes the load concrete. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language, and Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with the advice that no mandatory-subject lesson should run shorter than 25 minutes.

That guidance is Dubai's, and Al Ain schools sit under ADEK rather than KHDA, so the exact implementation differs and should be confirmed with your own school. The federal baseline applies regardless. The planning consequence is the same everywhere in the country: a DP2 student's week contains more timetabled lessons than the Diploma alone accounts for, and the hours families imagine are available for the essay are already committed. Any plan that assumes a Diploma-only timetable is overcounting.

There is an opportunity hidden in this as well. A confident Arabic speaker can register the essay in Arabic, which is a strong and under-used option, and questions touching on UAE social history, heritage or language policy sit naturally alongside the national subjects a student is already studying. The limit is supervisor availability inside a small school, which is the first thing to check rather than the last.

sections.heading: What Extended Essay mentoring costs, priced by block rather than by hour
paragraphs: Hourly rates are the wrong unit for this component, and quoting them is how families end up buying eight months of standing weekly sessions for a piece of work that needs perhaps ten hours of outside input in total. The honest way to price Extended Essay support is by block: a design block of two to four sessions, a draft review block of two to three, a reflection session, and optionally a subject-method block of two. That is six to twelve sessions across eighteen months, concentrated at the points where a decision is being made.

Converted to money using published UAE market rates, the picture is manageable. A qualified subject tutor working online is listed in the market from about AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. An IB specialist sits at AED 200 to AED 450 or above, where TutorChase publishes AED 270 and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table gives AED 200 to AED 450 and more. Budget online tutoring runs AED 45 to AED 150, with EdFlik from AED 45 to AED 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52, though at the Diploma core a general tutor is rarely the right purchase. A ten-session programme at specialist rates therefore sits in the low thousands of dirhams across two academic years, not per term.

Compare that with the monthly subscription framing most providers use. Packages advertised in this market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions, and Bestimate's monthly estimates for a single weekly hour run AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 or more for specialist examination-year support. A family on a standing monthly plan for eighteen months pays several times a block-based total and receives a great many sessions in the months when the essay needs nothing. The figures above are other providers' published rates with the source named, not IB Gram's price list.

One Al Ain-specific note on the in-home premium. Market rates for an in-home visit run AED 180 to AED 500 an hour, with Bestimate giving AED 180 to AED 350 and independent home tutors quoted up to AED 500, because travel sits inside the rate. In a city 130 kilometres from the capital, that premium frequently buys a generalist, because the number of people within driving distance who have supervised an Extended Essay in a specific subject is very small. The same spend online reaches someone who has read the criteria recently.

sections.heading: The supervisor, the mentor, and the line between them
paragraphs: Your child has one supervisor and that person is appointed by the school. The supervisor conducts the three mandatory reflection sessions, including the concluding viva voce, confirms the work is the student's own and provides the input the IB expects. A paid mentor from outside the school is an addition to that arrangement and cannot replace any part of it. A provider who offers to run the reflection sessions, sign anything, or act as the supervisor is describing something that does not exist.

What a mentor may legitimately do is well defined. Discuss and narrow the research question. Explain what each criterion rewards. Advise on method and on where evidence might be found. Read a draft the student has written and give feedback against the published criteria. Teach the writing skills the essay needs - how to evaluate a source, how to structure an argument, how to make a conclusion follow from a body. Prepare a student to speak honestly in the viva voce about their own research.

What a mentor may not do is equally clear. No part of the text may come from the mentor. No data may be supplied that the student did not gather. No source may be inserted the student has not read. No draft may be rewritten rather than commented on. No reflection may be composed for the student, because the reflections are themselves assessed. Work that is not the student's own is a malpractice matter for the IB, and the consequence falls on the candidate. Some operators in this market sell completed essays and completed internal assessments outright; that is the thing to walk away from, whatever the price.

There is a UAE layer to this as well. The private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued free of charge for two years through MoHRE, carries a code of conduct that bars a holder from tutoring students affiliated with their own school. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from paid private tutoring of students enrolled where they teach; that is press-reported rather than quoted from the policy document, so verify it against current ADEK guidance. The clean reading is that you should not be paying your child's own supervisor, and no reputable provider would arrange it.
